{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A makes the architectural decision that actually determines whether this system survives contact with reality: the router is a thin always-resident process that never touches the GPU, and the inference runtime is a separate child process it spawns and kills, so a CUDA crash or an OOM kill cannot take down the scheduler, the session store or the memory ledger. B ends by saying the design can be deployed as a single-process binary with an in-process GPU context, which contradicts its own claims about deterministic cleanup and OOM handling - an in-process CUDA fault takes the whole router with it. A also identifies the dominant real-world failure on a one-model box, the half-unloaded model or zombie CUDA context that silently holds VRAM, and designs against it end to end: the swap sequence verifies free VRAM after unload and force-kills and respawns the runtime if the check fails, and the ledger re-reads the driver every 60 seconds and treats a drift above half a gigabyte as a leak requiring a restart. B never addresses orphaned GPU memory at all. On swap policy A is both more concrete and better motivated - a sticky grace window justified by the actual interactive rhythm of reading and typing a follow-up, an anti-thrash cooldown that explicitly prevents the alternating ping-pong pathology, and lookahead pre-swapping so a benchmark job's swap cost is absorbed during the idle gap rather than paid in front of a user. B's hysteresis dwell time is the only one of these it has. B's swap cost model is actively wrong: it proposes serializing the resident model with torch.save to a temporary file before reloading the target from_pretrained, but the weights are already on disk, so this adds tens of gigabytes of pointless write traffic to every swap. Its watermark table is incoherent - low is under 60 percent VRAM free, critical is under 85 percent free, which makes critical a strict superset of low - and it conflates models with traffic classes in the swap trigger pseudocode by testing whether the current model equals interactive. It also asserts a measured 200 millisecond bound on cancel plus swap rollback, which is invented, and cites a torch.cuda.memory.record API that does not exist. A's cancellation section is the sharper of the two because it separates cancellation by SOURCE and gives each different partial-output semantics - a user pressing stop keeps and streams the partial text, a preemption discards it, a disconnect discards it - and it explains why cancellation must be cooperative at the token-batch boundary rather than per token. A's failure-mode section is ordered by pain and diagnostic difficulty, states what to measure AND why the measurement discriminates between competing causes, and closes with the genuinely insightful observation that one annotated VRAM-over-time timeline reveals thrash as sawtooth, OOM as a spike-and-crash and starvation as queued work against idle VRAM. B's failure list is broader in places - deadlock detection, priority inversion and fragmentation histograms are worth having and A omits them - but it is a flat catalogue of metric names without the reasoning that makes them actionable, and it reaches for PagerDuty on a single-machine setup where A correctly scopes instrumentation to a ring buffer and a JSON endpoint."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A's decisive advantage is conceptual: it opens by decomposing hallucinated citations into fabricated (the source does not exist), misattributed (the source exists but does not contain the cited claim) and irrelevant (the source is topically near but does not support the specific claim), argues that any agenda collapsing these into one number will mislead, and then threads that single taxonomy through all five experiments so results are composable and a given error type can be traced through the whole pipeline. That means B's entire agenda is structurally blind to misattribution - the hardest and arguably most dangerous failure, because the citation passes every database lookup and still misrepresents the source - and it is precisely the residual failure that A predicts constrained decoding will INCREASE, since a model forced to emit a valid retrieved document id will pick the nearest available document even when the claim is not in it. That predicted trade-off is the kind of non-obvious mechanism that makes an agenda worth running. A is also far stronger on experimental hygiene. It treats pretraining contamination as a first-class concern, reserving post-cutoff sources in every training and evaluation set, and frames the key scientific question of its preference-optimization experiment as whether the model learns a general honesty prior or merely memorizes not to cite specific papers - a shortcut-versus-principle test B never contemplates. It treats abstention as a measured quantity with its own precision, adds 200 questions whose answers lie outside top-k retrieval specifically to price false abstention, and states outright that a system which never cites is trivially accurate and useless. Its final experiment is a genuine factorial rather than another point comparison, motivated by the correct expectation that gating, verification and trained honesty interact non-additively, and it measures the gap between user trust and actual accuracy. {"choice": "B", "rationale": "B is right on the physics and A is wrong on it. Worse, A treats verification as a per-request cost amortized by batch (v/B), which inverts the central, well-established result: speculative decoding pays at small batch where decoding is memory-bound and the extra K positions are nearly free, and stops paying as batch grows and the verify pass becomes genuinely compute-bound at K times the FLOPs. B gets exactly this right, derives separate memory-bound (mu/(1+rho_m)) and compute-bound (K*mu/(K+rho_c)) expressions, uses the correct geometric mu = (1-alpha^(K+1))/(1-alpha) and even writes the general non-uniform form first, and solves S=1 for a critical acceptance rate in each regime, reproducing the user's 1.8x at alpha ~ 0.5 with a light head. B also contributes the insight that actually explains observed disappointment in practice: it is the positional decay of alpha_j, not the mean, that kills mu, so a healthy alpha_1 can coexist with a sub-1 speedup. Both propose a linear probe on hidden states as the pre-build experiment, but A arrives there only after two visible self-corrections ('Wait, that's not right', 'Wait, that's too high') that leave contradictory tables standing in the text, while B specifies the protocol properly: domain-representative sequences from the deployment distribution, consecutive (not marginal) acceptance measured per position, replaying the accept/reject logic to get mu empirically, the argument that a linear probe is a conservative lower bound on any non-linear head, an MLP probe to measure the remaining non-linearity headroom, and a go/no-go decision table that includes the batch-gated middle case. B is not flawless — its compute-bound column drops the K from its own boxed numerator, and the arithmetic-intensity expression in step 4 is garbled — but these are local slips inside a correct framework, whereas A's errors are the framework."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both answers contain real API errors — neither can build the mesh as written, since jax.devices() returns a list with no .reshape (A) and a flat list cannot be given two axis names (B) — so the decision rests on which one teaches the correct model of JAX sharding. That is wrong twice over: under plain jax.jit with NamedSharding inputs, GSPMD inserts the collectives for you, and the specific configuration A demonstrates — x sharded P('batch', None) against W sharded P(None, 'model') — is column-parallel, which requires no reduction at all; the psum is both unnecessary and un-runnable, because no axis_name is bound inside jit. A has confused column-parallel with row-parallel in its own worked example and then repeats it in the 'complete working example'. B gets exactly this right and makes it the substance of the answer: column-parallel splits W along N and needs no communication because X is replicated, row-parallel splits W along K so each shard holds a partial sum that must be all-reduced, with the matching specs given for each. That is the actual content of Megatron-style tensor parallelism, and B extends it to vocab-sharded embeddings and to why layer-norm and softmax are cheap. B's closing mental model — declarative specs say what lives where, single-device code says what to compute, the compiler derives the collectives — is the correct framing and is precisely what A's answer denies. B also offers the practical material that survives the code bugs: activations sharded on both axes cost 1/(data x model) memory, passing a sharded tensor where an op wants a replicated one silently inserts an all-gather so inspect the HLO, and checkpoints must be reloaded under the same NamedSharding for the layout to match. {"choice": "A", "rationale": "B has the broader catalogue — more metrics enumerated, a dashboard layout, instrumentation snippets, an alert table in three tiers — but A is the better engineered answer where the prompt is actually hard. Its stall conditions additionally require gpu_active to be false, so a wedged-but-spinning worker or an eviction thrash loop is classified healthy, and its thresholds are global constants (15s, 0.01 tok/s, STALL_THRESHOLD_MS) that cannot distinguish a request whose steady-state inter-token latency is 15ms from one legitimately sitting at 200ms under heavy co-batching. A also handles what B leaves out: prefill needs a separate rule because inter-token latency does not yet exist, and speculative decoding gets its own signature (inflated verify latency with zero acceptance over ten consecutive steps as draft divergence) rather than being folded into a generic idle check. On alerting, A is the more disciplined design: SLO error-budget burn with fast-burn paging and slow-burn ticketing, an explicit page/ticket/dashboard split, suppression when a high prefix-cache hit ratio or a saturated scheduler makes elevated latency expected, and exclusion of user-cancel terminations from SLO math. {"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is the better-calibrated survey and the sounder procedure. The two directly contradict each other on whether attention or FFN projections are more quantization-fragile, and A takes the better-supported side (the FFN projections, with down_proj in particular carrying the outlier burden, sitting above Q/K/V/O) while also hedging it; B asserts attention > FFN flatly and describes the whole pattern as 'remarkably consistent across architectures'. More importantly, A includes an explicit 'what is not settled' section — the ordering among attention sub-projections varies with GQA versus MHA and with the quantization scheme, stability across scale is open, and much of the cited evidence assumes weight-only quantization — which is exactly the calibrated uncertainty the question asks for and which B never offers. A also separates the mechanism from the correlation, grounding sensitivity in activation kurtosis and outlier channels, GPTQ's Hessian/curvature formulation, singular-value decay as a redundancy proxy, and residual-stream write magnitude, where B lists measurement approaches without explaining what drives the phenomenon. On procedure, B's Phase 1 contains a real methodological flaw: it quantizes each layer and leaves it quantized while measuring the next, so the score for layer i is taken inside a progressively more corrupted model and the scores are neither comparable across layers nor independent of traversal order. Calling this 'error propagation captured naturally' conflates propagation with confounding. A measures each tensor's perturbation against the clean full-precision baseline, adds a global KL-to-final-logits term to catch downstream amplification that a local L2 misses, and offers the cumulative variant separately while stating the additivity assumption it rests on and when it breaks. A also works at weight-tensor granularity (Q, K, V, O, gate, up, down, embedding, head, norms), which is where mixed-precision allocation actually happens, whereas B allocates per transformer block. A's assumptions are tabulated with the consequence of each violation, and its validation carries concrete acceptance thresholds (delta perplexity in nats, mean KL, top-1 agreement) plus generated-text divergence, activation-distribution preservation, spectral checks, and a knee-of-the-curve test that the chosen k should sit at — all on a held-out unlabelled slice, where B's refinement loop measures perplexity on the same calibration data it fit to. B is not without advantages: its pseudocode is concrete, its calibration-set sizing (128-512 sequences) is more realistic than A's 1-5k tokens, and it contributes two validation ideas A should have had — correlating the sensitivity proxy against per-layer perplexity impact to check the proxy itself, and benchmarking the allocation against uniform 4-bit and uniform 8-bit at matched memory, which is the ablation that determines whether the whole exercise paid. Its observation that public benchmarks require no new labelling is fair, though it partly sidesteps the stated constraint."}

A resolves it by having an admin route execute raw ALTER TABLE statements through the ORM, which is an operational and security anti-pattern, contradicts its own migration-first Prisma workflow, and sits badly beside its stated rule of never constructing raw SQL. A also misreads a stated requirement, specifying that the device listing filters by the requesting user's id when the brief says users should be able to read all records and update individual ones. B's other design choices show more thought about the actual workload: bulk updates as a CSV upload processed asynchronously through a job queue with batch size, progress tracking and real-time status, rather than a single synchronous transaction endpoint; an audit log table with user attribution as a first-class entity rather than an afterthought line item; optimistic locking on record updates; soft deletes; and cursor-based pagination. Its tickets are also more executable, naming concrete column lists per table, token lifetimes, lockout thresholds, hash cost factor and processing batch sizes, whereas several of A's task rows are one-line gestures. A is not without merit: it is leaner and less likely to over-build, its best-practices table explains why each choice was made rather than just listing it, and the quick-start command block is genuinely useful. But A carries avoidable errors, naming a non-existent form library, listing two overlapping validation libraries, and seeding a default admin with a trivial password in a proposal that claims to follow OWASP practice, and its architecture diagram is a cramped single line that conveys little. B's weakness is the opposite failure, pulling in Redis, a job queue, WebSockets and a dynamic permissions table without acknowledging that this is heavy for a small inventory app, and it too duplicates rate-limiting libraries. On balance the correct handling of the hardest requirement, the faithful reading of the role matrix, and the greater concreteness of the tickets outweigh the over-engineering risk."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both are detailed, credible engineering documents and agree on the big picture (shadow mode first, Triton on a small GPU at the site, drift monitoring, SaMD clearance, and integration rather than the model being the hard part). The user asked specifically for PACS specificity, and that is where accuracy decides it. B is confidently specific but wrong on several named protocol details: it repeatedly cites HL7 ORU^RDS as the radiology result message when the trigger event is ORU^R01, invents an ORU^OBS for escalation, describes MPPS as the modality worklist feed when MPPS is Performed Procedure Step and the worklist is MWL, and says pixel data is pulled via STOW-RS when STOW is the store direction and WADO-RS is retrieval. It also asserts that de-identification before pixel data leaves the archive is a hard FDA and HIPAA requirement, which is wrong for the production inference path inside a covered entity and is contradicted three paragraphs later by an output payload keyed on the real accession number. A names ORU^R01 correctly, keeps de-identification in the training-data acquisition stage where it belongs, and its only comparable slip is a garbled QIDO acronym. A is also the stronger answer on training methodology, which is half the question: explicit temporal and site-disjoint splits with same-patient leakage prevention, weak supervision from reports with certainty filtering, calibration to a stated expected-calibration-error target, sensitivity at fixed specificity as the headline metric, and pre-specified subgroup analysis across age, sex, scanner vendor and habitus. Its security treatment (network segmentation, DICOM TLS with mutual authentication, RBAC, audit fields) is concrete where B's is thin. B has genuine advantages that make this close: the design rule that the score is an annotation rather than a hidden re-sort, with a phased go-live that moves from shadow to badge to tiebreaker-only ordering, is the best clinical-safety reasoning in either answer; folding reason-for-exam and demographics from the HL7 feed into the feature vector is an idea A misses entirely; and the explicit justification for two-dimensional slice selection with set attention over a full three-dimensional model, with quantified latency, is better architectural argument than A's bare recommendation. But B derives that architecture from a sub-second latency requirement it asserts without justification, which is far tighter than triage actually needs and which A more realistically sets in the tens of seconds."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "A is well presented and has some good operational ideas (stage-duration percentiles with an automatic manager review when a deal lingers past the seventy-fifth percentile in Negotiate, a lost-deal rescue tier, what-if simulation of winning specific deals), but it inverts one of the four things the brief explicitly asks for. The user says to consider products that are far away from the target; A's Tier A requires the budget gap to be small or already met, its Tier C demotes deals whose product is far from target, its scoring formula multiplies by one minus the absolute gap so distance from target actively suppresses priority, and its closing takeaway restates the inversion. A never argues for the reversal, it simply contradicts the stated requirement, which is the most serious defect in either answer. A's priority tiers are also muddled in a smaller way, listing deals in the Won stage as candidates for top-priority acceleration. B tracks the brief item by item: it turns the 'deals lost because products not working' line into a first-class diagnosis task using topic modelling over free-text loss notes plus a structured-feature model, producing ranked loss themes per product that a product team can act on, and it treats distance from target as the trigger for action with explicit red-amber-green thresholds on forecast-versus-target gap. B also does the data work A only gestures at, naming four source tables with their granularity and the join keys that make product identity the spine across revenue, pipeline, budget and lifecycle, and it models the six-stage lifecycle explicitly as next-stage classification plus time-to-stage survival rather than folding it into a heuristic weight. Its delivery sequencing is better reasoned, shipping budget-gap alerts and product tiering first because they need only aggregate historical data before the deal scorer that depends on labelled closed-won and closed-lost history, and its evaluation section proposes an actual A/B comparison of reps using priority scores against a control rather than A's generic continuous-ops review. Both responses share the same blind spot, neither noting that ranking by probability of winning tends to prioritise deals that would close anyway and that incrementality is the correct objective, and B's eight to fifteen percent uplift estimate is asserted, though at least labelled conservative."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both plans are competent and share the core insight that this is a behaviour-change program wearing a technical costume, but A reasons more soundly and stays internally consistent. A sequences discovery -> pilot -> rollout -> lightweight governance with an explicit 'do not build' clause attached to each phase (not just a standalone table), and its deferral list is argued rather than asserted: no custom platform because maintenance outlives the builders, no bit-for-bit guarantee because non-determinism makes it unachievable and researchers do not need it, no separate reproducibility team because it converts a shared norm into someone else's problem. Its adoption measurement is properly layered into leading, core and outcome indicators, and it correctly flags that early support-channel volume is a positive signal - a subtlety B misses. Its risk section is the strongest part of either answer, naming the compliance backfire, champion dependency, and the leadership-incentive mismatch (rhetoric rewarding speed while asking for rigour) with matched mitigations. B is crisper, and its two real advantages are concrete numeric targets and a day-one toolkit (experiment.yaml, a run wrapper, a CI check) that make it more immediately executable; those are genuine strengths. But B contradicts itself in ways that matter: it identifies fake compliance and silent resistance as the sinking risk, then mitigates with hard mandates - a repro check gating commits from week 4, CI badges, and withholding funding, staff and data access with 'no grandfathered exceptions' - which is exactly the mechanism that manufactures the fake compliance it fears, and which assumes budget and access authority a 90-day program lead rarely holds. It also declares 'no new features after Week 4' while phases 5 and 6 build CI gates, auto-generated repro reports and a handbook. B's targets are also uncalibrated - 60 percent platform share and 85 percent badge rate by day 90 are stated without any basis from the day 1-7 baseline that is supposed to produce them. A's weaknesses are verbosity and an absence of numeric targets, which cost it some actionability but not correctness."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both are serious agendas with hypotheses, datasets, metrics and decision rules, and B has two real advantages: it names concrete verification substrates (Semantic Scholar, arXiv, PubMed Central, DOI validity), gives field-level error taxonomy (title vs author vs DOI), and pre-registers numeric pass criteria in a summary decision table that makes the branch logic auditable. But A is the better science. Its opening move is the one that matters - Experiment 1 is a controlled dissociation of retrieval failure, generation failure and verification failure by running the same prompts under source-provided, no-retrieval and full-RAG conditions, which is what turns a measurement study into a causal one; B's Experiment 1 is only a prevalence audit, so its later interventions are chosen without knowing which mechanism they are treating. A also carries a genuine calibration layer that B lacks entirely: an explicit falsifier for the whole agenda (if fabricated citations were memorized from contaminated pretraining data, then retrieval and verification are symptom treatment and the effort should move to data curation), stated limitations, the point that even a 5 percent residual rate may be unacceptable in medicine and law, and a dependency-annotated timeline with a named critical path. Its verification experiment is the more thoughtful one, anticipating second-order hallucination in self-critique loops and scoring net citation utility against a false-rejection rate rather than reporting hallucination reduction alone - important because the degenerate solution is a model that cites nothing, a failure mode A explicitly names as reward gaming. B has soundness problems at the edges: its Experiment 5 hypothesis that human detection is uncorrelated with automated metrics and that humans will catch 10-30 percent more hallucinations is confused, since the automated rate is defined by database lookup and is the more reliable instrument for existence checks - humans should be the noisier detector there, and the interesting divergence is about support and relevance, not existence; its Experiment 1 fallback treats a low measured rate as evidence that its own annotation was too lenient, which assumes the conclusion; and 50 seed questions is thin for the domain-stratified claims it later wants to make. Both overstate the precision of their expected effect sizes; A offsets this with its meta-section, B does not."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "A is the tidier document and more immediately implementable - a real SQLite schema, a cache-invalidation rule keyed on test-suite version, a weekly GPU budget with a FIFO queue, an override ledger with second-reviewer sign-off, a favorites list the system uses to flag suspicious overrides, and success metrics like P80 time-to-disqualify and zero unlogged overrides. Those are genuine strengths and A wins on structure and actionability. But B reasons better about the actual design problem. Its promotion criterion is incumbent-relative (a candidate must match the current champion within a stated margin of error, or beat it on some axis by a meaningful margin) rather than an absolute 60 percent floor, which matters because a fixed floor barely disqualifies anything among modern releases - A's funnel would not in fact fail fast at its own Stage 1. B states and uses the asymmetry between bounded false negatives (re-evaluate next week) and expensive false positives (they consume every downstream stage), and derives from it the correct threshold policy of permissive early and strict late, with the sanity gate written as a deliberately trivial bar. Its answer to avoiding redundant testing is the sharper one: a matrix of what changed - identical weights, requantization, fine-tune of a known base, same architecture retrained, new point release - each mapped to the stage you must resume from, which is the real question, whereas A's hash-plus-suite-version cache only handles the exact-duplicate case (A's downstream-invalidation rule is the one dedup idea B lacks). On honesty B is also deeper: alongside pre-registration, blinding and a no-exceptions kill switch with a documented re-evaluation protocol, it re-runs the champion every week as a positive control and invalidates the whole week if the champion fails - an instrument check that catches the silent pipeline breakage neither audit trail in A would detect - plus a rotating devil's-advocate critique required before final promotion. B has real flaws: the weekly-retrained performance predictor is speculative and its stated use is muddled (predicting failure should skip work, not schedule more), the funnel pass-rate percentages are framed as targets when they are observations, a sub-5-percent false-negative rate is not measurable without ground truth, weekly benchmark rotation contradicts its own pre-registration and champion-consistency check, and the ceremony and culture material is padding. Even discounting those, the core design reasoning is stronger than A's."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both reviews reach the right verdict - do not ship on p=0.03 alone - and both cover the standard hygiene list (SRM, novelty decay, segment heterogeneity, guardrails, phased rollout). B has three items A genuinely lacks and they are not trivial: optional stopping and the need for a sequential correction if the team peeked, pre-experiment covariate balance as a randomization check, and negative-control metrics that should not move. A better reviewer would have named peeking explicitly. But A is the stronger review overall because it reasons about the specific object under test rather than about A/B tests in general. Its position-bias section is the single best passage in either response: a ranking change is by construction a position change, so it demands position-level CTR and conversion curves to separate a genuine relevance gain from the model merely moving already-clickable items up the well-known position-bias gradient - and it makes that unresolved confound a standalone blocking condition. It is the only response that asks what 0.8 percent is a percent of, insisting the lift be re-expressed against the baseline and in business terms before anyone calls it a win, and the only one that treats the p-value correctly as not the quantity of interest, demanding a credible interval and then setting the decision on the lower bound rather than the point estimate. It also raises supply-side and ecosystem externalities (traffic shifted away from smaller sellers or creators, new-item discovery), concentration and diversity measures, concurrent-experiment interference on the same surface, a trimmed-window sensitivity re-analysis that drops the novelty and end-of-test days, and a long-horizon always-control holdout. Its decision section is the more useful artifact: instead of B's uniform pass-or-fail table, it enumerates branches - ship to 25-50 percent with pre-agreed kill criteria, ship only to the segment carrying the effect while holding the rest in control, or extend the test - each tied to which specific check comes back clean or dirty, and it explicitly prices the cost of being wrong in both directions. B is crisper and its rejection-trigger list is clean, but several of its points are asserted rather than argued (SRM as the number-one cause of false positives; a 0.8 percent lift being 'often material' with 'a strong business case' is listed as a reason to trust, which sits oddly against its own caution), and it never engages with the mechanism by which a ranking model could manufacture the lift."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "B is the more ambitious answer and contributes several real insights A lacks - that sparsity touches only the FFN so the KV cache is unchanged and long context erodes the same headroom, that MoE's read-amortisation assumes batched serving and at batch 1 you pay scattered expert reads that defeat prefetchers, that router quantisation is a discontinuous rather than graceful failure mode because a perturbed gate logit flips the top-k selection, that hot and cold experts justify mixed precision, that the shared attention and embedding path gets none of the redundancy protection, and that the dense ecosystem is simply better characterised. Had its arithmetic been right it would win. But its numeric spine is wrong in a load-bearing way: it states Mixtral 8x7B is 129 B total and about 65 GB at Q4, apparently by confusing the roughly 12.9 B active-parameter figure with the total, when the model is about 46.7 B total and roughly 26 GB at Q4. That error propagates into the per-token FLOP estimate, the entire budget table, the claim that a Mixtral-class model is unreachable below 32 GB, the 'about 60 GB on a 64 GB machine' sizing, and ultimately the headline advice to revisit MoE only when hardware crosses 32 GB - advice that is materially distorted, since Mixtral-class weights fit a 32 GB box and smaller sparse models fit well under 16 GB. It also contradicts itself, asserting the model 'becomes feasible' at 32 GB two paragraphs before pricing it at 45 GB even at Q3, and its quality-per-memory-byte section computes a 129 B-total MoE inside a 16 GB budget that its own memory section says cannot exist. Its claim that MoE beats dense at equal active count at Q4-Q6 because each active weight 'carries less representational load' is asserted rather than argued. A is far more compact but everything in it is correct, and it lands the one framing that actually resolves the question: the honest comparison is a T-total/A-active MoE against a dense model of size A, not against a dense model of size T, and it names the latter as the trap that produces the wrong conclusion. Its axis table is accurate, its quantisation reasoning (sparse per-expert calibration, group granularity colliding with small expert tensors, keeping the router in higher precision and that this eats the savings) is sound, it flags routing-induced token-rate jitter as mattering for interactive use as much as mean speed, and its three-branch decision rule keyed on what is actually binding, with a headroom allowance for KV cache and an instruction to measure on the real device, is directly usable. On soundness and calibration A wins clearly; B wins on breadth but pays for it with errors that change the recommendation."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Very close; both cover all six deliverables competently and neither is padding. A is better on two of them: its type-routed chunking table (functions for code, endpoints for API docs, steps for runbooks, version entries for changelogs) argues each choice rather than asserting it and adds a parent-child hierarchy enabling precise-versus-context retrieval, and its faithfulness evaluation is the more rigorous - claim decomposition with per-claim support checks, a 200-pair golden set that deliberately includes multi-hop and should-refuse cases, and a hard gate blocking deploys on a 5-percent regression. Its idea of verifying at the string level that a cited chunk actually contains the claimed text, rather than trusting an LLM judge, is the single best grounding detail in either answer, and its framing that all three failure modes reduce to the gap between faithful-to-retrieved-context and factually-correct is genuinely unifying. But B is better on the constraint that defines the problem and on two other deliverables. The corpus changes daily, and A responds with a nightly 3 AM batch, then lists the resulting 12-24 hour staleness as its own first failure mode with mitigations that are largely UI labelling plus ad-hoc refresh of 'critical' docs; B makes ingestion event-driven and delta-first with content-hash change detection, and actually handles the hard parts A skips - deletions and renames via soft-delete plus garbage collection, a dead-letter queue for failed embeddings, two retained embedding versions for rollback, and drift monitoring against a baseline. B's grounding degrades safely where A's does not: a reranker score floor that bypasses generation entirely and returns a structured no-evidence response, graded confidence tiers that route borderline answers to humans, an NLI check rather than only an LLM judge, plus RBAC enforced at retrieval time with audit logging, which A omits entirely despite this being internal engineering documentation. Its three failure modes are also the more earned: orphaned chunks that still resolve and therefore look confident, cross-reference fragmentation severing the links that engineering docs depend on, and terminology drift where newly coined service names and acronyms fall outside the embedding model's distribution so dense retrieval silently fails while BM25 could have caught it - all specific to this corpus, whereas A's second and third are generic RAG failures. B's flaws are real but cosmetic or local: a garbled phrase, a last-modified pre-filter that does not make sense as written, a latency symptom attributed to a recall problem, and an oracle-LLM regenerating golden answers, which is circular and weaker than A's curated set. Several of its thresholds are asserted with false precision, though it at least schedules calibration on 500 internal queries. Net, B's design survives contact with a daily-changing corpus and with production operations; A's is better reasoned in the abstract."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "A is a competent answer - it names the conflation, the binary cliff, the uncontrolled confounds and the point-versus-curve problem, and proposes two curves with EC50-style summaries. But it stops at the level of framework sketch, and it misses the two things that actually make such a metric work. First, position: the lost-in-the-middle effect means retrieval accuracy is a surface over (length, position), not a curve over length, and A mentions position only in passing while B makes it a first-class independent variable with an explicit position sweep, a 2-D heatmap, and a positional-asymmetry index. Second, and more importantly, A asserts that its two axes are orthogonal but provides no mechanism enforcing that: it merely sets the reasoning context 'above the retrieval EC50', which leaves every reasoning failure ambiguous. B installs a retrievability gate - probe each of the N target spans individually first, admit the item to the reasoning curve only if the spans were in fact retrievable, and report the excluded fraction as a separate statistic - which is precisely the control that makes the separation real rather than nominal. B is also better on threshold semantics, the part the prompt explicitly asks about: it defines retention relative to the model's own short-context ceiling rather than an absolute floor, correctly noting this keeps a model with an 82 percent ceiling comparable to one at 99 percent; it reports the derived length at several tau values rather than one; it adds a half-life as a worst-case bound; and it is explicit that the headline number is a convenience while the curves are the source of truth. A's choice of EC50 as the retrieval summary is weakly motivated and operationally far too permissive - fifty percent retrieval accuracy is not an effective context by any deployment standard. B further splits reasoning into two genuinely distinct axes, fact count N and inference-step count S, arguing they stress different bottlenecks (integration across attention versus chain length) and should not collapse into one complexity scalar, and it treats the result as a Pareto frontier rather than a scalar. Its composition formula factorising compound-task accuracy into a retrieval product times a conditional reasoning term is the concrete payoff of the decomposition - it lets an engineer decide whether to fix retrieval or shorten the reasoning chain - and it is appropriately hedged as approximate, though the independence assumption across spans is optimistic and B could have said so. B also specifies the operational details A omits: a length ladder, span length, sample counts, temperature handling, and a full reporting table. A's comparison tables restate its own claims rather than adding analysis, and its critique, while correct, is shallower than B's seven-point enumeration, which includes non-compositionality and entanglement with grader artifacts."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B covers the space better and is more accurate where it counts. It includes the three entries a reader would most notice missing from A - Unity WebGL, Three.js and PixiJS - and it handles the bonus criterion far more usefully by naming the actual longevity risks rather than awarding stars: Unity's WebGL target is a second-class citizen with 50-100 MB initial loads and the 2023 runtime-fee episode having damaged trust, Construct 3 carries subscription cost and vendor lock-in, Defold's momentum has slowed. That is what 'unlikely to be outdated soon' means in practice, and A's five-star ratings are asserted with no comparable evidence. B also makes the distinction that most determines the reader's workload - Three.js, PixiJS and Babylon.js are renderers or libraries where you supply the game loop, input, physics and scene management, while Phaser, Godot, Cocos and Defold are engines - and it quantifies the specific pain points (Phaser's small footprint, Godot's 15-30 MB web payload and weak mobile-web story, Construct's price). A's accuracy is the bigger problem. It attributes Godot's backing to a non-existent organisation, says Godot's web export 'requires the GDExtension or HTML5 module (still improving)' which is muddled, and then recommends it as an engine that 'might export to web eventually' when one-click HTML5 export has shipped - a claim it contradicts in its own pros column two lines earlier. It calls PlayCanvas 'not fully open source' and Cocos Creator a paywalled source-available product, both of which misstate the licensing, and it contains a garbled 'WebGPN'. B has its own slips - describing PlayCanvas as having real-time multiplayer built in appears to confuse the collaborative editor with networking, calling Babylon.js merely a library undersells its scene graph, GUI and physics integration, and the Defold and Cocos ownership claims are loose - but these are fewer and less decision-changing than A's. On structure both are clear; A's per-engine tables are handsome but repetitive, and its final recommendations restate the body. B's situation-to-pick matrix is the more useful closing artifact, and its closing shortlist of open-source, no-single-vendor options is the correctly reasoned answer to the question actually asked."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "A is well organised and its critique is sound - the decomposition of the metric into success rate times attempts per hour, the perverse incentive against thoroughness, the false precision of quoting 12.3 versus 11.8, and the cost-blindness (a dimension B never adds) are all good points, and its report card is clean. But A's four axes are not really four: its edit-competence axis is just pass rate at N retries, which measures retry persistence rather than editing skill, so the scheme fails at exactly the separation the prompt demands. B operationalises that axis properly - diff minimality against the gold diff, scope-creep outside the requested region, regression rate on previously-passing tests, multi-edit coherence, and style and context preservation - which is what 'does it change only that thing, correctly' actually means, and it correctly identifies rewrite-everything behaviour as the reason engineers distrust assistants. B's runaway axis is likewise far more developed, adding divergence over steps, hallucinated APIs checked against a dependency manifest, mid-task abandonment, and pass rate as a function of prior-context length, which catches the slow degradation that matters most for agent use. Its critique also lands the sharpest single observation in either answer: a model that loops for fifty-five minutes and then emits a correct three-line fix is rewarded by the metric even though that loop is the failure, and the time denominator silently mixes intrinsic generation speed, retry-cycle count and runaway time. It further notes the number is a property of the model-times-benchmark pair rather than of the model, taxonomises the four failure modes by operational consequence, and supplies the governing principle that the report should be a data table rather than a verdict, with weights stated so a reader can re-weight for their own workload without re-running anything. Its ordering of hard vetoes before any weighted trade-off, the shape-versus-point argument about integrating pass-rate curves against your own difficulty mix, and tracking the axes across model versions to catch silent edit-competence regressions are all beyond anything in A. B's flaws are real but minor: its worked example says two models both score 36 successes per hour when the arithmetic gives 3.6, its veto thresholds are loose and contradict its own table (which elsewhere calls any hallucination a hard veto), and the divergence score is hand-wavy. None of these damage the argument. A's answer would be adequate; B's is the one a team could actually implement."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both lay out a fully crossed design over a common task corpus and both refuse to overclaim, but A's statistics are right where B's are not. The prompt turns on the power argument, and B's central derivation is broken: rearranging its own sample-size formula at n=40, p-bar=0.5, alpha=.05, 80 percent power yields a detectable difference near 31 points, not the 15-18 it reports, and the displayed algebra omits the square root entirely; the paired 10-12 percent figure is then asserted with no derivation. That error runs the wrong way - it makes the budget look roughly twice as informative as it is, which is the single most damaging mistake this plan could make. A instead does an explicit variance decomposition, states that the task is the experimental unit and that treating 200 runs as independent would be badly anti-conservative, fits a logistic mixed model with a task random intercept, and carries the numbers through to a roughly 33-point minimum detectable effect, concluding plainly that the budget supports an omnibus test and a ranked list with intervals but is severely underpowered for any specific pairwise claim - and insisting that caveat appear in the abstract rather than a footnote. A's pairwise standard error is slightly conservative because it does not let the task effect cancel in a within-task contrast, but that errs toward honesty. On inconclusive reporting A is also the sounder document: it reports the design-stage MDE rather than post-hoc power, whereas B computes achieved power from the observed effect, a well-known anti-pattern that is a monotone restatement of the p-value and carries no information. A adds a pre-registered decision rule for declaring the study inconclusive, a practical-equivalence band that converts the binary significance call into a graded statement, posterior probabilities of exceeding a stated threshold, an explicit detectable-or-not column in the results table, and reporting of the full across-task distribution and ICC rather than means alone. It also plans contingencies keyed to the pilot's variance estimate, trading repeats against tasks or dropping a language. B's genuine advantages are real - spending every run on a distinct task rather than on repeats is a defensible and arguably better allocation for the language contrast, the McNemar framing makes the pairing explicit, and the tiered evidence-language table and worked example tables are concrete and usable. But its zero-repeat design leaves run-to-run stochasticity, which is substantial for an agentic harness, entirely unestimable, and it never acknowledges that source of variance; its claim that replication across five languages supplies the statistical repetition confuses the treatment with a replicate. A's weakest point is spending forty runs on a pilot and then excluding those tasks from the primary analysis, which wastes budget, but it flags them as a sensitivity check and the reasoning behind the pilot is sound."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A reasons; B mostly types. A commits to one architecture and defends it with numbers - slice-selection down to ~32 representative slices, a Swin encoder plus permutation-invariant set-attention aggregation, and an explicit argument for why a 3D backbone is rejected (twelve seconds per 500-slice study against a sub-second budget, and triage needs a global urgency signal rather than voxel segmentation). It carries a latency budget through to the serving stack, weights the loss against the stated ~8 percent urgency base rate, validates by leaving out whole centres rather than patients to avoid site leakage, and post-hoc calibrates because a worklist threshold needs a real probability. Its PACS section is the stronger half: sit alongside the PACS rather than replace it, pull pixels over DICOMweb rather than raw sockets, keep image bytes in the VNA and only metadata plus URIs locally, and - the best single design call in either answer - publish the score as an annotation with a badge rather than a silent re-sort, then phase it in through shadow mode with a stated acceptance criterion before allowing it to act as a tiebreaker within existing priority buckets. Drift monitoring via PSI, a concordance proxy fed by the report feedback loop, replay during re-fine-tuning, and a regulatory checklist that correctly identifies human-in-the-loop as the strongest argument all land. A is not error-free: ORU^RDS and ORU^OBS are not real HL7 trigger events, MPPS is conflated with the modality worklist, and de-identification is presented as a blanket requirement when it is really a condition on data leaving the institution. B's flaws are more serious because they sit inside the code it offers as the deliverable. Its calibration loss compares a constant bin centre to the label mean inside a hard mask and is effectively non-differentiable, so it would train nothing; the function it explicitly calls the most important safety metric computes the wrong quantity entirely, counting cases that are neither critical nor flagged and dividing by the critical count; the 3D backbone builder imports torchvision symbols, ignores them and returns an undefined class; the Orthanc plugin subclasses an API that does not exist and is mounted as a shared object; the Lightning metrics namespace was removed years ago; the batch endpoint loops one study at a time; and rotate-90 plus colour jitter are inappropriate augmentations for anatomical CT. Proposing to reorder a worklist via C-FIND and C-MOVE misunderstands what those services do. It also presents three architectures without choosing on any reasoned ground, then selects the one weakest for volumetric CT in a table whose rationale is simply best accuracy. B does contribute several things A misses and they are real - partial-study inference before all slices have arrived, alert fatigue, a rule-based fallback when the model is down, Kendall's tau against radiologist reading order, and a prospective randomised trial with time-to-critical-detection as the endpoint - but they are paragraphs in a document whose bulk is code that would not run. On soundness, clarity and actionability A wins clearly."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B is stronger on every criterion the rubric names. Its survey attributes each finding to a specific line of work (GPTQ, AWQ, LLM.int8, SmoothQuant) and separates the empirical patterns from the mechanisms that produce them - activation kurtosis and outlier channels, output-space Hessian curvature, singular-value decay as a redundancy proxy, and magnitude of writes into the residual stream. Critically, it includes a 'what is not settled' section conceding that the ordering among Q, K, V and O projections varies with architecture and scheme, that scale-stability of the ranking is open, and that much of the cited evidence assumes weight-only quantisation - exactly the calibrated uncertainty the rubric asks for, and something A never offers despite making flat claims (early FFN more fragile than late FFN) that are neither sourced nor hedged. B also makes the sharpest technical point in either answer: sensitivity is not purely local, because a layer that looks mild in isolation becomes critical once upstream quantisation has already shifted its input distribution, which is why a per-layer local metric can mis-rank layers. It then builds the scoring procedure around that insight, offering local output perturbation, final-logit KL under single-layer quantisation, and an incremental cumulative measure that prices error accumulation, with the distributional statistics acting as a prior where the perturbation signal is noisy. That single insight subsumes and corrects A's table. B's re-measurement section is correspondingly better: it separates re-measuring the execution profile from RE-DERIVING the evaluation configuration (do not inherit the laptop's Q4_K_M or its 4k truncation), forces a per-task truncation-validity recheck, catches that the candidate model set itself changes when 70B models now fit (and that expanding the set is a different study that must not be pooled into one ranking table), flags sampler/RNG backend differences as a comparability hazard, and notes that a larger trial budget requires re-deriving the minimum detectable effect. On report structure the two are close - A contributes a useful prohibited-patterns list, a transferability legend and a classification decision tree - but B's Transfer Analysis table with a binary Transfers? column and a stated reason per row, the fixed-schema hardware profile block that puts the laptop-equivalent line right next to the server config, the running header 'HARDWARE-DEPENDENT - DO NOT CITE AS MODEL PROPERTY', and a pre-publication checklist that requires the rank-reversal check to have actually been performed, are more enforceable. {"choice": "B", "rationale": "B answers the question that was asked; A does not. Crucially, B nails the mechanism that matters for the target workload: attention-magnitude importance scores correlate with frequent tokens, so rare-but-critical tokens - identifiers, imports, type names, cross-file references - are exactly what gets evicted, which is why pure eviction breaks whole-repo code reasoning; it then proposes a concrete hybrid (lexical-rarity-weighted composite scoring, mixed 8-bit recent / 4-bit background with per-channel outlier scaling, sink plus initial-token retention for file headers and imports, retrieval-fused chunks) and states plainly that no single technique suffices. B also adds a comparison matrix with an explicit 'fails on' column and a 'when to avoid this' section, which is better calibration than A offers. B is not flawless - 'LLM-Lion', 'Q-KV' and 'CompressedKV' look like invented or garbled references, its StreamingLLM description conflates initial-token sinks with top-K-by-attention, 'more sinks for code-heavy layers' is hand-waving, and the KV-cache fusion of retrieved chunks glosses over positional-encoding mismatch - but these are local blemishes against A's wrong-genre conclusion and misattributed quantization methods."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B is both more accurate and more insightful, while A is longer but contains several outright errors. B leads with the correct organizing fact - MoE cuts compute and weight-bandwidth per token but not resident memory, because you cannot know which expert the next token routes to - and then adds the subtlety that decides the whole question: the honest comparison is MoE(total=T, active=A) against DENSE(total=A), not against dense(total=T); the latter framing is the trap that makes MoE look bad for a deployment nobody would actually build. B also gets the latency mechanism right for this class of device: on bandwidth-bound hardware (CPU, Apple unified memory) an MoE reads fewer weights per token and is therefore faster than an equal-total dense model but not faster than an equal-active one. Its quantization analysis names real mechanisms - each expert sees few calibration tokens so per-expert calibration is poor, group-quantization granularity can collide with small expert tensors, the router is small but high-leverage and is usually kept at higher precision, which eats back some of the savings - and it flags streaming jitter from routing imbalance as mattering for an interactive assistant. The recommendation is correctly conditioned on what is actually binding (dense when memory is the wall or when you must go Q2/Q3; MoE when memory is plentiful and throughput is the constraint), with a concrete rule of thumb that reserves 20-30% headroom for KV cache. A reaches a broadly similar bottom line and its table structure is clear, but it is factually unreliable: it states Mixtral-8x7B has 1.6T total parameters (actual ~47B total, ~13B active), says a 7B model is 7GB at INT4 (about 3.5GB), and claims 'active params = 2-4% of total' which is far off for the models it cites. Worse, its central latency claim is wrong for the stated setting - it asserts MoE needs sparse-aware kernels and dedicated sparse hardware and is slower than dense on typical local CPUs/GPUs, when MoE's advantage on local memory-bandwidth-bound hardware is precisely that it reads fewer bytes per token; and 'top-1 routing adds one forward-pass overhead, top-2 doubles it' is a confused description of top-k. Its decision framework inherits these errors, gating MoE behind datacenter sparse hardware and thereby excluding the one local configuration (unified-memory Apple Silicon) where MoE is genuinely the right call - the case B identifies explicitly."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "These are both strong, and the gap is narrow. A has two genuinely better ideas: it splits the reasoning axis into fact count N and inference-step count S, correctly noting these stress different bottlenecks and should not be collapsed into one complexity scalar (B's K conflates them), and it defines its threshold as retention relative to the model's OWN short-context ceiling, which makes models with 82% and 99% baselines comparable in a way absolute cutoffs do not; its retrievability gate and its explicit factorization of compound-task accuracy into a retrieval product times a conditional reasoning term are also nice. But B is the more rigorous measurement design, and the prompt asks for exactly that. B is the only one of the two that catches the parametric-memorization confound and installs the needle-removed control (accuracy must fall to chance, proving the model is reading context rather than recalling training data) - without it the retrieval curve at short L is not measuring context use at all. B also specifies the confounds that actually move needle-in-haystack numbers - distractor topical and lexical overlap, needle uniqueness, near-miss distractors that test fact binding - and adds two controls A lacks: a leave-one-fact-out check confirming all K facts are necessary, and an adjacent-facts placement that isolates integration difficulty from localization difficulty, which is a cleaner way to achieve what A's gate attempts. On the threshold-semantics half of the question B is stronger still: multiple pre-registered crossings (L95/L90/L80/L50) whose SPREAD diagnoses cliff versus slope, chance-relative rather than zero-relative baselines with a pre-registered effect size, explicit warning about post-hoc threshold selection as a p-hacking vector, and bootstrap CIs on every number with the actual arithmetic (about plus/minus 6pp at n=50 near p=0.9). A never mentions confidence intervals at all, and its sampling plan - k>=200 per (L,p) cell across nine lengths and eight positions - is roughly 14,000 runs per model, proposed without any acknowledgement of cost and muddled by a parenthetical about temperature-0 determinism that would make repeated samples identical. B's worked before/after example, contrasting a single '112K effective context' claim with a paragraph reporting positional bands, K_max at two lengths, the retrieval-reasoning gap and the slope, is also the most directly actionable artifact in either answer."}

Its Experiment 5 is a proper 2x2x2 factorial aimed at interaction effects, with multi-turn sessions including a user challenging a citation to test error recovery, whereas A's integration experiment is a single combined system plus component ablations. A is not weak - its problem framing is clear, its 'what this changes about the next step' branches are explicit, and the timeline, dependency graph and self-critique section are nice additions B lacks - but its expected outcomes are studded with unjustified precise numbers (30-50%, 40-60%, ~60%, 2-5x, under 5%) presented as priors without derivation, its datasets are named but their construction and annotation protocols are thin, and several interventions are listed without design detail. On calibrated uncertainty A's explicit limitations section is a point in its favour; B compensates with per-experiment risk statements and a closing commitment that negative results redirect rather than dead-end the agenda."}

On avoiding re-testing, A's content-addressed cache keyed on sha256(weights_hash || quant || prompt_id || sampling_params) is the right primitive and yields three consequences A draws out explicitly - a re-release with identical weights is a total cache hit, a one-byte weight change forces re-test with no ambiguity, and a battery bump from v3 to v4 costs only the five new prompts. {"choice": "B", "rationale": "B is the deeper and better-constructed program. Its Experiment 1 does not merely measure a hallucination rate; it decomposes the phenomenon into pure fabrication, support mismatch (a real paper that does not support the cited claim) and metadata corruption, predicts that mismatch dominates, and predicts that existing DOI/URL and LLM-judge validators have low precision precisely on mismatches. That single structural claim then reorganizes the whole agenda - from existence verification toward claim-citation alignment - which is exactly the kind of 'what each result changes about the next step' the prompt asked for. B also builds a real experimental manipulation into the characterization phase by constructing low- and high-retrieval-recall subsets through deliberate corpus degradation, and states a differential prediction (fabrication rises sharply, mismatch does not), which is a testable interaction rather than a descriptive statistic; A's Experiment 1 varies only temperature and model and is purely observational. B specifies annotation reliability (two expert reviewers, Cohen's kappa above 0.75, target 500 annotated failures per domain) while A's ground truth rests on a single annotator and a 'no match after a 10-minute search' heuristic that is neither reproducible nor auditable. B's interventions are also more concretely specified and more honest about their side effects - constrained citation emission gated on a cross-encoder threshold, contrastive positives built from the exact supporting sentence and negatives from same-domain different-subtopic pairs, and an explicit prediction that constraining generation will INCREASE fabrication under low recall, which then motivates the safe-refusal module in the next phase. Treating abstention as a trained objective with its own metric, adding calibration error, and closing with adversarial corpus poisoning, multi-hop grounding and an eight-week expert deployment gives the agenda a coherent arc that A's cross-domain stress test and human-correlation study do not match. A has genuine merits: its summary table of numeric pass criteria per experiment is the cleanest decision logic in either answer, it includes explicit fallback branches (if fine-tuning underperforms, revert to RAG), and its Experiment 5 on human-versus-automated metric divergence is a good idea B only partially absorbs into its deployment study. But A's technical specification is thinner and in places unsound - the hallucination-penalty loss 'up-weights tokens that generate ungrounded citation strings' presumes token-level groundedness labels the design never produces, and 'inject at each generation step the top-3 most similar citations' is left undefined. Both responses over-report precise expected numbers; B is the worse offender (82% verifier catch rate, ECE 0.18 to 0.06, 2.3x fabrication), which costs it on calibrated uncertainty, but not enough to outweigh its stronger taxonomy, controls and sequencing."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both build a real cost model, and both contain one significant error, but B's is localized while A's is systemic, and B's proposed experiment measures the right quantity. B gets the accounting right: mu = (1 - alpha^(K+1))/(1 - alpha), which correctly includes the free bonus token the target emits from the verify pass. A sums alpha^j from 1 to K and so drops that token, and the off-by-one then propagates into every number it quotes - its expected-accepted table, and above all its headline claim that speculation cannot clear breakeven below alpha ~ 0.45 at K=4. At alpha = 0.45, rho = 0.05, small batch, the true speedup is roughly 1.7x, so A's central 'when it cannot pay off' threshold is wrong by a wide and practically consequential margin. B's numeric table is internally consistent and it usefully back-solves the user's observed 1.8x to alpha ~ 0.5 with a light head in the memory-bound regime, which directly answers the 'sometimes faster' half of the question. B's other strong contribution is identifying non-uniform positional decay as the real killer - worked through explicitly (alpha_1 = 0.7 but alpha_4 = 0.03 yields mu ~ 1.85, not the 2.5x you would extrapolate from alpha_1) - which is exactly why real deployments underperform the uniform-alpha formula. A gestures at sequential rejection but never quantifies it. B's error is the compute-bound branch: the boxed S_comp carries a spurious factor of K, which contradicts its own table (the table uses the correct mu/(K + rho_c)), and that bad box generates both the claim that the compute-bound regime is 'easier to make profitable' and the absurd alpha_c ~ 0.045. A's opposite conclusion there - that with a fully FLOP-bound verify pass no acceptance rate can rescue you - is the correct one, and A's continuous phi(B) interpolation between the two regimes is more elegant than B's two discrete cases. But B's own numbers all show sub-1.0 compute-bound speedups and its summary concedes the throughput ceiling sits below the no-speculation baseline, so a reader still reaches the right operational conclusion. The experiment is the decider. B fits a linear probe on saved hidden states to predict the K tokens THE TARGET ITSELF EMITS, then replays the accept/reject logic to recover the per-position consecutive acceptance curve - that is precisely the quantity speculative decoding consumes, it captures the positional decay, and the argument that a linear probe lower-bounds any non-linear head (with an MLP probe to measure the remaining non-linearity headroom) makes the go/no-go decision principled. B closes with a decision table that includes gating speculation on batch size. A's probe instead compares the target's greedy self-continuation against GROUND-TRUTH corpus tokens, which is not draft-target agreement, approximates p_j by p_1^j, and converts to acceptance via an invented 0.85 discount factor. A does add a genuinely good operational idea - stratify calibration by domain and gate speculation at runtime on the target's top-1 logprob - and its optimal-K discussion is a fair topic, though the formula it prints (K* = 1 + ln(alpha)/ln(alpha)) is garbled and evaluates to 2 for all alpha."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "The decisive difference is that A's central mechanism contradicts the literature it cites. A allocates 8-bit to the layers with the largest Frobenius norm, justified by 'larger weights carry more information' -- but the consistent finding from the outlier-aware quantization line of work is that salience is driven by activation magnitude, not weight magnitude, and selecting salient channels by weight norm specifically underperforms activation-based selection. Frobenius norm also scales with matrix dimension, so the ranking will largely recover 'which projections are biggest', not 'which are most sensitive'. A's validation compounds this: checking that the top-k layers by norm also have the lowest relative reconstruction error is circular, since layers quantized to 8-bit necessarily show lower relative error than 4-bit ones regardless of whether the selection was correct -- it tests that the quantizer ran, not that the allocation was right. A also asserts a 'U-shaped' curve with specific layer bands (1-3, N-3 to N) with more confidence than the evidence supports. B's summary is more faithful and better differentiated: it separates embeddings and lm-head from attention projections and from early versus middle-to-late FFN, names the actual correlates of sensitivity (activation range and outlier density, Fisher/Hessian-diagonal approximations, proximity to embedding and head), and correctly notes that a few hundred unlabelled sentences suffice for calibration. Crucially B identifies the insight that makes the no-labels constraint a non-problem -- next-token cross-entropy is self-supervised, so per-layer sensitivity can be measured directly by the loss increase from quantizing that layer, rather than guessed from a weight statistic -- and builds a greedy budgeted allocation around that measurement. Its validation is also stronger, adding activation-distribution KL against the full-precision model and, best of all, a stability check that re-runs the procedure on different unlabelled subsets to confirm the same layers get promoted. B is not flawless: its greedy stopping rule is garbled (it says to keep a layer at 8-bit if the increase exceeds a threshold given as 'less than 0.5 percent'), its per-layer ordering in Step 4 contradicts its own earlier remark that early MLP layers degrade faster, the 0.5-1.0 perplexity-point success criterion is arbitrary, and the code snippet adds nothing. Even so, B is sounder, deeper and more actionable."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both cover every requested section, but B shows markedly better API judgment and its reasoning is load-bearing rather than decorative. B gets the hard calls right and explains why: cancel is POST /jobs/{id}/cancel rather than DELETE because a cancelled job must stay inspectable with logs, timings and exit code, so DELETE would be a semantic lie; queue-full returns 503 while per-owner rate limiting returns 429, with the correct distinction that a full queue is our failure and not the client's; cancelling an already-terminal job returns 200 with the current state rather than 409, deliberately trading honesty for making cancel unconditionally safe to fire-and-forget; an idempotency key replayed with a different body returns 409 with the original job ID rather than silently returning the wrong job; and server-generated UUIDv7 IDs are chosen for sortability while closing tenant enumeration and IDOR. It also makes cancelling a public state with an explicit contract -- the API never promises cancel equals stopped, only stopped within grace plus kill timeout -- and records force_killed and a classified error.reason, which is exactly the observability a caller needs. Two further touches are genuinely strong: separating liveness from readiness so an orchestrator can drain by refusing new work while letting the running job finish, and declaring the state enum open with a client requirement to ignore unknown fields, which is what actually makes additive evolution safe within v1. A is competent, more visually elaborate, and has a richer Prometheus and logging section plus a separate result endpoint, but its judgment is weaker in several places. Its versioning section says unversioned /jobs should route to the latest stable version, which silently breaks clients on a major bump and contradicts the section's own stated principle. It rejects SSE for status and then specifies SSE-style log following. Its rejected-tradeoff on client-side idempotency key generation argues against the approach and then adopts it, which reads as confusion rather than a tradeoff. It has no multi-tenancy, no auth, no per-client rate limiting, and no protection against one caller filling the bounded queue. And its state diagram is cluttered enough that the transition table has to carry the meaning. B is also the only one to reject synchronous create on proxy-timeout grounds and to reason about silent retries causing double side effects on an expensive single GPU. B is tighter, sounder, and more insightful."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B is a design; A is a code dump that substitutes implementation volume for reasoning, and the implementation does not hold up. A's Request dataclass places a non-default field after defaulted ones, which will not even construct; swap_model takes _loading_lock and then calls load_model, which takes the same non-reentrant asyncio lock, a guaranteed deadlock on every swap; the priority formula derives both recency_bonus and wait_penalty from the same wait_time so they collapse to a single linear term and the 'penalty' is meaningless; and the starvation boost of +80 lets a benchmark request overtake interactive after 30 seconds, directly contradicting A's own stated rationale that interactive always preempts benchmark. The KV rebuild after reload, which is the crux of the whole swap story, is a bare pass. B instead earns its conclusions. It makes the single most consequential isolation call explicitly -- the inference engine runs as a child process so a segfault in llama.cpp or vLLM costs a 5-10 second respawn rather than the daemon -- and it names and rejects an obvious alternative (keeping a small model resident during loads) with a real argument about doubled state-machine complexity and violated user expectation. Its preemption mechanism is the correct one and A misses it entirely: when interactive arrives mid-benchmark on the same model, do not kill the benchmark; finish the token, save kv_offset, serve the interactive request, then resume. Its swap procedure is concretely sequenced with a step-by-step timing budget and an honest total user-visible stall, it handles the awkward case of an interactive request arriving mid-load with a cost heuristic on abort-versus-complete, and it spills KV synchronously to pinned RAM while writing NVMe asynchronously, with the reason stated. The memory accounting predicts peak before dispatch and reconciles bookkeeping against the driver every five seconds, treating divergence as the bookkeeping bug it is. Most importantly for a system serving unattended benchmark traffic, B prioritises instrumentation by consequence and puts silent data corruption first -- KV checksum mismatch on restore, stale KV after preemption, weight-shard hash mismatch -- ahead of liveness and QoS, because a wrong benchmark number is worse than a visible stall. A's failure list is competent but conventional and leads with load failure and OOM. B also shows calibration A lacks, noting mid-table that a 70B Q4 simply will not fit the 24 GB example and sizing down."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A gets the central statistical question right and B gets it wrong. A identifies the task as the experimental unit, crosses all tasks across all five languages so comparisons are paired, and states explicitly that the two repeats per cell are technical replicates that estimate within-cell noise but do not create 200 independent observations -- warning that any analysis treating them as independent is severely anti-conservative. B allocates 40 runs per language and then powers the study with a chi-square test of homogeneity on n=40 independent trials per group, which assumes away exactly the task-level clustering that dominates variance in code-generation evaluation; it also specifies a random intercept per run, which in a Bernoulli model is unidentifiable, suggesting the mixed-effects framing is decorative rather than load-bearing. B's arithmetic does not survive checking either: with the noncentrality it states (lambda = 50, df = 4, critical value 9.49) power is essentially 1.0, not the claimed 0.81, and at w = 0.30 (lambda = 18) it is near 0.88, not 0.54, so the headline numbers do not follow from the stated inputs. Most damagingly, B's inconclusive-reporting protocol centres on computing achieved power from the observed effect size, which is a known fallacy -- observed power is a monotone transform of the p-value and carries no information beyond it. A instead prescribes the correct tool, the minimum detectable effect at the achieved sample size, with a worked number (roughly 33 percentage points) and instructions to put a 'Detectable?' column in the results table rather than a footnote. A's honesty is also its strongest feature: it concludes that 200 runs buy a reasonably powered omnibus test but leave pairwise language comparisons at roughly 6 percent power under Bonferroni, and it says that belongs in the abstract. It adds a pre-registered inconclusive decision rule, a pilot that spends 40 of the runs estimating the variance components the power argument depends on, and explicit contingencies for rebalancing if the task variance comes back far from the assumed value. B is not without merit -- TOST against a stated ROPE, Bayes factors, Wilson intervals, a reproducibility appendix, and richer outcomes including latency and a blind quality rating -- and A would be improved by measuring more than pass/fail. But A also offers Bayesian posterior statements and practical-equivalence bands, so it covers most of B's reporting ground while resting on a design and a power argument that are actually correct."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B is far stronger on every criterion. Its survey is more faithful and more granular: it goes below the layer to the projection level (FFN down-projection more sensitive than up/gate because the dimensionality reduction concentrates error, attention output projection next, Q/K/V least), notes that norm parameters are kept at full precision because they are tiny and rescale activations, and offers an actual mechanism for why middle layers tolerate 4-bit (redundancy plus averaging of independent quantization noise in the residual stream, with the boundaries having nowhere to average). It then correctly separates layer-level allocation proxies from within-layer salience proxies, which A conflates. The procedure is the right one: measure sensitivity by leave-one-out -- quantize a single matrix to 4-bit, re-run the calibration forward pass, and score the normalized logit deviation -- with the GPTQ diagonal-Hessian trace as the cheap alternative, then greedy top-K assignment under an explicit bit-budget constraint, force-protection of the embedding and LM head regardless of score, and a swap-based local refinement that explicitly compensates for isolated scores failing to predict joint degradation. A's core proposal is unsound by comparison: it ranks layers by Frobenius norm on the rationale that larger weights carry more information, which contradicts the outlier-aware literature it cites (salience tracks activation magnitude, and weight-magnitude selection is specifically known to underperform) and which will mostly recover matrix dimension rather than sensitivity. A's validation is also partly circular -- confirming that the 8-bit layers have lower relative reconstruction error than the 4-bit ones tests only that the quantizer ran, not that the selection was correct. B's validation is the best part of either answer: alongside held-out perplexity on a corpus disjoint from calibration and logit KL / top-k agreement, it proposes directly measuring the actual per-matrix perplexity increase and checking Spearman correlation against the proxy scores, with an explicit instruction to switch proxies if the correlation is low; it checks allocation stability by re-running on a different calibration sample and requiring high overlap in the chosen set; and it ablates the force-protected matrices to confirm the prior. B's assumptions are also better calibrated, naming approximate additivity of errors as the weak point near the boundaries, noting the ranking can shift for out-of-domain deployment, and flagging that the residual-stream prior does not transfer to non-transformer architectures."}
