{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both land on the same defensible bottom line -- start dense on memory-constrained hardware -- but B reasons about the right mechanisms while A rests on a conceptual error that runs through its entire latency and hardware analysis. A repeatedly treats mixture-of-experts as a form of weight sparsity requiring 'sparse-aware kernels', structured-sparsity hardware support, and 'custom edge ASICs with sparse support', and concludes MoE is slower than dense on ordinary devices due to cache thrashing and irregular access. That is wrong: expert FFNs are ordinary dense GEMMs selected per token, and on a bandwidth-bound local decode the relevant fact is that MoE reads far fewer weight bytes per token than a dense model of the same total size. A's recommendation to consider MoE only on datacenter GPUs follows from the misconception rather than from the memory-bandwidth reality of local inference. A also states that Mixtral-8x7B has 1.6 trillion total parameters, off by more than an order of magnitude from roughly 47B, and that error is load-bearing since the whole memory argument turns on total parameter counts. B's framing is the sharper one and gets to the crux of the question: it explicitly separates quality per active parameter, quality per total parameter, and quality per byte of resident memory, and correctly identifies the third as the metric that governs the device-constrained decision, with the conclusion that MoE shifts the Pareto frontier upward only if it fits. It is also the only response to budget the KV cache alongside weights and to note that context length can dominate memory. Its quantization section is materially better: it names the failure mode that actually matters -- quantization noise distorting router logits into degenerate or imbalanced routing -- and supplies a concrete diagnostic, monitoring routing entropy after quantization, plus per-expert importance scoring for mixed precision. B is not clean either: its '70B MoE with 8 experts means 560B of storage' is confused arithmetic, treating inactive experts as statically identifiable ignores that routing is per token, and the claim that MoE implies smaller hidden dimensions and hence smaller KV cache is not generally true. But its decision framework is more usable, with memory tiers, explicit latency targets, a fit-in-fast-memory gate, and the correct final instruction to benchmark against the practitioner's own prompt distribution rather than trusting synthetic numbers."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both are clear and correct, and B deserves credit for opening with the unifying identity, for supplying numeric anchors a reader can sanity-check (roughly 1-5 percent online conversion against 20-40 percent in store), for decomposing online revenue by acquisition channel, and for naming omnichannel cannibalization, which A omits. But A carries the deeper idea. Its central observation is that online forecasting is partly a planning exercise rather than pure extrapolation -- you largely choose your traffic by choosing your ad spend, so the model becomes a scenario tool ('if I spend X at CAC Y, I get Z orders'), whereas a brick-and-mortar forecast is dominated by exogenous local demand you cannot dial. That single distinction explains most of the downstream differences and B never surfaces it. A is also the only response to treat capacity as a real constraint: store hours, shelf space, staffing and warehouse throughput cap physical revenue in a way that has no online analogue, which matters because a forecast that ignores the ceiling will overshoot every peak season. It adds several other things B lacks -- re-forecasting cadence (weekly to biweekly online, monthly in retail with tighter cycles over holidays), an instruction to track leading rather than trailing indicators with concrete examples for each channel, the warning that search and social algorithm changes can break historical patterns overnight, and the point that a ten percent lift in repeat-purchase rate can outweigh a ten percent lift in new traffic. On the uncertainty criterion the two are close: B's mistakes list is a nice device and explicitly calls for best/base/worst modelling and conservative conversion assumptions, but A independently recommends conservative/base/aggressive scenarios rather than point estimates and warns against relying on a single method. {"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is a design that reasons from the binding constraint; B is a large code dump whose implementation does not hold together. A opens by deriving everything from the cost of a swap and then defends specific, numbered policies against that cost: a 90-second sticky grace window justified by the read-think-type pattern, a 30-second post-swap cooldown motivated explicitly by the ping-pong thrash failure, a bounded swap timeout so a stuck load fails loudly instead of hanging, and opportunistic pre-swap during an expiring grace window so benchmark work absorbs the stall. Its swap sequence contains the detail that separates a working single-GPU router from a broken one -- verify VRAM actually returned after unload and force-kill plus respawn the runtime if it did not -- grounded in the correct diagnosis that a zombie CUDA context from a crashed runtime silently holds memory and makes the next load OOM. That also motivates its process-isolation argument and its 60-second ledger-versus-cudaMemGetInfo drift check. Its cancellation section is the sharpest part of either answer, distinguishing three cancellation sources by partial-output policy (keep for user stop, discard for preemption, discard for disconnect) and deliberately locating that distinction in the router rather than the runtime. And it answers the question actually asked about instrumentation by tiering failures into pre-ship and first-week, giving a reason per metric, then naming one annotated VRAM timeline in which thrash, OOM and starvation each have a distinct visual signature. B has surface breadth -- traffic classes, a decision matrix, a failure table, a telemetry collector -- but the substance is weaker and the code is broken in ways that matter: the Request dataclass puts a non-default field after defaulted ones and will not construct; swap_model holds the non-reentrant loading lock and then calls load_model which takes the same lock, deadlocking every swap; the priority formula derives recency_bonus and wait_penalty from the same wait_time so they collapse into one linear term and the penalty is meaningless; and the starvation boost lets benchmark requests overtake interactive after 30 seconds, flatly contradicting B's own rationale table that interactive always preempts benchmark. The KV rebuild after reload, which is the crux of what a swap costs a user, is a bare pass. B also never addresses swap thrash in policy, only as an alert. That is true for the jit plus NamedSharding (GSPMD) path but precisely false for shard_map, where the programmer owns psum/all-gather; A's own attention example shards the head dimension and then runs a softmax with no collective, which would be silently wrong. Its pipeline-parallelism section is also not pipelining - reshaping to a 'pipe' axis and shard_map-ing each layer does not create stages or schedule micro-batches - and its training-loop snippet passes an opt_state pytree under a single PartitionSpec. B is not clean either: jax.devices() returns a list with no .reshape, and its headline claim that psum is required under plain jit is wrong in two ways, since collectives are not callable outside a named-axis context and, for the column-parallel spec P(None, 'model') it actually uses, no reduction is needed at all (the all-reduce belongs to the row-parallel case). But B gets the primary sharding API right, places psum inside shard_map where an axis name genuinely exists, and adds real breadth the reader can act on - a pattern table distinguishing tensor, pipeline, attention-head, vocabulary and FSDP-style sharding, plus a gotchas table and links to the actual docs. A is better written and its axis-to-mesh mental model is well stated; B is more correct where correctness decides whether the code runs, so B edges it."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B identifies the threat that actually defines this product class and A largely misses: indirect prompt injection, where hostile instructions arrive inside the material the agent is paid to read - a comment, a README, a dependency's docs - so the agent is compromised through its normal workflow rather than through a tampered binary. B makes that AP-1 and rates it Critical/High-likelihood, and its Phase 1 set is coherent against it: human-in-the-loop for shell, filesystem scoping, secret pre-flight scanning, and crucially default-deny network egress, which is the control that converts a successful injection from exfiltration into mere local noise. A treats injection only as the model emitting a bad command in response to the user's own prompt, and defers egress filtering to the later tier, leaving the exfiltration path open during the window that matters most. A's proposed input sanitisation - stripping shell metacharacters from user text against a character allow-list - is a web-appsec reflex misapplied here; the hostile content is the repository context and the model output, not the user's typing, and metacharacter filtering does nothing against a benign-looking curl. Its inclusion of full-disk encryption and Secure Boot as mitigations is off-target for a model about an authorised process misbehaving as the user. B is also better calibrated (explicit likelihood ratings, and every Phase 2 item carries its stated trade-off: container overhead, policy-engine usability burden, second-model latency, anomaly-detection false positives) and contributes genuine design insight A lacks - progressive autonomy from read-only to write to shell, diff-based edits so changes are reviewable and reversible, local-model backends to shrink the remote-provider boundary, and a kill switch with an incident-response path. A's real advantages are that it ships sandboxing and a dedicated least-privilege account in the first tier where B defers containerisation to Phase 2, and its roadmap is calendar-sequenced; B's M6 proposal to strip comments and strings from context is impractical for a coding agent. Those do not offset B's stronger threat identification and prioritisation."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "A's literature summary is serviceable, but its procedure undercuts it: having just argued that sensitivity is positional and driven by error propagation through the residual stream, it then allocates precision purely by the Frobenius norm of each weight matrix, a statistic that tracks matrix dimensions and initialisation scale far more than it tracks quantization sensitivity, and that ignores the positional structure A itself established. The stated rationale (larger weights carry more information) is asserted rather than argued, and since quantizers are scale-adaptive, absolute norm is close to irrelevant to relative reconstruction error. A also leaves the unlabelled calibration data on the table entirely, and one of its three validation checks is circular: confirming that the 8-bit layers show lower weight reconstruction error than the 4-bit layers tests the arithmetic of quantization, not the allocation heuristic. B does what the problem actually calls for. Its sensitivity signal is measured rather than assumed - per-layer output perturbation under 4-bit quantization on a small unlabelled calibration set - and it measures sequentially with predecessors left quantized, so the compounding error it identified in the survey is captured in the score rather than merely described. It uses a scale-invariant metric with a reason given, carves out the components every method in the literature treats specially (embeddings, LM head, LayerNorm) and adjusts the budget accordingly, and layers GPTQ or AWQ error compensation on top. Its assumptions are stated where they bite (calibration representativeness, approximate layer independence, perturbation as a proxy for downstream quality), and the validation plan is the right one: correlate the sensitivity ranking against measured per-layer perplexity damage, ablate against uniform 4-bit and uniform 8-bit at matched memory, check allocation stability across calibration sets, and note that standard benchmarks are automatically scored so they need no labelling - a point A misses. B also enumerates failure modes. Its weaknesses are minor: the attention-over-FFN claim is more contested than presented, and the iterative one-layer-at-a-time refinement loop is costly without a stated budget."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is the deeper and more genuinely scientific agenda. It opens by operationalising the construct three ways - nonexistent reference, real reference misattributed in its metadata, and real correctly-identified reference cited for a claim it does not support - and then carries that distinction through every experiment, which matters because the third class is the residual the whole agenda ends up fighting and is invisible to any metadata-existence check. Its designs contain real experimental thinking rather than condition labels: a factorial battery crossing specificity, domain rarity and requested citation count so the drivers can be separated; deliberate retriever degradation at 10/30/50 percent to measure fabrication-under-miss as a dose-response rather than a single number; a forced-citation versus free-choice contrast that isolates whether the model ignores good retrievals; explicit treatment of the refusal-example ratio as the tunable that trades fabrication against over-refusal; and a confidence head evaluated not by headline AUROC but by a precision-recall sweep to an abstention operating point plus ECE, with a cross-architecture transfer check that could reduce the contribution from an artifact to a methodology. Its branch logic is the strongest part - the point that if self-correction precision is low the second pass must be made asymmetric (allowed to delete citations, forbidden to add them) is a non-obvious design consequence, as is routing expensive external audits only to low-confidence citations. It also budgets annotator hours, sequences experiments on a calendar with dependencies, and pre-registers the pivot if RAG turns out to increase misattribution. B is clean, readable, and its decision table with numeric pass criteria is a nice touch; the cross-domain robustness experiment is a legitimate axis A treats less directly, and grounding domain differences in database coverage and name conventions is a real insight. But B is thinner where it counts: 50 seed questions cannot support per-domain subgroup claims at n=20/20/10, injecting top-3 citations at each generation step is not a specified pipeline, the Experiment 3 loss term that up-weights tokens generating ungrounded citation strings is hand-waved rather than defined (grounding is not decidable at the token level during training), and its Experiment 5 hypothesis that human detection is uncorrelated with automated metrics is an odd prior for a metric that is itself defined by database lookup. Both over-specify expected effect sizes, but A at least gives ranges tied to mechanisms."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "The two overlap heavily - both open by refusing the premise of a single answer, both land on niche specialisation plus land-and-expand plus subscription pricing plus partner channels as the winning combination - so the decision turns on what each adds beyond that shared core. B covers the part of the answer that actually determines whether a managed-services GTM works: the unit economics and the retention side. It names CAC payback of 12-18 months and an LTV:CAC target of 3:1 as steering numbers, identifies churn as the primary failure mode for MSPs, and prescribes onboarding investment and quarterly business reviews as the retention mechanism - which matters because in a recurring-revenue business net retention, not new logos, is where the compounding happens. It also specifies the consultative sales motion concretely (lead with a free or low-cost assessment, then proposal, pilot, full engagement), and closes with a pitfalls list that is mostly the inverse of its own advice but still useful as a checklist. A is the better-written document and has the two sharpest individual insights: the outcomes-not-hours reframe with concrete before-and-after phrasings (99.9 percent uptime rather than 2,000 support hours), and the channel play of recruiting partners who already own the customer relationship but lack delivery capability so you become their back end - a genuinely non-obvious move that B's generic partner bullet misses. A also prioritises explicitly, calling niche choice the single highest-leverage decision, and usefully asks for the service type and company stage before going deeper. But A says nothing at all about churn, retention, customer success, or any acquisition-cost discipline, which is a substantive hole given it is recommending a subscription model. B's demerits are that its distinctive figures (40-60 percent of revenue through partners, expansion revenue 3-5x initial contract) are asserted without sourcing or a range caveat, and several bullets stay at the level of received wisdom. Coverage of the economics that decide the outcome edges out the sharper prose."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both are strong and reach the same headline conclusion - four axes reported separately, runaway behaviour treated as a gate rather than a dial - so the margin is narrow. B has the single sharpest observation in either response: decomposing the metric as success_rate times attempts_per_hour and then noting that a model stuck in a loop shows up as low throughput, arithmetically indistinguishable from a model that is merely slow, so the metric silently reclassifies a reliability failure as a latency property. Its runaway definition is also the more operational of the two (token budget exceeded by more than 2x, detected repetition, timeout) and it is the only response to carry confidence intervals into the actual report card and to attack the false precision of ranking 12.3 against 11.8. A nonetheless edges it on the decision framework, which is half the question. It sequences the trade-off correctly and without self-contradiction: disqualifying gates first, then an explicit written-down capability floor tied to the use case, then visible documented weights over the remaining axes, then an obligation to narrate the actual trade to the stakeholder in prose, then re-running the profile when the use case shifts. B states a value equation that includes a runaway-risk term and then says two paragraphs later that runaway must be a veto and you do not trade off safety - the same tension A resolves structurally. A's critique is also broader in ways that matter: Goodhart pressure once the number becomes a target, the total loss of partial credit when nine of ten tests pass, the invisibility of how a success was obtained (deleting the failing test, or shipping correct-but-injectable code), and the metric's uselessness as a diagnostic. Its most valuable structural point is that edit competence cannot be derived from a single-shot benchmark at all and requires a separate multi-turn refactoring corpus, with scope adherence measured by diff analysis and behaviour preservation by existing tests staying green - concrete instrumentation B gestures at with iteration counts but does not specify. A's weakness is that its fourth axis drifts from runaway behaviour toward general safety and hallucination, so the non-termination failure mode B nails is underweighted, and its sample profile card omits the intervals its own principles demand."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B is the better design document on nearly every criterion the prompt sets. It gets the cheapest disqualifier genuinely right by opening with a zero-GPU static triage stage - license allow-list, max_position_embeddings against the longest real prompt, parameter count against what fits at target precision, architecture compatibility - so half the weekly cohort dies before a single weight is loaded; A's first stage already loads the model, skipping the free filters entirely. B's economics are checked rather than asserted: per-stage GPU-hour budgets, stated survival rates, and an arithmetic reconciliation showing a full week lands near 110 of a 120-hour budget. Its caching is the correct design - content-addressed on (weights hash, quant, prompt_id, sampling params), so a re-release with an unchanged config is a total cache hit, a one-byte weight change forces a full re-test, battery version bumps regenerate only the new prompt ids, and a known_results table prevents the specific mistake of re-queuing a model that failed three weeks ago on unchanged weights. A's 28-day cache expiry actively contradicts its own determinism claim: if the inputs are hashed and the tests are seeded, an expiry only buys wasted compute. B also includes what A omits entirely - regression prompts run against the incumbent production model, so the funnel answers 'is this an improvement' rather than 'does this clear an absolute bar'. On honesty B is far deeper: pre-registration of the week's expectations before results arrive, thresholds as versioned constants with no eyeballing, an asymmetric re-run policy (one re-run for a failure with a logged technical reason, and passes never re-run to confirm - the latter blocks the classic confirmatory-rerun ratchet), blinded randomised human spot-checks, a favourite flag that changes nothing but forces a visible log entry, a weekly calibration note tracking whether the operator's enthusiasm predicts outcomes, and best of all a quarterly re-run of the battery against three reference models to distinguish 'my favourite regressed' from 'my validator broke'. B also states what the funnel does not do (it gates, it does not rank) and enumerates the funnel's own failure modes. A is coherent and covers caching, audit logging and blinding at a surface level, but it reads as a generic CI template rather than a design for one machine and one operator: the capability gates are statistically hollow (3-of-3 trivial prompts, 6-of-10 MMLU questions), the proposed chi-square on pass/fail distributions across models is not a meaningful bias test, and HMAC-signed S3 buckets, PDF dashboards and an annual ML-ethics review are enterprise apparatus that the stated single-machine scope cannot support. B's weakest element is using BLEU-1 against hand-written references as a coherence gate, which is a noisy instrument for open-ended prompts."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B answers more of the question and answers it more coherently. It gets the single most important semantic right - conversation history survives a swap while the KV cache cannot, because KV state is model-specific - and builds the session cache around that distinction, preserving messages in RAM while deallocating KV on unload. Its swap policy is a proper decision matrix by traffic class, and it contains the key amortisation insight A never reaches: batch all queued benchmark requests targeting the same model and serve them behind a single swap, so swap cost is paid once per cohort rather than per request. Its failure-mode section is exactly what was asked for - ranked into three priority tiers, each with a named metric, an alert threshold, and a recovery action - whereas A gives a flat undifferentiated list. A's substantive errors are in the areas the prompt centres on. Its watermark table is internally contradictory (Low is defined as under 60% VRAM free and Critical as under 85% free, so the Critical band strictly contains the Low band); its swap cost model proposes torch.save of model state to a temp file on unload, which is not how a resident model is evicted (you free it and reload from the checkpoint that is already on disk); and throughout Section 5 it conflates traffic class with model identity, testing current_model == interactive, which muddles the one-resident-model invariant the whole design exists to enforce. The claim that cancel plus swap rollback completes in under 200ms 'measured in benchmarks' is a fabricated number in a design document. A does have genuine strengths B lacks - a minimum dwell time after a swap as a structural anti-thrash mechanism rather than merely an alert, a swap-budget bid from benchmark clients, cancellation checks at every forward pass with deterministic cleanup, and memory attributed across three buckets with a fragmentation histogram. B's own weaknesses are real but more localised: its priority function subtracts a wait_penalty that grows with wait time, which is backwards and partly cancels its own aging bonus, and the starvation boost lets benchmark overtake interactive two paragraphs after the docstring promises it never will; swap_model re-acquires a non-reentrant asyncio lock it already holds; the Request dataclass orders non-default fields after defaulted ones; and cancel() scans only the queue, so in-flight requests - the case that matters - are unreachable despite the cancel_event being plumbed into generate. Its memory accountant is also declarative bookkeeping over ModelSpec estimates with no reconciliation against real allocator readings, which A at least gestures at."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B identifies the actual physics and A gets it backwards. The reason verification can be nearly free is that single-stream decode is weight-read bound: at small batch the target re-reads the same weights whether it scores one position or eight, so T_v is roughly T_t; as batch grows the model crosses onto the arithmetic ridge and each verified position costs a full token's matmuls. B parameterises exactly this with phi(B), derives Speedup = E[accepted] / (1 + r + (K-1)*phi(B)), and then reads the failure modes straight off it, including the important structural one: as phi approaches 1 the denominator approaches K + r, so no acceptance rate can rescue it and the fully compute-bound regime is a dead end. That directly answers 'when it cannot pay off'. A asserts the opposite on the same axis - that larger batch amortises verification and makes speculation more profitable, with a summary matrix recommending skip at B=1 and build at B=8, which inverts the regime where speculative decoding actually wins. A's formal apparatus does not survive inspection either: its expected-accepted formula (1-(1-AR)^N)/AR does not tend to N as AR tends to 1 (it tends to 1), contradicting the limit A claims one line later, and the verify-cost law c = N^alpha * B^(1-alpha) is invented pseudo-physics standing in for the memory/compute ridge. A is also badly calibrated, presenting fabricated authority - a named citation with a correlation of 0.94, a draft-cost law 'validated across 10+ architectures', and prediction errors of plus or minus 0.08 verified on three named models - none of which a design analysis can support. B's experiment is also the better answer to the question asked: it needs no head at all, deriving the acceptance ceiling from the target's own K-step predictability in one teacher-forced pass, measuring phi from a single two-token verify timing and r from timing a head-shaped proxy, then stratifying the calibration set by code/prose/chat to explain the 'sometimes 1.8x, sometimes slower' observation and to propose gating speculation on a runtime confidence signal rather than applying it uniformly - the most practically useful idea in either response. B is not flawless: its expected-accepted sum omits the bonus token the verification pass emits for free, which makes its never-helps claim in the compute-bound limit slightly too strong; step 3 muddles the acceptance ceiling by scoring the target's self-continuation against ground truth rather than against what a head would have to mimic; the 0.85 head-recovery discount is an unsourced constant; and the K* expression reduces to a tautology."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both correctly diagnose the metric as a binary point estimate that confounds two abilities, but A's replacement is a usable measurement protocol where B's is a framework sketch. A supplies the controls that make the separation actually hold: a needle-removed condition that must land at chance, which is the only way to prove the model is reading context rather than answering from parametric memory (B never addresses contamination at all); a leave-one-fact-out check confirming all K facts are genuinely necessary; and, most importantly, an adjacent-facts control in which the same K facts are co-located in one paragraph, which is the manoeuvre that isolates reasoning difficulty from retrieval difficulty rather than merely asserting the two axes are orthogonal. A also controls distractor construction quantitatively (30-60 percent content-word overlap with a differing answer value), reports position bands with an explicit middle-to-edge asymmetry ratio for lost-in-the-middle effects, and treats the statistics seriously - at least 50 needles per cell, bootstrap intervals, and the observation that a single Bernoulli trial near p=0.5 is a coin flip being read as a capability. Its threshold semantics are the better answer to the question as posed: multiple pre-registered crossings (L95, L90, L80, L50) whose spread itself diagnoses cliff versus graceful slope, baselines set against position-matched chance rather than zero, and an explicit warning that post-hoc threshold selection is a p-hacking vector. B's decisive weakness is structural: it fixes context length at some level known to be sufficient for retrieval and then varies reasoning demand, producing a one-dimensional reasoning curve that never measures how integration degrades as context grows - exactly the interaction the prompt is asking to expose. A's ReasonAcc(L, K) surface with K_max(L), L_max(K) and a retrieval-to-reasoning gap at fixed L captures it directly. B's EC50 is also a poorly chosen operating point, since a 50-percent-accuracy retrieval length is not a usable capability boundary, and it acknowledges the curves interact while offering no measurement that would quantify the interaction. B is clearly organised and its comparison tables are readable; A's example report paragraph shows concretely what the replacement buys a reader, which B's suggested format does not."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Close call, and B has the better epistemics section - an explicit 'what is not settled' listing the unstable Q/K/V/O ordering, uncertain scale-invariance and weight-versus-activation interaction, with accurate author-year citations - plus two validation ideas A lacks: sweeping k to plot a degradation curve and checking the chosen allocation sits at the knee, and spectral comparison of singular values per quantised matrix. But A is sounder where soundness decides. A states the U-shaped picture (embedding and LM head worst, early and late blocks worse than middle) and explains it mechanistically via redundancy plus error averaging in the residual stream, which is what makes 'most layers at 4-bit' viable at all; B's depth row asserts the opposite direction - that early error is washed out by later non-linearities so deeper layers are more sensitive - which sits badly against the error-propagation argument and against B's own later claim that first and last layers are disproportionately fragile. A also specifies a workable calibration set (128-512 sequences) where B's 1-5k tokens is an order of magnitude too small to estimate per-channel outlier statistics stably. On procedure, A names the isolation-versus-joint-degradation problem as an explicit assumption and then does something about it, with a swap-based refinement that promotes and demotes across the 8-bit boundary while watching calibration perplexity; B's composite score folds four heterogeneous signals together behind unspecified weights alpha through delta and then concedes that two of them dominate, which is not a reproducible recipe. A's validation is tighter on the two checks that matter most for a label-free setting: rank-correlating the cheap proxy against directly measured per-layer perplexity damage, so the allocation signal is shown to be real rather than noise, and re-running the whole scoring on a different calibration slice to require better than 80 percent overlap in the selected set - a stability check B never performs despite calibration representativeness being its assumption A4. Both share one unaddressed flaw: they rank by sensitivity alone while the budget is in bits, so a large low-sensitivity matrix can crowd out several small critical ones; B compounds it by claiming the integer program is trivially solved by the same greedy sort, which does not hold for heterogeneous tensor sizes."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "The requirement that admins can create and eliminate database fields is the one genuinely hard call in this brief, and the two responses diverge on it decisively. A exposes a REST endpoint that executes ALTER TABLE against the live devices table on request, with a type whitelist and a soft-delete grace period. That is a serious anti-pattern for a production web app - DDL takes locks, diverges the schema from committed migrations across environments, puts user-controlled identifiers into SQL where parameterisation cannot protect them, and breaks any ORM or cached query plan - and A never surfaces the risk. B explicitly refuses raw DDL, proposes an attribute-definition table plus a JSONB values column validated against the active attribute schema, states the reasoning (safer, no migration storms, no schema drift), and flags in a dedicated note that it is interpreting the requirement rather than implementing it literally. That is the professionally correct answer and the well-calibrated way to deliver it. B's library choices are also cleaner: Prisma for parameterised access and typed migrations, Zod schemas shared from a packages/shared directory, BullMQ so bulk updates do not block the event loop (a real scalability point A misses), PgBouncer, Testcontainers for integration tests against real Postgres, and auto-generated OpenAPI. A's stack shows less care - it recommends express-mongo-sanitize then an express-mysql-sanitize for a PostgreSQL application, which is both the wrong ecosystem and the wrong control given parameterised queries are already mandated, lists uuid as 'deterministic ID generation', and stacks Redux Toolkit, TanStack Query and an AuthContext for the same state. A is not without real advantages: its RBAC matrix is mapped directly onto the stated roles, it honours the requirement that all users may update individual records where B silently narrows users to device:update:own without flagging the change, it adds optimistic locking on PATCH via an updated_at version check, it returns a per-row success/error report from CSV bulk upload, and it closes with genuine operational depth B lacks - k6 load testing against a p95 target, dependency and image scanning, Sentry and Prometheus, and a Definition of Done per sprint. Its tickets are also sliced so a working system is demoable after sprint three rather than layer by layer. Those are meaningful, but they are refinements on top of an architecture with a structural flaw at its centre."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A opens with the decomposition that actually settles the question - separating knowledge gaps, which retrieval fixes, from behaviour gaps, which prompting has a ceiling on and fine-tuning addresses - and then makes that distinction operational by demanding a tagged eval set of 200-500 real interactions as the artifact every later decision reads from. Its experiments are designed to discriminate rather than merely to compare: fine-tune on behaviour alone with factual content deliberately excluded, then fine-tune again with facts added, so the delta between the two isolates whether the bottleneck is knowledge or behaviour; a staleness test on questions whose answers changed in the last thirty days, which prices the maintenance tax directly; and a composition test that watches specifically for the fine-tuned model beginning to ignore retrieved context, a real and frequently missed failure mode. Its cost model is a twelve-month P&L with the lines teams forget - model-upgrade cost, since retrieval is checkpoint-agnostic while fine-tuning locks you to one, and ongoing labelled-example curation - and it locates the crossover sensibly as volume times knowledge-churn with a usable heuristic (retraining more than once a quarter likely eats the inference savings). It also refuses the false binary and says why. B is organised and readable, and it contributes two experiments A lacks (a retrieval ablation and a data-volume knee curve), plus concrete dollar ranges. But its core decision logic is unsound at the point that matters most: it routes hallucination-critical domains - medical, legal, financial - to fine-tuning and claims a 30 percent hallucination reduction 'thanks to aligned weights', inverting the standard grounding argument, and its flowchart repeats the error. Its pilot is undersized (200 tickets split into train and holdout supports neither a meaningful LoRA run nor a discriminating eval) and leans on exact match and F1 against gold agent replies, a poor proxy for support quality. Its TCO figures are precise but unsourced, which reads as less calibrated than A's qualitative table plus an explicit crossover rule."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is the more current and more useful curriculum. Its coverage reaches the material that actually defines the field now - RoPE, tokenization, LoRA and QLoRA, RLHF/DPO/GRPO, KV-cache and continuous batching, GPTQ/AWQ quantization, FSDP and ZeRO, vLLM and PagedAttention, speculative decoding, state-space models, and mechanistic interpretability with sparse autoencoders - whereas B's advanced phase tops out around BERT and GPT-2 with no parameter-efficient fine-tuning, no alignment, no retrieval, and no modern inference stack, which leaves a learner well short of employable in 2025. A's projects also escalate properly, from hand-derived backprop and NumPy gradient descent, through a from-scratch single-head Transformer on a small corpus, to a QLoRA fine-tune of an 8B model and a multi-GPU FSDP training run logged to W&B and served with vLLM; B's capstones stay at the transfer-learning-plus-Gradio-demo tier. A additionally handles the prompt's vagueness structurally, with explicit pacing variants for full-time, part-time and already-experienced readers, entry points for skipping phases, four optional specialisation tracks, and a weekly read-code-write-teach loop that turns the map into a habit. Both responses fabricate attributions, which is the main quality problem here. A is the worse offender: Elements of ML credited to Cortes and Vapnik (it is Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman), a named YouTube PyTorch tutorial and an LLM book with invented authors, a CS229W course that does not exist, and DPO miscategorised as a pre-training objective alongside CLM and MLM. B has its own: Grokking Deep Learning attributed to Khalid rather than Trask, a mini-project applying logistic regression to Boston house prices (a regression target, on a dataset withdrawn for ethical reasons), and a garbled DDIM/Predictor line. B's genuine advantages are a self-assessment matrix that locates the reader before prescribing anything, timelines tied to three distinct goals (career pivot, job-ready, grad school), and a practical tips section on reading loss curves, seeding and portfolio building. Those do not offset a syllabus that is roughly half a generation out of date."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A describes the stack people actually build today and is honest about where the difficulty lives. Its architecture is Llama-style - RoPE, grouped-query attention, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, weight tying, dispatching to F.scaled_dot_product_attention so Flash kernels are used - where B's is GPT-2 era with learned absolute positions, LayerNorm and a hand-rolled quadratic attention. A also covers the parts of 'from scratch' that decide whether the project succeeds and that B omits or fumbles: data curation as a first-class stage (MinHash dedup, quality and perplexity filtering, weighted domain mixing, PII removal), a comparison of the parallelism strategies with what each actually shards (DDP, tensor, pipeline, ZeRO-3/FSDP, sequence), inference optimisation (KV-cache, PagedAttention, speculative decoding, INT4/INT8), post-training as a distinct run with its own much lower learning rate, and a staged build order that starts at nanoGPT scale and says when to move up. Its closing judgement - that the architecture is the easy part and data quality plus distributed-training stability are what actually bite - is the most valuable sentence in either response. B's advantages are real: a blunt cost reality check up front, concrete quality-filter heuristics, a complete Trainer class, and the only evaluation section in either response (perplexity, which A never mentions at all - a genuine gap), plus a sensible fallback to fine-tuning GPT-2. But B carries a load-bearing correctness bug: its dataset already returns x as tokens[:-1] and y as tokens[1:], and then train_step shifts a second time with logits[..., :-1, :] against targets[..., 1:], so the model is trained to predict two tokens ahead - and the same double shift is repeated in evaluate and in the perplexity function. It also instantiates a fresh GradScaler inside every mixed-precision step, destroying the scaler state, recommends DataParallel for multi-GPU, and strips all non-ASCII in cleaning, which silently discards multilingual data without comment. A is not clean either - the tokenizer trainer call has its arguments reversed, the FSDP auto-wrap call is not a real API, GradScaler is used with a bfloat16 autocast that A itself later says needs no scaling, the EOS check in generate is nonsense, and the stated ~10M parameter count is off by more than 2x given a 32k vocabulary at dim 512 - but those are peripheral snippets rather than the training objective."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both are well-organized and cover the same ground, but A reasons where B mostly enumerates. A anchors both models in the shared Revenue = Traffic x Conversion x AOV identity and then explains *why* each variable behaves differently (soft vs. hard capacity ceilings, catchment-area economics, fixed-cost floors setting a higher break-even bar, replenishment latency of days versus hours), and closes with a genuinely useful synthesis: online forecasting is a demand-and-channel problem while physical retail is a location-and-capacity problem. Its actionability is also more concrete (forecast per-store then aggregate, model cannibalization for omnichannel, build an explicit weather/event adjustment band, channel-level rather than blended conversion). B is competent and does name a few forecasting techniques A omits (same-store sales, regression on local variables, time-series/ML), which is a real if narrow advantage, but its content is largely a bulleted inventory of data sources and variables with little causal explanation, and its comparison table restates surface facts rather than deriving implications. Both are appropriately hedged; neither overclaims. A's greater depth, mechanism-level insight, and sharper practical guidance outweigh B's slightly broader method vocabulary."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "The two are close in form and both are well-structured, appropriately hedged, and directly usable as a thesis Scope-and-Limitations section, but A is the more complete and more operationally specific document. A adds two scope elements B lacks entirely: an explicit performance-metrics subsection naming the actual dependent variables (radial deviation from theoretical center, concentricity, positional repeatability, coefficient of variation) and a drilling-scenarios subsection that bounds the process parameters (bit diameter, feed rate, spindle speed, flat vs. curved vs. machined surfaces) — which is what makes a scope statement testable rather than aspirational. A also names concrete guide geometries (V-groove locators, concentric ring fixtures) and contributes limitations B misses, notably hole depth and high length-to-diameter-ratio and off-axis drilling, and an explicit caution against extrapolating the tolerance findings to other machine classes. B's genuine advantages are real but narrower: its measurement-resolution limitation (instrument calibration imposing a detection floor that could mask sub-millimetre deviation) is the single sharpest item in either response and A should have had it, and its n >= 30 per condition is better calibrated to the prompt's 'many repeated trials' than A's 10-25. Those two points make the gap small, but A's broader and more concrete coverage of both scope and boundary conditions carries it."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both identify the same correct core thesis — niche focus, productized outcome-based offerings, land-and-expand, subscription pricing, partner leverage — and A states it crisply with a memorable one-sentence playbook. But A largely stops at the what, while B supplies the how: a concrete sequencing plan (validate the niche with 10-15 discovery calls, build 2-3 packages, secure 2-3 vendor partnerships with deal registration, then build the pipeline engine), the operating metrics to manage against (CAC, LTV, gross margin, NRR, partner-sourced revenue, utilization), an explicit pitfalls list, and — most valuably — a stage-conditioned adaptation section that tells a sub-$2M-ARR firm to skip the channel motion that will take 6-12 months to mature, which is exactly where A's undifferentiated 'build a channel engine' advice would mislead an early-stage reader. B also notices that 'managed services' need not mean IT and maps the framework to facilities/HR/logistics, whereas A only surfaces that ambiguity as a closing question. It also deliberately makes cancel-after-terminal return 200 and argues the case (fire-and-forget safety beats pedantic honesty), whereas A returns 409 and pushes a pure-noop race onto every client. B catches several things A misses entirely: a required, server-capped timeout_seconds so nothing can occupy the single GPU forever; server-generated UUIDv7 justified by both sortability and IDOR/enumeration surface; a cursor-paginated list endpoint and tenant scoping; separate liveness and readiness so an orchestrator can drain rather than kill mid-run; and a real versioning policy (additive-in-v1, open state enum clients must not treat as exhaustive, Deprecation/Sunset headers with 12 months' notice) against A's single sentence about URI versioning. {"choice": "A", "rationale": "The decisive design question under a 200-run cap is how to buy power, and A gets it right: a single common task corpus ported into all five languages makes every comparison paired, so task difficulty is differenced out and McNemar-style analysis extracts materially more signal per run than independent groups. A then explicitly addresses the repeats dimension the prompt names — zero within-task repeats, justified as trading sample reliability for task diversity because the cross-language pairing already supplies the replication — whereas B's 'repeats: 40 independent generation attempts per language, fresh prompt, different random seed' conflates repeats with distinct tasks and never resolves whether the 40 are tasks or re-draws, abandoning pairing in the process. A's inconclusive-reporting section is also the more useful artifact: effect sizes with CIs, an explicit required-n statement, Bayes factors on the Jeffreys scale, a tiered evidence vocabulary tying claim strength to CI width and power, sensitivity re-analyses, and a summary table that states in plain language that inconclusive means the study cannot separate no difference from a meaningful one rather than establishing equivalence. Both plans have real defects and neither is clean. A omits any multiplicity correction across ten pairwise language comparisons, and its own example table would flag a p=0.01 result as significant when it likely would not survive Holm; its MDE arithmetic also drops a square root, so the honest unpaired detectable difference at n=40 is nearer 30 percentage points than the 15-18 claimed, and the paired 10-12 is likewise optimistic. B's errors are larger and better hidden: with N=200, w=0.5 and df=4 the noncentrality it itself computes (lambda=50) implies power far above 0.99, not the stated 0.81, and w=0.3 gives roughly 0.90, not 0.54, so the central budget justification rests on numbers that contradict its own formula; a 'random intercept per run' in a Bernoulli model is not identifiable; and the ICC-lifts-power aside is asserted rather than shown. B does contribute two things A lacks and should have had — TOST against an explicit ROPE, which is the correct way to claim equivalence rather than merely disclaiming it, plus latency and blinded quality as secondary outcomes and a reproducibility appendix. Those narrow the gap but do not close it against A's stronger core design and clearer handling of the allocation question actually asked."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both land on the same honest headline — roughly 40 runs per language buys only a ~30 percentage-point pairwise MDE — and B deserves credit for drawing the right strategic conclusion from it, namely that the study should be repositioned from ranking languages to locating difficulty-tier failure modes. But A does substantially more real design work. It runs a 20-run pilot outside the budget to seed the success-rate priors the power argument depends on, rather than asserting them; it allocates runs proportionally to Bernoulli information p(1-p), which is the correct justification for over-weighting the Medium tier and is an argument B never makes; it authors each task once as a single semantic specification translated into all five languages, with a per-language idiomaticity panel, giving within-task pairing and controlling the confound that a 'Rust task' may simply be a harder task — a lever B leaves entirely on the table by never specifying whether tasks are shared; and it models tasks as a random effect and then actually pays the price for it, computing a design effect from an ICC and deflating the effective n from 36 to 28 before quoting the MDE, whereas B's 31pp figure silently assumes independence across clustered repeats and is therefore optimistic. A also reports three separate MDEs (language ~30pp, difficulty ~10pp, interaction ~65pp) and flags the interaction as severely underpowered instead of quietly including it, reserves a 20-run buffer governed by a pre-registered reallocation rule rather than post-hoc judgement, and adds a threats-to-validity table covering memorization via hidden-test variants and model-snapshot pinning. Its inconclusive-reporting protocol is the stronger of the two: it shares B's good instincts (CIs, mandatory MDE disclosure, TOST against a pre-specified 15pp margin, required follow-up budget) but adds a Bayesian supplement reporting P(effect > 5pp) and P(effect > 15pp), and an explicit list of what it will not do, including refusing to drop noisy tasks post hoc and refusing to let a non-significant omnibus F-test bury a large two-language gap. A is not flawless — it says repeats use a fresh random seed in one section and a fixed seed in another, its proportional-allocation shares do not quite sum, and its range-versus-pairwise derivation is muddled before it abandons it. B has a clean arithmetic slip of its own (5 tasks x 2 repeats is 10 runs per tier per language, not the 20 it claims). On depth, rigor, and honesty about what the budget cannot resolve, A is clearly ahead."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A models the threat that actually defines this product class and B largely misses it. A names the reverse trust boundary explicitly — untrusted content flowing into the agent from files it must read to do its job — and ranks indirect prompt injection via a comment or string literal in the repo as attack path P1, with the correct justification that it requires zero external compromise and the input channel can never be closed. B treats prompt injection almost entirely as a network MITM concern and then proposes, as a first-ship control, stripping shell metacharacters from user text against a character whitelist; that is SQL-injection thinking transplanted into a domain where the hostile input is ordinary-looking prose arriving from a source file, and it would both fail to stop the attack and break legitimate use. B's companion rule to reject any model output containing a metacharacter has the same problem. A's mitigations are correspondingly better engineered and better sequenced: structured typed tool calls instead of raw shell strings so injected shell syntax is inexpressible, filesystem scoping named down to the concrete primitive per OS (landlock/seccomp, sandbox-exec, AppContainer), credential isolation achieved by making the files unreadable rather than by asking the agent not to read them, a default-deny egress proxy with pre-registered registries and a separate rule for the model API, a hash-chained audit log deliberately written outside the sandbox root so the agent cannot rewrite it, and later a reader/executor split where the context-reading model has no shell tool at all. Its ordering has an articulated principle — v1 shrinks blast radius because a contained failure is recoverable, v2 shrinks probability — and it closes with a residual-risk section that honestly concedes the sandbox cannot stop an injected agent from misusing an allowed action, that the developer remains the root of trust, and that a local model removes the cloud-exfiltration path entirely. B is competently organized and contributes a few things A does not (a dedicated unprivileged OS account, hardware second-factor for high-risk commands, a dated rollout calendar, a closing red-team suggestion), but its attacker and asset tables stay generic, several later-stage items are off-target for this threat model (full-disk encryption and secure boot defend against offline physical attacks, not an autonomous agent), behavioral anomaly detection is asserted rather than designed, and it offers no residual-risk accounting at all."}

Experiment C is the standout: ablate retrieval from the fine-tuned model, because if quality collapses the fine-tune learned how to use retrieved context (durable and healthy) whereas if quality holds it baked knowledge into weights (a maintenance liability that rots on every policy change). {"choice": "A", "rationale": "A reads like a review written by someone who has actually invalidated experiments, and it front-loads the checks that most often kill a result of exactly this shape: sample-ratio mismatch, pre-experiment covariate balance and whether the randomization unit is user or session, optional stopping with a demand for the peeking curve and an O'Brien-Fleming style correction, multiple comparisons across variants and metrics, and the winner's curse inflating the observed effect if the test was underpowered. It is also the only one of the two to take seriously that a ranking model can win on the primary metric while damaging the system — guardrail metrics for diversity, spam and toxicity, creator and advertiser impact, negative-control metrics that should not move, and the specific gaming signature of CTR up with time-spent-per-session down — and it converts the whole review into a decision: an explicit pass/fail table, named rejection triggers, and a rollout plan with a 1 percent canary, a minutes-scale kill switch and a four-week persistence check. But B undercuts itself with a repeated statistical error, insisting twice that the result is inconclusive or unshippable if the confidence interval spans zero — at p = 0.03 the 95 percent interval necessarily excludes zero, so the stated criterion cannot bind and signals the reasoning is pattern-matched rather than worked through. It also misstates the power problem, claiming an underpowered test can yield p = 0.03 for a trivial effect, when the actual hazard is the opposite: low power means a significant result must be an exaggerated one. B is a competent sketch; A is the review that would actually protect the launch."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B is the more complete and more technically disciplined survey, and it answers the 'where does it cost you' half of the prompt far better by characterizing the shape of each failure rather than just its magnitude: the sliding window is a cliff not a curve, score-based eviction is silent and distributed, quantisation error is uniform across the sequence with no lost region, gist compression loses granularity rather than coverage, and fixed sparse patterns produce targeted blindness. It also covers the single biggest lever A omits entirely — architectural KV reduction via grouped-query and multi-query attention, an 8x reduction that is essentially free and should be the first move — plus low-rank and layer-shared factorisation, gist-token compression, and CPU-paged external KV. Its sharpest analytical point is that attention-mass scoring is myopic by construction: it rewards tokens that were attended to, not tokens that will be, so a declaration at the top of a long file is evicted precisely before it is needed. That observation then drives a recommendation that hangs together — keep the full sequence, refuse hard eviction, and instead re-allocate precision asymmetrically using an AST-derived structural score rather than attention mass, protecting identifiers, signatures and type annotations at high precision while compressing whitespace and boilerplate hard; add a symbol-aware code retriever for genuine cross-file references; and treat gist tokens as a pointer index rather than a substitute. It closes with explicit memory arithmetic and a stated quality cost, which is the calibrated way to end. {"choice": "A", "rationale": "A reads like a review written by someone who has actually run ranking experiments, while B reads like a competent generic statistics checklist. A leads with the check that should come first and that B omits entirely, sample ratio mismatch, correctly treating it as a binary validity gate that invalidates the test before effect size is even discussed, and it names realistic causes (bot traffic, cookie-clearing duplication, misconfigured experiment layers). It is the only one to identify the confound specific to this class of model: a ranking change is a position change, so a CTR lift can be an artifact of moving already-high-CTR items up the position-bias gradient rather than a relevance gain, and A makes inability to separate those a standalone reason not to ship. It also surfaces the guardrails that matter for ranking and that pure user-metric analysis hides, result-set diversity and concentration collapse, supply-side and creator traffic redistribution, reformulation rate, and concurrent-experiment interference on the same surface. Its decision framework is genuinely decision-shaped: four ordered gates, a lower-bound-of-interval criterion rather than a point estimate, explicit cost of being wrong in both directions, and four conditional branches that map distinct evidence patterns to distinct actions including segment-only shipping and phased rollout with pre-agreed kill criteria. B covers the standard ground well and contributes two things A lacks, an explicit demand to disambiguate 0.8 percentage points from 0.8 percent relative, and an online-versus-offline agreement check to detect overfitting or distribution shift, plus a sensible note that bootstrap or permutation intervals suit ranking metrics better than normal-theory tests. But B is shallower throughout and contains two statistical slips: it repeatedly conditions its no-ship decision on the confidence interval including zero, which cannot happen at 95% given a two-sided p of 0.03, and it claims an underpowered test can yield p equals 0.03 for trivial effects, when the actual hazard is the reverse, that low power inflates the magnitude of any estimate that does reach significance, a Type M error A captures implicitly via its achieved-power audit and its insistence on the interval's lower bound. A's multiple-comparisons treatment is also more pointed, asking specifically how many metrics were pre-registered versus scrolled to post hoc. Neither is over-hedged; A's calibration is stronger because it separates what would make the result trustworthy from what it currently is, a hypothesis rather than a conclusion."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "The procedures diverge on a point that decides correctness. A measures sensitivity by walking forward, quantising layer i while leaving every earlier layer quantised, and scores the local output perturbation of that layer; it calls this capturing error propagation, but the effect is that each score is contaminated by accumulated upstream drift, so later layers are scored under a degraded input distribution and the resulting ranking is confounded with measurement order rather than being a clean per-layer comparison. A also scores local reconstruction error at the layer boundary, which is exactly the quantity known to correlate poorly with end-to-end damage, since a large perturbation in a redundant middle block can be absorbed while a small one at the head is not. B instead perturbs one matrix at a time against the unmodified full-precision reference and scores the change in output logits, which is a properly controlled one-factor-at-a-time measurement, then adds a greedy demote/promote swap pass explicitly justified as correcting for the fact that isolated scores do not predict joint degradation. B also allocates at matrix rather than block granularity and actually writes the budget constraint over parameter counts, which matters because an 8-bit assignment to a wide FFN matrix costs far more than to a small projection; A's pseudocode simply adds the embedding and LM head to the 8-bit set without the budget adjustment its own prose calls for, and never restores precision between measurements. On the literature summary B is both more accurate and more mechanistic: it identifies the FFN down-projection and the attention output projection as the sensitive matrices within a block with Q/K/V least sensitive, and explains boundary sensitivity via redundancy and error averaging in the residual stream, whereas A asserts the broader and more contestable claim that attention projections are generally more sensitive than FFN weights, and offers propagation as the only mechanism. B's validation is the decisive advantage: alongside held-out perplexity against both an all-4-bit and an FP baseline on a corpus disjoint from calibration, it proposes logit KL and top-k agreement as a finer instrument than perplexity, an ablation confirming the force-protected matrices really are disproportionately costly at 4-bit, an allocation-stability check across calibration draws with a concrete overlap threshold, and above all a Spearman rank-correlation check between the cheap proxy and the actual measured perplexity delta, with an explicit switch-proxies decision if the correlation is weak. That validates the instrument rather than only the artefact. B's assumptions are also better calibrated, naming where each breaks (domain shift for code versus prose, boundary layers for additivity, 2-bit for non-interference, non-residual architectures for the middle-layer prior). A contributes a clear pseudocode sketch and a reasonable iterative upgrade loop, and its benchmark suggestions are practical, though presenting MMLU and GSM8K as label-free is loose. B is the sounder design."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both answers are well organised, correctly identify the shared multiplicative skeleton of traffic times conversion times order value, and correctly locate the divergence in where demand originates and what caps it, so the decision comes down to coverage of the actual practitioner toolkit and to depth of insight. {"choice": "A", "rationale": "B looks far more substantial, offering schemas, a full class, an architecture diagram and a decision matrix, but its core modelling is unsound in ways that would invalidate the deliverable. The win/loss classifier derives its target from deal_stage and then includes deal_stage in the feature matrix after filtering to stages 4 and 5, which is perfect target leakage: the model can only learn the identity mapping, every reported accuracy, F1 and AUC is meaningless, and the feature-importance table is noise. The code also does not run as written: the growth block aggregates a deal_count column that does not exist in the revenue frame and then merges on product_name while it is still an index, and pd.qcut with labels HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW assigns them in ascending order, so the lowest-priority tercile is labelled HIGH and the sales team would be pointed at exactly the wrong deals. Presenting randomly generated demo data through this pipeline, where no signal exists by construction, completes the illusion of validation. A is thinner and stays at blueprint level, with no code, but it is sound: it maps each of the user's questions to a defensible analytical approach, separates descriptive, predictive and prescriptive work with a staged roadmap, defines expected revenue as deal size times win probability, proposes survival and stage-duration analysis with a 75th-percentile stall trigger that is genuinely actionable, and closes the loop from lost deals back to product and budget decisions. Its weaknesses are real but lesser: the priority formula multiplies by one minus the absolute budget gap and the top tier favours products already near target, which sits in tension with the user's explicit instruction to focus on products far from target, and A never flags that tension; the stage weights also assign a nonzero score to already-won deals. Neither response expresses much uncertainty or proposes an evaluation protocol worth the name, but A's omissions are gaps whereas B's are confident errors presented as a finished system."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both lay out a sensible phase structure (environment, tokenizer, architecture, data, training, inference) and both give runnable-looking PyTorch, so the split comes from correctness on the part that matters and from coverage of the rest of the stack. A decoder language model trained without a causal mask is not a language model at all, and the failure is silent except for a suspiciously low loss, which is exactly the trap a beginner cannot diagnose. Its generate function compounds this: the token list is concatenated with a tensor, the multinomial index is used directly as a token id instead of being mapped back through the top-k indices, and the top_p argument is accepted but never used. B's architecture, by contrast, is correct where it counts: rotate-half RoPE with the standard duplicated cos/sin table, GQA with correct head repetition, SwiGLU with the right three projections, RMSNorm, pre-norm residuals, weight tying, and scaled_dot_product_attention with is_causal set. {"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is both more rigorous and more usable. A also recognises a fourth category B lacks entirely: measurements that were impossible on the laptop and are therefore new rather than re-measured, such as multi-GPU scaling and NVLink collective behaviour, and it encodes this in a four-state legend (transfers, re-measure, re-optimise, new) rather than a binary. B's substance is also thinner on the model-evaluation side, reducing mechanisms to script portability, pip installs, and sampling-parameter trends, whereas A covers quantization sensitivity by layer, KV-cache and eviction behaviour, attention diagnostics, and failure-mode taxonomy. The hardware particulars matter here too: A's figures for H200 and B200 capacity and bandwidth are right, while B's are wrong on both parts and wrong on PCIe generation, in a document whose entire subject is hardware-specific care. B does contribute real enforcement ideas A partly lacks, notably device-prefixed metric syntax, a read-only baseline archive with an as-run disclaimer, artifact tagging of driver, CUDA and OS build, and a transferability-assessment section that records which mechanisms failed and why; A's per-platform re-measurement checklists are less specific about protocol details such as p50/p99 capture and one-second thermal logging. Against that, A's evaluation table is sloppy in places (a retrieval precision target expressed as at most 0.30), its two-phase self-verification is an LLM checking an LLM without the independent NLI instrument B specifies, and running a judge on 100 percent of answers is asserted without cost reasoning. {"choice": "A", "rationale": "A identifies the mechanism that actually explains the user's observation, namely that the arithmetic changes qualitatively between the memory-bound small-batch regime, where verifying K extra positions is nearly free because time is dominated by streaming weights, and the compute-bound large-batch regime, where the verify pass genuinely costs K times a decode step and speculation buys latency at the price of throughput below the no-speculation baseline at the same batch. It then reverse-engineers the reported 1.8x to a consistent operating point (uniform acceptance near 0.5 with a head about five percent of the target's streamed parameters), and its memory-bound numbers check out exactly, with the correct expected-tokens identity including the bonus token from the verify pass. Its deepest contribution is insisting that the positional acceptance curve, not a single averaged alpha, governs the economics, and showing numerically how a healthy first-position rate coexists with a collapsing tail that drags the speedup far below what the uniform-alpha formula predicts. The proposed experiment matches that insight and is genuinely minimal and faithful: fit a linear probe from saved hidden states to the K subsequent tokens, replay the accept-reject logic to get consecutive per-position acceptance on the deployment distribution, and treat the result as a lower bound on any nonlinear head, with an optional MLP probe to measure the remaining nonlinearity headroom and a decision table that gates the build on batch regime rather than giving one verdict. A is not flawless: its boxed compute-bound speedup carries a spurious factor of K, and the critical-alpha derivation that follows from it is wrong, though the accompanying table, the surrounding prose, and the cannot-pay-off discussion all use the correct expression and reach the right conclusion, so the error is localized rather than load-bearing. B is cleaner to read and its break-even framing is serviceable, but it is wrong in several places that matter. Its worked numbers do not follow from its own formula (alpha 0.7 with k=4 gives about 2.53, not 2.73; alpha 0.5 with k=8 gives about 2.0, not 3.8). More seriously, its treatment of the batch axis, one of the four the prompt names, is backwards: it claims larger batch amortizes and reduces the effective verify cost and can turn a slowdown into a speedup, when increasing batch is precisely what pushes the system into the compute-bound regime where the K-token verify stops being free and speculation stops paying. Its predictive experiment substitutes target-model top-1 confidence or entropy for acceptance, which measures how predictable the target is rather than how well a head reading the hidden state agrees with it, offers a calibration constant attributed vaguely to published data, and describes an upper-bound estimate as conservative, which inverts the safety direction of a go/no-go decision."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B is built on the decomposition that actually decides this question: separate the knowledge gap, which retrieval fixes, from the behavior gap, which prompting has a ceiling on and fine-tuning addresses, and then make the first deliverable a set of 200 to 500 real interactions tagged by which kind of failure each one is. B's justification for its 50 percent threshold is simply wrong for this task — chance accuracy on short-answer extraction is near zero, not one half, so the psychophysics analogy does not hold — and its worked report line conflates positions with accuracies confusingly.
