A also answers the repeats part of the prompt properly -- 20 unique tasks times 2 repeats per language -- and gives the right reason, that k=1 cannot separate a flaky harness from a weak one while k>2 buys reliability at the cost of task coverage, and it plans a mixed-effects model with tasks as random effects to exploit that structure. B's design has no repeats at all despite labelling a section Repeats: 40 fresh prompts with 40 seeds is 40 singleton observations, which forecloses any flakiness estimate, and its stated model puts a random intercept per run, which is unidentifiable when each run contributes one Bernoulli outcome. B's power numbers are also wrong in the direction of overclaiming: with N=200, df=4 and w=0.5 the noncentrality is 50 against a critical value of 9.49, giving power near unity rather than the claimed 0.81, and w=0.3 gives roughly 0.94 rather than 0.54, so the central budget justification does not hold; the appeal to simulation-confirmed prior LLM evals for a 10-15% power lift is asserted without support. B's reporting section is its strongest part, adding Bayes factors, a ROPE and a reproducibility appendix with a per-run tagging schema, but it also prescribes post-hoc power computed from the observed effect size, which is a known fallacy that conveys nothing beyond the p-value. A's reporting is narrower but clean -- intervals over point estimates, a mandatory MDE statement attached to every null comparison, TOST against a declared margin, Cohen's h for tier transitions, and the follow-up budget needed to resolve the question -- with only a minor slip in that follow-up sample-size figure."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is more accurate, more complete, and answers the bonus question with an actual mechanism rather than a score. It covers eight options ordered along a coherent spine from web-first frameworks to general engines with a web export path, and its cons are specific and verifiable in a way that would change a real decision: Godot's web target being its weakest, with large WASM payloads, multi-second first loads and a COOP/COEP header requirement that breaks on some hosts; PlayCanvas's engine being open source while the editor is a proprietary cloud product, so the risk is losing the workflow rather than the code; Kaboom being effectively a single-maintainer project. That last set is exactly the right framing for unlikely to be outdated, and A generalises it explicitly into a governance argument -- foundation-governed and standard-setting projects are safest, single-company cloud products and single-maintainer projects least safe -- which is more useful than B's unexplained decimal ratings of 8.5 versus 7 out of 10, a false precision that is not derived from anything stated. B has the better coverage decision in one respect, including Unity, which A omits entirely despite it being the most popular engine overall, but B pays for it with two outright factual errors: it says Phaser is community-maintained with no corporate backing when a funded company maintains it, and its comparison table marks PlayCanvas as not open source when the engine is MIT-licensed, which is precisely the fact that determines its longevity risk. B also omits Three.js from its list while referencing it as a yardstick elsewhere, leaving out the dominant 3D library on the web. B's closing criteria for durability and its use-case matrix are genuinely good, and A's Babylon governance description is loosely worded, but on soundness and the specific bonus criterion A is clearly ahead."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "These are close: both organise by mechanism, cost and fit, both correctly separate the cliff-shaped failure of window methods from the uniform blur of quantisation and the silent, distributed failure of attention-score eviction, and their coverage is complementary, with A adding low-rank/latent factorisation and fixed sparse patterns while B adds StreamingLLM attention sinks and cross-layer sharing (CLA/YOCO) that A folds away. B wins on two things that matter more. First, calibration: its numbers are stated as typical benchmark drops rather than confident per-technique perplexity figures, and it makes the sharper observation that for code the benchmark average understates the risk because the real damage is tail-case symbol loss, not mean degradation; A's quantitative claims (10-30% for eviction, 20-50% for gists, 10-200 ms retrieval latency, a final 2-5% and 3-8% split) are precise beyond anything that could be supported. B is also more accurate on SnapKV, describing the trailing observation-window pass, where A calls it a single importance head. Second, the recommendation: B reframes the problem correctly, arguing that a coding agent should retrieve a few thousand tokens of relevant code with a tree-sitter symbol index before filling the cache at all, so that quantisation, a structure-aware importance floor for def/class/import/type tokens, and middle-layer sharing only have to be adequate rather than heroic. That is the right diagnosis of where the leverage is, and B states the underlying asymmetry crisply -- in a repo the heavy hitters are structural rather than statistical, and eviction must decide before the model knows which signature it will need. A reaches a partly similar place but insists on retaining the whole sequence and proposes per-token asymmetric bit-widths driven by an AST pass plus a CPU-resident full-repo KV store with a code-aware retriever, which is creative but hand-waves serious kernel and engineering costs it never prices, then closes with a memory and quality estimate stated with unjustified confidence. A's mechanism explanations are vivid and its breadth is slightly greater, which makes this a narrow rather than decisive call."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both are unusually good and both refuse the common failure of pretending 200 runs can settle pairwise language questions, but A covers more of what was asked and covers it with more rigour. A allocates across all three requested axes rather than two: it defines difficulty tiers with concrete shapes and pilot-estimated pass rates, then justifies the 30/90/60 split by Bernoulli information content, since a run at p near 0.5 carries roughly four times the information for estimating a difference as one at p near 0.25, and it is candid that it over-weights Medium beyond the strict proportional split because that is where the language contrast is identifiable. It then computes minimum detectable effects separately for the language main effect (about 30 pp), the difficulty main effect (about 10 pp) and the interaction (about 65 pp), and names the interaction as the design's honest weak point rather than hiding it, closing with an explicit not-powered-for list. The 20-run buffer governed by a pre-registered stopping rule with a repeat cap, the threats-to-validity table (hidden-test variants against memorisation, idiomaticity review so a Rust task is not intrinsically harder, a SHA-pinned model snapshot), and the reporting protocol that mandates stating the MDE beside every null, adds TOST at a declared 15 pp margin, a Bayesian supplement and a list of things it will not do, together make it the more complete instrument. B lands the sharper single insight -- that the task is the experimental unit, that two repeats reduce residual noise without creating 200 independent observations, and that any analysis treating them as independent is severely anti-conservative -- and its 20 unique tasks is the better allocation given that items buy power while repeats buy reliability, which is the real soft spot in A's nine-task base. But B's budget is internally inconsistent, computing its standard error and 33 pp MDE from 20 tasks while the summary table spends 40 of the 200 on a pilot and leaves only 16 tasks in the primary analysis, and it treats difficulty only as a stratification covariate rather than as an axis with its own power consequences, so it answers the difficulty part of the prompt more thinly. Both assume an implausibly low task-level ICC, so neither's headline power figure should be taken at face value."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both design five progressive sessions with a tangible artifact per session, timed agendas and sensible sequencing, so the gap is in facilitation craft, which is what the role in the prompt asks for. B does not just list activities, it explains the mechanism behind each one: the One-Sentence Test to expose the gap between the story the team tells itself and what customers hear; an explicit anti-message per pillar; a Reach-by-Relationship-Depth two-by-two paired with the observation that teams over-invest in shallow high-reach channels; dependency mapping named as the place launches actually fail; specific crisis cards rather than a generic what-could-go-wrong; a deliberately uninformed attendee in session four as a red-team device standing in for the people who will be told about the launch rather than build it; and verbal rehearsal in session five, where each owner says aloud their action, trigger, backup and escalation, which is a genuinely strong technique for surfacing ambiguities invisible on paper. B also varies participants per session rather than carrying one fixed roster, tapers durations from three hours to two as the work shifts from generative to operational, matches room setup to phase, defines the facilitator's stance per phase (provocateur, architect, red team, conductor), and closes with a single testable rule for whether a session is finished. A is clean, well-paced and easier to skim, and it beats B in two places worth naming: a dedicated KPI and dashboard block with targets, data sources and named reporters, and a launch-readiness checklist that covers the website-specific items B mostly omits, including redirects, SEO, accessibility, analytics tracking and email deliverability. But A's facilitation notes stay generic (parking lot, dot voting, note-taker) where B's carry reasoning, and A's single fixed participant list of ten to fourteen people across all five sessions is a weaker call than B's role-tailored attendance. On depth, insight and operational actionability B is ahead; A's edge on measurement and technical readiness narrows the gap without closing it."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B is the more serious design at nearly every stage. Its chunking is routed by document type with a stated rationale per type (function boundaries for code, one chunk per endpoint for API docs, per-step for runbooks, per-version-entry for changelogs) rather than a single hierarchical recipe, and the parent-child pointers give two distinct retrieval modes -- precise chunk match versus parent expansion for grounding -- that it actually uses later in the pipeline. The refresh design shows real operational thinking that A lacks entirely: a change manifest as an explicit artifact, and deterministic chunk IDs derived from doc_id, chunk index and text hash so that re-running the same manifest is idempotent, which is exactly the property a daily delta pipeline needs when a job fails halfway. Retrieval adds intent classification, query rewriting, separate code and text indices, reciprocal rank fusion to combine incommensurable score scales, and cross-encoder reranking confined to the top 50 for cost -- each justified rather than listed. Grounding is where the gap is widest: B requires per-claim citations, runs a second verification pass, and crucially proposes string-level verification that a cited chunk actually contains the claimed text rather than trusting an LLM judge, and it budgets the context window arithmetically. Its evaluation has numeric thresholds, a golden set that deliberately includes I-don't-know and multi-hop cases, and a regression gate that blocks deployment on a five percent drop. The failure modes each carry mitigations and are unified by the sharpest observation in either answer -- that all three are the gap between faithful to the retrieved context and factually correct. A is coherent and covers the same section headings competently, with a good incremental-upsert sketch and a reasonable hybrid-plus-reranker retriever, but it stops at description: no idempotency, no citation verification beyond a prompt instruction, a generic metric list, and failure modes with root causes but no remedies, the third of which muddles corpus growth with context-window overload. B's flaws are minor by comparison: text-embedding-3-large is 3072-dimensional rather than the 1536 in its schema, and its retrieval-precision threshold row is labelled backwards."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A covers ten options against B's five and organises them by a taxonomy that actually matters for this question -- 2D-focused, 2D-plus-3D, and browser-native 3D with no export step -- so a reader can find their bucket before comparing. It also includes the categories B drops entirely: Three.js and PixiJS, which between them account for most 3D and high-performance 2D on the web, plus a no-code option in Construct 3. On the bonus criterion A is both more granular and better calibrated, attaching a per-engine outdated-risk rating with a stated reason and closing on the underlying principle that the safest bets are open source with no single-vendor dependency, whereas B assigns decimal scores out of ten that are precise without being derived from anything. A's judgements are also sharper where it counts: it flags Unity's WebGL target as a second-class citizen with heavy builds, poor mobile-browser performance and trust damage from the 2023 runtime-fee episode, and rates its web-specific risk as medium-high, while B calls the same pipeline mature and highly optimised and hands Unity a 9 out of 10, which is not defensible for web delivery specifically. {"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is the stronger design on every section the prompt names, and its advantages are substantive rather than merely longer. On idempotency it defines the piece B omits entirely -- a 409 when the same Idempotency-Key arrives with a different spec, which is the failure that actually bites in production -- plus the key namespace scoped to (api_key, key) so tenants cannot collide, a stated TTL with garbage collection, and a clear 201-versus-200 distinction between first submit and replay. On cancellation it separates QUEUED (immediate) from RUNNING (SIGTERM, configurable grace window, then SIGKILL), returns 202 with the explicit reasoning that the request completes when the signal is sent rather than when the process dies, makes repeat cancels no-op 200s on terminal jobs, and handles partial artifacts with a flag. B is internally inconsistent here: it calls cancelling an internal transient state and then returns it to the client, its state diagram has an unexplained running-back-to-queued edge, and it returns 409 for cancel on a completed job while returning 200 for cancel on an already-cancelled one, which breaks the idempotency of the operation it just described. B also rejects hard cancel outright on the grounds that it corrupts model state, which leaves no answer for a process that ignores the signal, whereas A's escalation path covers it. A's back-pressure separates the queue-depth gate from a per-key token bucket and argues clearly why a full queue is 429 rather than 503, and its observability offers polling, SSE, cursor-paginated logs backed by a ring buffer that spills to object storage, webhooks as an explicit optimisation rather than the primary channel (because a public client may have no reachable endpoint), and operator metrics. B rejects SSE in favour of webhooks on reliability grounds without confronting that gap. A additionally covers what B does not touch at all: cursor pagination under a mutating queue, artifacts and logs resources, a stable machine-readable error code with request_id, deprecation and Sunset headers with 410 after the window, tenant scoping that returns 404 rather than 403 to avoid leaking existence, and crash recovery. B is tidier and contributes a few good touches -- queue_position and eta in the submit response, queue-depth headers on every response, and sensible scope rejections around batching, multi-GPU and resume -- but it is a sketch beside a specification."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "On a question that is almost entirely about API correctness, B is the less wrong answer by a wide margin. B builds on the actual modern surface -- Mesh, PartitionSpec, NamedSharding to bind a spec to a mesh, and device_put to realise it -- and its gotchas and pattern tables (tensor, vocab, head and pipeline sharding, combining two mesh axes on one tensor axis via a tuple) are mostly accurate and immediately reusable. A repeatedly invents APIs that do not exist: shard_map.ShardSpec(spec, mesh) is used three times in place of NamedSharding, the Flax section decorates __call__ with param_with_axes and a nonexistent nn_partitioning.initializers and the wrong compact, and the pipeline section passes a resource_axis_names argument to pjit. A also specifies P('mp','mp'), sharding two axes of the same weight over a single mesh axis, which is not a legal partition spec, and repeats it. Its training loop takes jax.grad of a function whose out_specs is a per-device vector rather than a scalar, and its transformer block drops q while generating weights inside the forward pass from fixed PRNG keys. Most importantly, A inverts the central semantic distinction: it asserts that shard_map implicitly inserts the necessary collectives, when shard_map is precisely the manual mode in which the user writes psum and all_gather, and automatic insertion is what jit with NamedSharding does. B makes the mirror-image version of that same mistake -- calling jax.lax.psum inside a plain jax.jit, which requires a mapped axis context, and claiming that without it JAX errors or returns wrong results, when for its own spec (contracting dimension replicated) no reduction is needed at all -- so neither response has the duality straight. But B's error is one repeated idea inside otherwise-valid scaffolding, whereas A's code is unrunnable in most blocks and would mislead a reader about which functions exist. A's extra breadth on training loops and pipelining adds volume rather than value because that material is the least correct part of it."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "The prompt demands specificity about PACS, and specificity is only a virtue when it is correct -- which is where B collapses. Nearly every DICOM tag B cites is wrong or invented: it labels (0008,0051) as C-STORE when that is Issuer of Accession Number Sequence, offers (0054,0016) and (0054,0017) as AI Algorithm Name and Version when those belong to radiopharmaceutical information, repurposes (0042,0011) and (0042,0012) from encapsulated-document tags into SR identifiers, calls (0008,0100) Image Type when it is Code Value and then uses it to auto-select windowing, and calls (0008,0021) SOP Instance UID when it is Series Date. It uses WADO-URI to query for new studies, which WADO-URI cannot do (QIDO-RS is the query service, which A names correctly), proposes writing an SR by C-STORE to the same SOP Instance when an SR is necessarily a new instance, invents a Modality value of AI, cites a nonexistent EfficientNetV3-S backbone, and recommends middleware products (MIMIC-NAS, Rubik) that do not appear to exist. Its mediastinal and bone window values are also wrong. An engineer following B would burn days discovering the tags do not mean what they were told. A is specific in ways that hold up: QIDO-RS and WADO-RS for retrieval, a concrete comparison of Orthanc versus dcm4chee versus AWS HealthImaging with the right reasons, de-identification per PS3.15, a CPU preprocessing worker in front of GPU inference, realistic GPU sizing and queueing for a 500-to-2000-study day, and rendering results in the existing viewer rather than a new one. Its ML choices are also better reasoned -- ordinal urgency with CORAL so that grading a massive PE as routine costs more than the reverse, modality-specific low-rank adapters instead of per-modality retraining, patient-level splits, sensitivity at fixed specificity rather than AUC, and an explicit temperature-scaling calibration phase. B contributes two genuinely good ideas A underweights: the three-way deployment taxonomy (in-PACS plugin, middleware gateway, cloud bridge) with tradeoffs, and DICOM SR as the return artifact, which is more idiomatic than A's FHIR Observations. That is not enough to offset a PACS section built on fabricated identifiers. A's own lapses -- a stray reference to 92 COCO-style classes and loose VRAM figures -- are cosmetic by comparison."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is stronger on all three parts of the task. Its literature summary identifies mechanisms rather than just patterns -- activation outliers and kurtosis as the dominant practical driver, the Hessian/curvature formulation that GPTQ makes explicit, singular-value decay as a redundancy proxy, and the residual-stream write magnitude -- and it separately flags what is not settled, including the unstable ordering among Q/K/V/O across architectures and the open question of whether the ranking holds across scales. That calibration is exactly what the prompt asked for and B offers none of. B's central heuristic is the decisive weakness: ranking layers by the Frobenius norm of their weight matrix is not a sensitivity measure, because quantisation step size scales with the weight range, so relative reconstruction error is roughly scale-invariant and a large-norm layer is not thereby fragile; the real driver, which B's own summary gestures at, is the activation distribution multiplying those weights. B also declines to use a calibration forward pass at all, discarding the most informative available signal, whereas A treats weight-statistics-only scoring as an explicitly degraded fallback when no text exists. Worse, B's second validation check is circular: eight-bit layers will always show lower weight reconstruction error than four-bit ones and the top-k by Frobenius norm are the eight-bit set by construction, so the test can never fail and tells you nothing about whether the allocation was right. A's validation is substantive and mostly non-circular -- held-out perplexity delta with a stated acceptance band, mean logit KL and top-1 agreement rate with thresholds, generated-text divergence to catch compounding error that single-step KL misses, activation and spectral preservation checks, and best of all a sensitivity curve swept over k with the requirement that the chosen point sit near the knee, which genuinely can refute the allocation. A also pins embeddings, lm_head and norms outside the ranking for stated reasons, expresses the budget as a small integer program, and lists six assumptions each with the consequence of violation. Its flaws are minor by comparison: a few loose citation attributions, and a depth-sensitivity claim that sits uneasily beside the U-shaped picture B describes."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both open honestly by denying that a single formula exists and both converge on the same core answer -- niche down, land and expand, lean on partners, retain through QBRs -- so the separation is in depth and usability. B goes further in three ways that matter. It insists on ICP precision as a distinct step (revenue, headcount, stack maturity, specific pain, willingness to pay for managed versus break-fix) and then uses that ICP to filter outbound, partnerships and content, which is the mechanism that makes niching operational rather than aspirational. It couples GTM to delivery explicitly, arguing the motion only scales if onboarding is standardised, RMM/PSA automation is in place and SLAs are KPI-driven, and it names the actual tooling category, which is the kind of domain-specific detail that signals the writer knows the industry. And it closes with a concrete adaptation path -- the one-sentence positioning test, reverse-engineering an ICP from your top five existing clients, a ninety-day commitment to one channel plus one introducer, a single proof asset, and one weekly GTM metric -- which converts advice into a plan. Its pitfalls are also causal rather than listed, each tied to the consequence it produces, and the observation that technically strong MSPs underestimate the selling half of a service business is the sharpest line in either answer. A is cleaner and more scannable, and it owns one area B skips entirely: unit economics and pricing structure, including per-device versus per-user versus tiered packaging, a CAC payback window, an LTV-to-CAC target, and the well-reasoned point that hourly billing misaligns incentives in a managed model. That is a genuine gap in B. But it is one section against B's broader and more executable treatment, and both answers state their benchmark numbers without sourcing, so neither has a calibration advantage; B's only internal slip is that its pipeline-mix percentages in the prose and in the summary table do not quite match."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A's critique is the deeper one: it names non-transitivity explicitly, showing how a cyclic set of pairwise strengths gets crushed into a total order that hides exactly the dimension you care about; it separates capability from reliability, which a point estimate cannot represent; it frames benchmark optimisation as Goodhart in slow motion; and its error-bar argument is quantitatively right, since a 500-item eval does carry roughly a four-point interval, so ranking 72.4 above 72.1 is ranking noise. B's eight-row table covers similar ground plus two items A misses (cross-lab pipeline non-comparability, arbitrary aggregation weighting) but states them as assertions rather than mechanisms. The larger separation is in how uncertainty is actually presented, which the prompt asks for directly. A requires repeated runs and reports cross-run standard deviation alongside the bootstrap interval, so consistency is visible as a distinct property from the mean, and it instructs the writer to state in plain words when two models are statistically indistinguishable. B reports intervals but never tells the reader what to conclude when they overlap -- and in its own worked table the top two accuracy intervals do overlap while the recommendation text treats the gap as real, which is the precise failure mode the critique was about. A also pre-commits a decision rule before results are seen and then perturbs the threshold to report whether the recommendation flips, converting a fragile point choice into a robustness statement, and it catalogues the worst twenty examples per model with annotations, which is the evidence a reviewer six months later actually reads. B is broader in ways that matter and should not be dismissed: it covers latency, cost curves, integration fit and SLAs, which A omits entirely and which often decide a real selection; its evidence-grading scheme, with aggregation only within a grade and cross-grade comparisons flagged as informal, is a genuinely good idea for conflicting evidence; and its governance apparatus of triggers, rollback runbook and signed decision ledger is more complete than A's versioned repo and re-evaluation cadence. But B resolves conflicts with a fixed lexicographic priority order and a per-dimension Winner column, which quietly reinstates the ranking it set out to replace, whereas A keeps the trade-off as an explicit value judgement the team must make and defend. Statistical discipline is harder to retrofit than missing cost columns."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both open by denying a single formula and both land on niching as step one, but A explains mechanisms where B mostly enumerates practices. A's strongest contribution is productization, which B omits entirely: turning a vague we-will-manage-your-stuff engagement into fixed-scope, fixed-price tiers with defined SLAs, and the stated consequence that this collapses a six-month custom RFP into a two-to-four-week evaluation and gives content and inbound something concrete to point at. That is a causal chain, and pricing structure is a load-bearing part of any managed-services GTM that B never touches. A's channel table is also better reasoned, ordered by return with referrals and existing-client word-of-mouth first on the grounds of highest close rate and lowest acquisition cost, then partnerships that pre-sell for you, with outbound scoped realistically to a list of five hundred to two thousand ideal accounts rather than fifty thousand. B instead assigns forty to fifty percent of pipeline to outbound and never names referrals as a channel at all, which is a weak empirical claim for this industry, and its percentages are given with false precision and do not match between the prose and the summary table. A's closing insight -- that GTM here is a retention engine wearing a growth costume, that the first ninety days of a new client is the real GTM, and that most firms invert the right ratio of effort between new logos and existing accounts -- is the sharpest and most defensible observation in either answer, and it connects delivery quality to acquisition rather than treating them as separate sections. B is genuinely better in two places: its ICP definition is concrete where A leaves it implicit, and its five-step adaptation path with a weekly metric plus its consequence-linked pitfalls give a reader something to execute on Monday. Its delivery-led growth section with named RMM and PSA tooling also shows domain familiarity. But that is breadth against A's depth, and on the substance of what actually drives managed-services growth A is the more reliable guide."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both documents get the shape right -- cheap metadata triage, a load-and-sanity gate, a short battery, then progressively expensive stages -- so the decision rests on how mechanically enforceable each design is. A is far more concrete: every threshold is a named constant in a versioned YAML config, the stage budgets reconcile against a stated GPU-hour ceiling, and the pass rule is stated in a way that forecloses argument (0.39 passes, 0.41 fails, no eyeballing). Its answer to avoiding repeated work is the strongest section in either document: a content-addressed output cache keyed on weights hash, quantisation, prompt id and sampling parameters, so a re-release with an unchanged config is a full cache hit and a one-byte weight change forces a re-test with no ambiguity; incremental battery evaluation that generates only newly added prompt ids; and a known_results table whose primary key literally encodes the invalidation conditions. Its cross-model delta-testing shortcut is explicitly flagged as a heuristic with a per-model override. B's equivalent -- a lightweight predictor retrained weekly that lets you skip the benchmarks a model is predicted to pass -- is unsound, since not running the tests you expect to pass is how false positives get through, and weekly retraining on a handful of releases is not feasible. On honesty A is also better matched to the stated setting of one operator on one machine, designing controls that work without a second person to approve exceptions: pre-registration written into the log before the run, blinded and randomised human spot-checks, an asymmetric re-run policy, an explicit logged entry when a flagged favourite fails, and a quarterly battery audit against known-good reference models that catches the subtle case where the favourite is failing because a validator broke rather than because the model regressed. The end-of-week calibration note tracking whether the operator's enthusiasm predicts outcomes is a genuinely good idea. B contributes two things A does not: the crisp framing that a false negative is bounded because you can re-evaluate next week while a false positive is unbounded, and the Champion's Burden of re-running the incumbent every week as a pipeline control that invalidates the week if it fails. Its scenario-to-re-entry-stage deduplication table is also cleaner than A's prose. But B's Stage 3 rule contradicts itself, disqualifying on falling below the champion on any benchmark while promoting on exceeding the champion on at least one, its false-negative and false-positive rate targets are unmeasurable without ground truth it cannot have, and much of its honesty apparatus presumes a team with a rotating devil's advocate and independent approvers that the one-machine framing does not supply."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both responses cover the requested five layers and produce the two requested rankings, but A is the sounder and better-calibrated piece of work. A's ranking is internally consistent, it explicitly reconciles the two axes into an effectiveness-per-cost recommendation (the actionable payload the prompt implies), and it closes with the one genuinely important caveat -- that repetition penalties and loop detectors can truncate legitimate self-correction, so thresholds must be tuned against held-out good long traces. B is broader and its tables are denser, but the extra surface comes with real defects: the numeric scores (4, 4.5) are pseudo-precise with no stated basis, the 'By Expected Effectiveness' list is not actually sorted by its own scores (a 4.5 serving item sits at position 7 below several 4s), the 'zero-code fix' recommends editing the sampling function, and several entries are conceptually muddled -- the 'n-gram loop detector' is defined via rolling entropy, 'entropy-regularized sampling' is glossed as a bonus for low-probability tokens, and 'zero-quality impact if penalty is smooth' is an unsupported claim about exactly the quality constraint the prompt asked to protect. B also rates prompt-level loop-breakers at 4 with no acknowledgement that long-horizon instruction adherence decays, where A flags that failure mode directly. On reasoning soundness, clarity, and calibrated uncertainty A wins; B's edge in enumeration does not offset its inconsistencies."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both designs are competent and follow a sound discover-to-deliver arc with per-session deliverables, but B is the more runnable artifact. B gives timed agendas down to the block, and -- crucially -- specifies the mechanics of each exercise (the awareness x stakeholder 2x2, the 'When I / I want to / So that' JTBD prompts, rating sample copy 1-5 on four voice adjectives, rewriting the Big Idea per channel format, the hour-by-hour launch-morning role-play), so a facilitator could actually run it without inventing the method. A more often names a technique ('Socratic Questioning & Iteration', 'Data Specification', 'Kanban Style Review') without saying how it is run, which leaves the hard part to the reader. B also shows better calibration to the real constraint: it anchors the series to launch day (finish 6-8 weeks out, sessions 1-2 weeks apart), sizes and names the room, and hardens the plan with a readiness checklist, trigger thresholds on contingencies, and a T+1/T+4 feedback loop. A's genuine advantages -- explicit decision protocols (fist-of-five, disagree-and-commit), stakeholder power/interest mapping, go/no-go criteria, psychological-safety and hybrid-logistics notes -- are real facilitation craft and the main reason this is close, but they sit in a generic appendix rather than in the sessions, its cadence guidance (three weeks apart) is unmoored from the launch date, and the heavy emoji styling plus the closing sales pitch ('Shall we proceed with customizing Workshop 1?') add noise rather than clarity. On actionability and structure B wins; on facilitation meta-craft A does, and the former matters more for the brief as stated."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both build a cost model and both get the batch-size physics partly wrong, but A is substantially sounder. A uses the correct expected-accepted-tokens expression for sequential prefix acceptance, E = (1-a^k)/(1-a), whereas B uses E = k*p, which treats acceptances as independent and badly overstates yield at low p -- the single most important term in the whole analysis. B's headline 'key insight', that verification amortizes as v/B so at B=32 any acceptance rate above k*p > 0.05 wins, is backwards: batched decode does not divide per-sequence verification cost by B, and the well-known behaviour is that speculative decoding is strongest in the memory-bound small-batch regime and degrades as batch grows and decode becomes compute-bound. B then builds three tables and a decision tree on that inverted premise, which is actively misleading for the stated local-model case. B also leaves two unresolved 'Wait, that's not right, let me recalculate' passages with a superseded wrong table still in the text, argues incorrectly that a fast target model makes SD unprofitable (speedup is a ratio), and its 'refined' minimal experiment -- train a linear probe on the final hidden state to predict the token the model itself argmaxes at that position -- would simply re-learn the LM head and return acceptance near 1.0, so the centerpiece of its proposal does not work as written. A has real flaws of its own: setting v ~ k for k-token verification misses that verifying k tokens is one target forward pass, and its claim that larger batch helps by sharing prompt processing has the mechanism and the direction wrong. But A's impossibility conditions, its optimal-k discussion, its explicit go/no-go thresholds (S>1.1 build, S<0.9 skip, else pilot), and its hedged framing of rules of thumb make it more usable and better calibrated, and its entropy / top-1-probability proxy is a genuinely cheap, defensible predictor that needs no draft head -- exactly what was asked."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B is the stronger piece of research on every axis the rubric names. Its taxonomy is both wider and better carved -- nine families including GQA/MQA, low-rank/layer-shared KV, gist-token compression and token merging, all of which A omits or conflates -- and its citations are real and correctly attributed (H2O, SnapKV, PyramidKV, ToMe, AutoCompressor, ICAE, BigBird/Longformer), whereas A leans on several names that do not correspond to actual work ('LLM-Lion', 'Q-KV', 'CompressedKV', 'KVCache-Quant') and miscategorises LongRoPE/YaRN (context-window extension, not cache compression) and Ring Attention (which A itself concedes is not compression) inside a single grab-bag section. More importantly, B answers the 'what does it cost and where' half of the question mechanistically rather than with a generic percentage: the eviction scorer is myopic because attention mass is backward-looking, so a symbol declared early and needed late is silently dropped; quantisation error is uniform and compounding across layers rather than localised; sparse patterns cause targeted blindness; merging conflates parse(int) with parse(str). It also names the failure mode that actually governs the recommendation -- silent symbol loss, wrong-but-plausible identifiers -- and reasons from it. The recommendation follows from the analysis instead of stacking every technique: keep all tokens, reallocate precision asymmetrically using a cheap AST/syntactic pass rather than attention mass, retrieve cross-file KV with a code-aware retriever, use gist tokens as a pointer rather than a substitute, and an explicit avoid-list with reasons. A's recommendation is a laundry list of libraries to combine with little account of whether they compose, and its 'inject retrieved chunks' KV into the active window' glosses the positional-encoding problem that makes KV reuse hard. B is not flawless -- its closing arithmetic double-counts GQA as if it were a runtime lever rather than a property of the checkpoint you already chose, and the 80 GB to 2-5 GB figure is loose -- but these are quantitative sloppiness on top of correct structure, where A's errors are in the taxonomy and the evidence base."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both produce a usable scope-and-limitations section and both correctly mirror the three elements of the brief (repeatability, alignment-guide functionality, variation across dimensions and materials), but A is markedly deeper and more operational. A commits to how effectiveness will actually be measured -- radial and axial deviation, mean, standard deviation and coefficient of variation, n >= 30 per condition -- names a representative material set spanning hardness and machinability, and states that dimensional bounds are set by the tool's rated capacity and fixture limits, so a reader can tell what the study will and will not do. Its limitations are individually reasoned rather than generic: the measurement-resolution floor imposed by the available instruments (which bounds the smallest detectable deviation and is the single most important caveat for a precision study), the inability to separate the tool's contribution from residual operator variability, specificity to one drill press and its spindle runout, exclusion of interrupted-cut and high-feed dynamics, and the absence of any comparison against self-centering bits or CNC/laser positioning, which correctly disclaims any relative ranking claim. B is competently written and its single-paragraph scope matches conventional thesis style, but it stays at the level of category labels -- 'a variety of materials', 'standardized machine parameters', 'finite set of combinations' -- without specifying metrics, trial counts, materials, or instruments, and it omits the measurement-resolution and comparative-benchmark caveats entirely while listing tool wear and dynamic forces only in passing. B also mildly contradicts itself, folding operator technique into limitations without ever having scoped how operation is standardised. On depth, actionability and calibrated uncertainty A is the stronger document; B's only advantage is brevity, which the rubric discounts."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "These are both strong, correctly skeptical reviews that converge on the same verdict and share the core checklist -- SRM, pre-registration and multiple comparisons, daily treatment-minus-control time series, segment breakdowns, guardrails, confidence interval over p-value, phased rollout -- so the decision turns on the unique material each brings. A is the better review of *this* experiment because it reasons about the specific failure modes of a ranking change rather than a generic metric move: the position-bias confound (is the lift a relevance gain or just items shifted up the CTR-by-position curve, which is exactly how a ranking A/B manufactures a fake win), concentration/diversity collapse in the top-k, and supply-side externalities where traffic shifts away from newer sellers or creators and never appears in any user-level metric. It also carries the more usable decision apparatus: ordered gates with validity as a hard binary pass/fail before effect size is even discussed, an explicit requirement that the CI lower bound clear a practical threshold rather than zero, a cost-of-being-wrong comparison in both directions, and branch-by-branch ship rules including the segment-only ship. Its MDE-versus-observed-effect point and the demand for achieved power are correctly framed, and its SRM threshold (p > 0.01) is the conventional one, where B's p > 0.05 is loose. B is genuinely sharp and catches things A misses -- the stopping rule and sequential-peeking question, which is the single most likely explanation for a p of 0.03 landing at three weeks; partial weekly cycles from a mid-week launch; winsorization and bootstrap robustness on heavy-tailed metrics; latency as a guardrail; and the demand for an explainable mechanism. Those omissions are real and keep this close. But A covers more ground overall, its unique items are more specific to the system under test, and its ship framework is more decision-ready, so A takes it."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both are serious designs that cover all five requested areas, and A has genuine virtues -- the grace-window/cooldown/anti-thrash triple, the pre-swap lookahead that hides swap latency in the idle gap, the three-source cancellation table that distinguishes keep-partial from discard-partial semantics, and the 'one chart that shows 90% of your problems' (VRAM over time annotated with swap events and arrivals) which is exactly the right instrument for a single-box system. But B is more complete and more technically sound. B opens with an explicit contract table per traffic class (latency SLO, preemption rights, cancellation granularity, queue behaviour), which makes the scheduler rules derivable rather than asserted; it correctly notes that a KV cache is architecture-specific and therefore cannot survive a swap, so only the message list carries over and re-prefill is the real user-visible cost; it handles the case A omits entirely -- an interactive request arriving mid-load -- with an abort-versus-complete heuristic keyed to load progress; and it suspends rather than kills preempted benchmark work by saving kv_offset when the model is unchanged, which preserves expensive unattended compute. Its memory accounting is predictive at dispatch time rather than only at swap time, and it accounts for pinned CPU RAM used by spillover, a real exhaustion path A never mentions. Crucially for unattended benchmark traffic, B puts a data-corruption tier above liveness -- KV checksum on restore, per-token tagging to catch stale KV after preemption, weight-shard hashes against a manifest -- because silently wrong benchmark results are worse than a crash, and it adds ECC and thermal-throttle polling that would otherwise show up as inexplicable result drift. B also shows better calibration: it names and rejects the keep-a-small-model-resident trick with reasons, and closes by marking what is out of scope. A carries two real technical errors that B does not: it claims a 70B model 'generates a batch of 8-32 tokens per forward pass' and builds its cancellation-latency bound on that, when decode is one token per pass and batching is across sequences; and it sizes a 32k-token conversation's KV at ~2 GB on a 70B model, which is off by roughly 5x. B's own overclaims (a 6 GB device-to-pinned-RAM copy in 50 ms is well past PCIe bandwidth) are smaller and less load-bearing."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B is the stronger answer on every dimension that matters here. Its critique is mechanistic rather than a list of labels -- it names the compression from a high-dimensional performance surface to a scalar, works a concrete example of two models sharing an F1 of 0.847 with opposite error geometries, quantifies the illusion of precision (a 0.008 gap against a roughly +/-0.018 binomial CI on 5,000 examples), and adds the social point that leaderboard authority is an organisational artifact rather than an epistemic one. The proposed design then follows from the critique instead of quietly reinstating it: the Role Charter is written before any model is evaluated, asymmetric costs are stated as a ratio (1:200), hard constraints are pass/fail so a failing model is flagged as a different category of object rather than ranked, and the single expected-cost figure is *derived* from the role's cost structure and presented last, after the full profile. Several elements are genuinely original and hard to get elsewhere: the cross-model failure-overlap matrix and its direct implication for whether ensembling can help, the worst-5%-most-confidently-wrong analysis and whether those cases form a coherent type present in production, calibration framed as the primary input whenever a downstream workflow is confidence-gated, and stress evaluation on a different time period or source to separate fragile from robust winners. For the six-month test specifically, B records what was rejected and why, the acknowledged uncertainties with the numeric condition under which the ranking would flip, the revisit triggers, a named owner, and -- the best touch -- the dissenting view on record, which is exactly what the post-mortem question 'did we miss something?' needs. A is competent and has two things B lacks (an explicit weight-sensitivity sweep and a copy-paste template), but it has a structural problem it never acknowledges: its scorecard assigns fixed weights of 0.4/0.3/0.2/0.1, which is a weighted aggregate score in all but name, the very instrument it just critiqued. Its worked example is also internally inconsistent -- the scorecard shows B at 0.78 versus A at 0.81 on performance, while the trade-off matrix claims B beats A by +12% F2 in one place and by +3% in another, and a latency cell is missing entirely -- which undercuts the defensibility it is arguing for."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "The two designs cover nearly the same ground -- structure-aware chunking, content-hash incremental re-embedding, hybrid BM25 plus dense with RRF and cross-encoder reranking, prompt-level grounding with citations, claim-decomposition faithfulness judging -- so the decision turns on reasoning quality and the non-obvious moves. B reasons rather than lists: it justifies each choice with the failure it prevents (a fixed window slices a function in half and orphans a table from its caption; stuffing twenty chunks degrades attention and invites blending contradictory sources), and it pushes back on the premise, pointing out that 'daily' is a floor not a ceiling and that a nightly batch bakes in a 24-hour staleness window users will hit -- webhooks or a 15-minute poll instead. It contributes several things A lacks that materially change behaviour: parent-document expansion so a high-scoring fragment brings its sibling chunks and section outline (the direct fix for its own third failure mode), refusal calibration via few-shot 'I don't know' examples on the grounds that a model never shown a refusal will hallucinate to avoid one, a citation-accuracy check that verifies the cited chunk actually contains the claim (catching the model that cites plausibly while paraphrasing training data), and a regression harness with explicit pre-deployment gates on faithfulness, recall@10 and refusal precision. Its failure modes are argued with mechanism and ordering rationale -- staleness is first precisely because the window is invisible until someone deploys the wrong retry count -- and it closes with a defensible prioritisation: make the incremental indexing pipeline boring and observable before tuning the prompt. A is genuinely strong on operations and governance, and its RBAC-at-retrieval-time plus audit logging is a real omission in B for an internal corpus; the dead-letter queue, embedding versioning for rollback, drift monitoring, graph-based cross-reference boosting and launch checklist are all valuable. But A asserts a thicket of precise thresholds (0.35, 0.85, 20%, 60%, 15%) with almost no statement that they must be calibrated, proposes running RAGAS on every production query without acknowledging the cost, includes an inert metadata filter (last_modified < query_date), and -- most damagingly for an evaluation design -- proposes regenerating golden expected answers with an oracle LLM when docs change, which quietly converts the ground truth into model output and undermines the very test set it is meant to protect."}

Its only real blemish is a slight inconsistency between the stated three-week span and the weekly check-in cadence. A offers nothing comparable in depth, and its closing offer to expand is filler."}

A routes this through a custom_fields metadata table plus JSONB values, with soft-deactivate preserving data, an explicit cascade flag required for destruction, pg_advisory_lock against concurrent schema mutations, and a versioned record of each admin change -- avoiding user-driven DDL entirely. B instead proposes 'safe schema migration that adds columns without downtime', i.e. real DDL driven by admin input, and never addresses the injection, locking, or rollback exposure that creates. A's tickets carry endpoints with HTTP verbs and status codes, per-ticket estimates, dependencies and a Definition of Done, and cover genuinely hard details: optimistic locking with 409 on conflict, 202-plus-jobId for bulk with SSE progress and a dead-letter queue, idempotency keys, async audit writes, read-replica routing with failover, graceful degradation when Redis or Bull is down, load-test targets with p95 budgets, and a runbook. B's ticket lists are flat and vague by comparison ('implement permission checking middleware', 'create admin panel for managing database fields'), have no acceptance criteria, and duplicate admin user management across tickets 4 and 5 while re-opening RBAC in ticket 4 after ticket 2 already built it. B's library list also shows less care: pg-hstore is irrelevant to this stack, and it includes both rate-limiter-flexible and express-rate-limit for the same job. B's architecture diagram depicts three separate React SPAs per role, which contradicts its own single-app protected-route tasks and would triple the build. A is not flawless -- recommending express-mongo-sanitize in a SQL application is a real slip, repeated in the OWASP section -- and B contributes a password-reset flow and data export that A omits, but these do not offset the gap in rigor, actionability and soundness."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "A is a solid, well-organised checklist and covers the standard hazards -- peeking, multiple comparisons, novelty, Simpson's paradox, guardrails, power audit, forest plots across segments -- with a tidy four-way ship/monitor/don't-ship/extend matrix. But B does the sharper analytical work. It leads with a stated recommendation rather than deferring one, and it interrogates the number itself: it asks for the confidence interval instead of the p-value and shows why the answer changes the decision ([0.1%, 1.5%] versus [0.4%, 1.2%]), asks for the effect in standard errors and the achieved power, and demands the sample-ratio-mismatch chi-squared test *before* looking at any effect size -- the single highest-yield validity check in experiment review, and one A never mentions at all. It also asks the operationally decisive question A leaves implicit: what was the stopping rule, since a p of 0.03 landing at exactly three weeks is the classic signature of someone watching the dashboard until it crossed. B adds several checks absent from A -- launch-day alignment and partial weekly cycles biasing the estimate, winsorization and bootstrap for heavy-tailed metrics, experiment-layer interaction with concurrent tests, latency as a named guardrail, and a mechanism requirement with the correct justification that an unexplained lift will regress at full traffic. Its ship framework is quantitative where A's is qualitative: decide on whether the CI lower bound clears a pre-agreed minimum practically meaningful effect, extend with a pre-committed stopping rule if it straddles, soak at 10-20% with a kill switch when the mechanism is unclear, and escalate guardrail trade-offs to the product owner as a product decision rather than a statistical one. A's corresponding bar -- 'consistent across all segments' before shipping immediately -- is unrealistically strict, since segment estimates always scatter. B's only blemishes are minor arithmetic looseness ('one-third of a standard error' from the threshold is closer to a fifth) and the omission of Simpson's paradox and a long-term holdback, neither of which offsets its greater precision and decisiveness."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both correctly diagnose successes-per-hour as a throughput number masquerading as a capability number, but B's critique is mechanistic where A's is a list of headings. B constructs the decisive case -- two models with opposite profiles landing on the same rate -- and names the perverse incentive precisely: a model that loops for 55 minutes and then emits a correct three-line fix is *rewarded* by the metric, even though that loop is the runaway incident you were trying to detect. It also makes the distribution-sensitivity argument properly (the number is a property of the model x benchmark pair, not of the model) and supplies a failure-mode taxonomy mapping each mode to its distinct operational cost. The reporting scheme is where the gap widens. B's axes are populated with measures that are specific to coding agents and actually measurable: diff minimality against the gold diff, scope-creep outside the requested region, regression rate on previously-passing tests, multi-edit coherence, hallucinated APIs checked against a dependency manifest, abandonment rate, and a pass-rate-versus-prior-context curve for context degradation. Latency is decomposed into TTFT, throughput, steps-to-convergence and a planning-versus-emission split, which separates 'slow per token' from 'needs six attempts' -- exactly the confound the original metric creates. A's axes are largely generic (pass@k, fix-rate, ms/attempt, flag counts), and two entries are muddled: 'edit distance preservation' is defined as test-passing status, and 'iterative fix-rate' is defined as a percentage of models rather than of tasks. On the trade-off question, both use the right shape -- hard floors first, then explicit weights -- but B adds the more useful guidance: report shape rather than points, integrate the difficulty curve against *your* workload distribution rather than the benchmark's, treat the report as a data table rather than a verdict so it can be re-weighted without re-benchmarking, and track axes across versions to catch a silent edit-competence regression that a faster-on-easy-problems aggregate would hide. A's contributions that B lacks -- explicit Pareto-frontier language and weight sensitivity analysis at plus-or-minus 20 percent -- are real but narrow. B's one visible flaw is arithmetic: its worked example yields 3.6 successes per hour for both models, not 36, though the equality that carries the argument holds."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B does the actual intellectual work the prompt asks for. It establishes a crisp two-class taxonomy with the right asymmetry stated explicitly -- a mechanism predicts *what* will happen on new silicon, a verdict tells you *how much* -- and then supplies a falsifiable classification test ('would this still be true on an MI300X? true-but-different-number means verdict'), which is what makes the scheme usable rather than aspirational. It then partitions finding-by-finding and, crucially, allows split classifications: the peak-memory formula is a mechanism while the fits/does-not-fit conclusion is a verdict that can *reverse*; the FLOP/byte analysis is a mechanism while the operator-time ranking is a verdict; the existence of a thermal ceiling is a mechanism while its location is a verdict. It also catches the single sharpest trap in the whole exercise, which A gets backwards: model quality is only invariant at *identical numerical precision*, so a laptop FP16 evaluation does not transfer to an FP8 or FP4 server deployment, and the quality-versus-precision *curve shape* is the mechanism while the laptop's specific delta is not. A instead lists 'prompt-to-output consistency' and accuracy under 'no re-measurement required', which is exactly the error the report is meant to prevent, and it contradicts its own FP8/INT8 row a page later. On report design both propose gated sections and tagging, but B adds the two devices that do the real work: the cross-hardware table with an explicit Transfers? column telling the reader whether three numbers are three measurements of three machines or one property stated thrice, and the Discrepancy subsection that shows a carried mechanism's prediction against the server measurement with the quantitative reason (crossover batch moving 4 to 32 to 48 as the compute-to-bandwidth ratio changes). Its process guardrails are also better calibrated -- write mechanisms before verdicts so the separation is structural, pin every library version because a cuBLAS change is itself a verdict, run twice so a verdict has a spread, and do not assume B200 equals 1.67x H200 because the curve shape can differ. B is not flawless (its L2 figure for H200 is wrong, and the laptop envelope figures are loose), but A's hardware table misstates H200 and B200 memory bandwidth by roughly a factor of four and garbles a power figure, and A's transferable list contains the category error the whole study exists to avoid."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both correctly identify successes-per-hour as a throughput number wearing a capability costume, and both propose four separated axes with thresholds before trade-offs, so the decision rests on depth and on one structural disagreement. A's critique is sharper and covers ground B misses: the selection pressure the metric creates toward models that guess fast rather than reason carefully; the loss of partial credit (nine of ten tests passing scores identically to complete failure); the reward-hacking case where a model 'succeeds' by deleting the failing test; and the fact that correct-but-insecure code scores the same as correct-and-safe code. Its axis metrics are also more operational and more specific to the stated dimensions -- calibration via Brier/ECE, scope adherence measured by diff analysis, context retention compared at turn 15 versus turn 1, explicit negative-constraint ('change X but not Y') compliance, incremental-modification F1, the latency-versus-quality curve that tests whether extra thinking time actually buys anything, hallucinated-API rate, and whether the model escalates under uncertainty instead of guessing. A adds a methodological point B never makes and that matters a great deal in practice: edit competence and safety require *different* benchmarks and cannot be derived from the single-shot suite at all. The decisive difference is the treatment of runaway behaviour. A argues it is a gate rather than a trade-off axis -- disqualify below threshold, never let it be weighted -- and justifies it with exactly the failure mode at issue: otherwise a fast, capable model that occasionally destroys a production database can win a throughput contest. B instead folds a RunawayPenalty term into a weighted utility function, which permits precisely that compensation. A also closes better by insisting the report narrate the actual trade in prose so the decision-maker sees what is being given up. B is competent, and its unique contributions are real -- weight sensitivity analysis at plus-or-minus 20 percent, an explicit Decision Context section, and the observation that wall-clock rate is meaningless without a hardware tag -- but its metric definitions are looser and two are garbled ('edit distance preservation' defined in terms of test-passing status; 'iterative fix-rate' defined as a percentage of models rather than tasks), and its example table carries a stray percentile typo."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "This is close: A is broader and has the single best unique idea in either answer -- grading each piece of evidence on relevance, sample size, contamination risk and methodology transparency, with the rule that you aggregate only within a grade and flag cross-grade comparisons as informal signals -- plus a stronger governance apparatus (version hashes, archived raw outputs and eval code, an explicit list of re-evaluation triggers, a rollback SLA, stakeholder sign-off, a fillable template). But the prompt names two things specifically, uncertainty presentation and conflicting evidence, and B handles both better. {"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is the more soundly reasoned and internally consistent design, and it is the one an implementer could actually build from. Its status-code semantics are correct and justified rather than asserted: 429 with a computed Retry-After for a full queue with an explicit argument that 503 would wrongly signal a broken service, 202 for cancel-while-RUNNING because the request completes when the signal is sent and not when the process dies, and a 200 no-op for cancel on a terminal job, which is what makes cancel naturally idempotent. It separates the two distinct back-pressure surfaces (queue-depth gate versus per-key token bucket) and correctly notes that zero free GPU slots is not itself a back-pressure condition. Its idempotency contract is complete in the ways that matter in practice: namespaced by (api_key, key), a TTL with GC, 201 on first write versus 200 on replay, and a 409 when the same key arrives with a different spec, which is the specific footgun most designs miss. It also reasons cleanly about why the idempotency key and the resource id are orthogonal concerns, exposes CANCELLING so clients can distinguish draining from done, defines a grace period with SIGTERM then SIGKILL, and handles partial artifacts with an explicit flag. The rejected-tradeoffs section is the best part of either answer: ten entries, each naming a concrete mechanism (gRPC-Web needs a proxy; DELETE implies resource removal but the record must persist for audit; priority queues let one tenant starve others on a single GPU; per-GPU endpoints force clients to make placement decisions the scheduler owns), rather than generic pros and cons. B covers the same checklist but is noticeably looser and contradicts itself repeatedly. It returns 409 Conflict for a full queue in the back-pressure section while its own rejected-tradeoffs row claims the design uses 429 back-pressure. It returns 409 for a cancel on an already-terminal job, which breaks the idempotent-cancel property it claims two paragraphs earlier and forces clients to special-case a benign race. It models cancellation as PATCH with an {\"action\": \"cancel\"} body, which is RPC tunnelled through PATCH, while a rejected-tradeoffs row specifically dismisses RPC-style verbs for breaking REST discoverability. It has /v1/ready return 503 when the queue is merely saturated, which would pull the instance out of load-balancer rotation for an entirely healthy condition. Smaller problems compound: snake_case URLs paired with camelCase bodies for no stated reason, an unmotivated PENDING state distinct from QUEUED, a muddled transition diagram, a client-facing POST .../result upload endpoint that does not belong on this surface, Idempotency-Key mis-cited to RFC 7231, an overclaim of exactly-once submission where at-most-once within a TTL is what is actually delivered, and a deployment note about an 'embedded SQLite/Vectorized job store' that is not a coherent thing. B's observability section is respectable and its OpenTelemetry tracing is a genuine addition A lacks, but A's SSE-versus-WebSocket argument, ring-buffer-then-object-storage log path, cursor pagination chosen because the queue mutates concurrently, and signed webhooks as an explicit optimisation rather than the primary channel are deeper. {"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is both more accurate about the literature and more coherent as a procedure. It works at the right granularity - per weight matrix rather than per layer - and gets the within-block ordering right (FFN down-projection and attention output projection more fragile than Q/K/V, norms kept in full precision), while also offering a mechanism rather than just a list: boundary matrices like the embedding and LM head have no downstream layers over which independent quantisation noise can average out, which is exactly why middle blocks tolerate 4-bit. It states the budget as an explicit constraint with the bit-accounting equation, force-protects the embedding and LM head regardless of measured score, and then adds a swap-based local refinement pass justified by the observation that per-matrix scores measured in isolation do not perfectly predict joint degradation - which is also declared as an explicit additivity assumption rather than assumed silently. Its validation section is the decisive advantage. Beyond held-out perplexity on a corpus disjoint from calibration and FP-versus-mixed logit KL and top-k agreement, it proposes validating the proxy itself: measure the actual per-matrix perplexity increase and check Spearman rank correlation against the sensitivity scores that drove the allocation, with an explicit fallback (switch from logit-MSE to Hessian trace) if the correlation is poor. It adds an ablation confirming the force-protected matrices really do degrade disproportionately, and a stability check requiring high overlap in the chosen 8-bit set across calibration resamples. That is a genuinely well-calibrated, label-free validation design. B covers the same ground at a shallower level and contains several real defects. Its central allocation rule in Step 5 is garbled: it upgrades a layer to 8-bit and then keeps it at 8-bit 'if the loss/KL increase exceeds a threshold', but upgrading precision should reduce loss, so the acceptance criterion is inverted and the parenthetical '<0.5% of baseline' contradicts the word 'exceeds'. Its sensitivity ordering contradicts itself - the prose says early MLP layers degrade faster while middle-to-late MLPs tolerate 4-bit, then the ranked pattern in Step 4 places Late-FFN above Early-FFN. It labels the activation second-moment matrix a 'weight-Fisher approximation', conflates a perplexity-point reduction with a percentage loss increase in its success criterion, and closes by claiming the mixed config should beat uniform 4-bit 'while keeping the same model size', which is false since 8-bit layers cost more. Its budget handling is vestigial - the threshold rule and the bit-budget stop condition are never reconciled - and the included validation script computes a single loss value while the comparison logic lives only in a comment. B does have modest merits: it names outlier density and activation-range statistics as cheap proxies, notes that per-channel or per-token scaling changes attention-layer tolerance, and includes the same cross-subset stability check. But on soundness, internal consistency, and the rigour of the validation plan, A is clearly ahead. A's own small slip - implying GPTQ's diagonal Hessian comes from a backward pass when it is built from activation second moments - is minor by comparison."}

On chunking, B handles document normalisation first, makes code blocks and table rows atomic by snapping split boundaries even at the cost of oversized chunks, serialises table rows with their column headers so a row is self-contained when retrieved alone, and adopts parent-child indexing so small chunks drive vector similarity while the generator receives the surrounding section. A's hierarchical chunking is reasonable but stops at description. On retrieval, B specifies fusion concretely (RRF with k=60, explicitly justified by dense and sparse legs ranking differently) and adds two things A lacks entirely: a query-understanding stage that rewrites colloquial phrasing and infers metadata filters, and a calibrated confidence gate that refuses rather than forcing an answer. Its grounding section enforces citations by post-processing rather than trusting the prompt, adds a contradiction-flag rule for conflicting retrieved values, and a recency-preference rule keyed to doc_version - all three directly motivated by a daily-changing corpus. Its evaluation is layered and falsifiable: per-sentence NLI entailment with a numeric target, citation-precision checks that catch fabricated tags, a 500-question gold set stratified by intent including a 'changed last week' stratum with forbidden-claim lists, a judge model deliberately different from the generator to avoid self-bias, and a regression page threshold. A's three are plausible but loosely reasoned, and its third conflates context-window overload, failure to prune vectors, and outright hallucination into one item with a hand-wavy root cause. B's three are mechanistically specific, timed, and each carries mitigations that engage the design above: the staleness case distinguishes the read-during-reindex race from the harder case of old and new versions coexisting and returning contradictory chunks, and fixes it with version-aware retrieval plus a canary shadow pipeline against the previous snapshot; the recall-gap case correctly predicts that a gold set written in document vocabulary will mask failures on colloquial user phrasing, and traces the failure through RRF and the reranker to a false refusal; the confabulation case identifies the subtlest real problem - one relevant chunk among five near-misses, blended into a fluent cited answer that NLI scores 'neutral' rather than 'contradiction' and so passes automated checks - and answers it with a per-chunk relevance floor below the refusal threshold, per-doc-type NLI calibration where 'neutral' is a failure for config docs, and at least 30 percent refusal examples in the fine-tuning set so the refusal path is not under-trained. Its standout contribution is making contamination a first-class control throughout, culminating in Experiment 4's decisive test - hold out post-cutoff sources and check whether preference training reduces hallucination on documents the model could not have memorised. A states plainly that if post-cutoff rates drop while in-distribution rates do not, the model learned a shortcut rather than a principle, and pre-commits to pivoting to a retrieval-grounded reward model in that case. That is the single best-designed piece of inference in either agenda, and B has no equivalent. A's conditional branching is genuinely conditional rather than a fixed roadmap: which sub-type dominates in Experiment 1 determines whether Experiment 2 targets grounding or abstention; whether verifier precision clears roughly 0.9 determines whether Experiment 4 aims at training the generator or at strengthening the verifier. A also anticipates the specific perverse outcome that structured-output gating drives fabrication to zero by construction while raising misattribution because the model picks the nearest retrieved document, and it pairs every abstention metric with a false-abstention cost so a system that refuses everything cannot score well. Its final experiment is a proper 2x2x2 factorial motivated by the expectation that interventions interact non-additively, with a trust-versus-accuracy correlation designed to surface the uncomfortable possibility that users cannot detect misattribution. B is impressive in other ways and is not far behind. It names real seed corpora (QASPER, PubMedQA, CaseHOLD, CourtListener), specifies dataset sizes and construction procedures more concretely, adds a metadata-corruption failure type A folds into fabrication, supplies per-domain calibration with ECE, and contributes an adversarial dimension A lacks entirely - corpus poisoning, metadata manipulation, multi-hop grounding - plus an eight-week expert beta and a clean handoff-trigger table. {"choice": "B", "rationale": "B gets the physics right and A gets it backwards, which decides this regardless of presentation. B captures this with an explicit arithmetic-fraction term phi(B), derives T_v = T_t[1 + (K-1)phi], and then proves the sharp result that in the fully compute-bound limit the requirement becomes E[accepted] > K + r, which is impossible since E[accepted] is bounded by K - so speculative decoding can never pay off there no matter how good the draft head is. That is the single most useful statement in either answer and A does not have it. A instead writes Speedup = k*p / (D/T + v/B), amortising verification cost by dividing by batch size, and concludes the exact opposite: that large batches make speculation easier, that at B=16 a 4 percent acceptance rate yields 1.8x, and that 'multi-token heads work so well at batch sizes >= 4'. This inverts the real regime and would lead a reader to enable speculation precisely where it hurts. A also models accepted tokens as k*p, ignoring that acceptance is sequential and one rejection discards every later position; B uses the correct geometric expectation alpha(1-alpha^K)/(1-alpha), tabulates it, and flags the cliff below alpha ~= 0.5 as the usual reason a model sometimes speeds up and sometimes regresses. A's answer is also visibly unpolished, containing two abandoned derivations left in the text ('Wait - that's not right' and 'Wait, that's too high'), including a proposed acceptance proxy (mean max probability) that it introduces, plugs in to get a nonsensical 6x, and then discards. On the requested minimal experiment B is again stronger and more faithful to the constraint 'before building its draft head': one teacher-forcing pass over calibration data yields the target's own K-step self-continuation accuracy, which is the correct ceiling on any drafter since an MTP head is a lossy compression of the target's own prediction; two short timing benchmarks give r and phi; a stated 0.85 discount converts the ceiling to expected head-level acceptance, with an honest note that this factor is the only approximation and can be tightened with a single-layer probe if the estimate lands near breakeven. It closes by stratifying calibration across code, prose and chat to explain the 'sometimes fast, sometimes slow' observation directly and suggests gating speculation on a cheap runtime logprob signal. {"choice": "B", "rationale": "B is substantially more expert and more useful. Its three-way decomposition of quality-per-parameter (per total, per active, per memory byte) is the crux of the question and resolves it cleanly, and its decision tree is grounded in a measured M after subtracting OS/runtime/KV cache, with a named crossover (~32 GB) and a directive to profile TTFT and inter-token latency on the actual chip rather than trusting paper numbers. A is well-organised and reaches a similar bottom line, but it is shallower and contains a serious factual error — stating Mixtral-8x7B has 1.6T total parameters, off by more than an order of magnitude — and it repeatedly confuses MoE conditional computation with hardware structured-sparsity kernels, framing MoE viability as requiring 'sparse-aware kernels' and data-center sparse hardware, which misdiagnoses the actual bottleneck. B's own Mixtral total-parameter figure is also inflated, but its reasoning chain and the ratios it depends on remain internally consistent, and its hardware guidance (unified memory, llama.cpp/MLX per-tensor precision) is concrete and correct where A's is misdirected."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A demonstrates markedly better command of the actual mechanics. It gets the single most important correctness fact right and reasons from it: a KV cache is architecture-specific, so it cannot survive a model swap, and therefore the only thing that persists is the message list plus a re-prefill cost — which A then names as the dominant user-visible penalty and designs around (spill to pinned CPU RAM synchronously, NVMe asynchronously, because the user is watching a spinner only during the swap). B never confronts this and instead implies KV caches survive swap-out/swap-in, with a swap cost model built on torch.save of model state to disk, which is not how weight loading works and would be absurdly slow. A's traffic-class contract is precise (I is never preempted by B but may be suspended; B is suspended at a token boundary rather than killed, and resumes from kv_offset only when the model is unchanged), it handles the genuinely hard case of an I-request arriving mid-load with an explicit abort-vs-complete heuristic, and it correctly forbids mid-token cancellation because it would corrupt the KV cache.
