B is organized and its failure-mode table is a reasonable list, but it is shallower throughout and contains real defects: the watermark table is internally inconsistent (High is '60-85% VRAM free' while Critical is '<85% free', which overlaps and inverts), the swap logic conflates traffic classes with models ('current_model == interactive'), it asserts an unearned '≤200ms, measured in benchmarks' bound, and it recommends PagerDuty alerting for a single local machine. A covers blinding and override logging too, but its statistical guard is confused (a chi-square over pass/fail distributions flagging favourites with 'unusually high pass rates' does not test the bias it claims to), and its trivial-task gate demanding 3/3 exact answers is brittle enough to disqualify capable models on formatting. {"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is the more rigorous and internally consistent design. Its state machine is fully specified as a transition table with explicit triggers and declared terminal states, and it covers the case B omits entirely — validation failure moving pending to failed. Its idempotency section handles the subtle part correctly: a replayed key returns the original job and, critically, replays the original validation error rather than re-running the request. Its cancellation semantics are the most operationally honest part of either answer: DELETE returns 202-style 'cancelling, poll for final state', SIGTERM followed by a bounded grace period and then SIGKILL, with grace_period_seconds exposed as a query parameter so the client can trade cleanliness against latency, plus a cancellation-latency histogram to observe whether the grace period is well-chosen. Back-pressure is a 503 with Retry-After and queue-depth headers, with a separate queue-state model (open/full/paused) that gives the operator a drain switch. The rejected-tradeoffs section — which the prompt explicitly demands — is where A wins decisively: it rejects priority queues on starvation grounds, job chaining on state-complexity grounds, webhooks on delivery-guarantee grounds, blocking POST on connection-exhaustion grounds, and in-response results on caching/streaming grounds, each with a reason specific to a single-GPU host rather than generic REST doctrine. B's rejected table is shorter and several entries are strawmen (metric-only observability, RPC verbs). B also contains real self-contradictions: section 5 returns 409 Conflict for a full queue while its rejected-tradeoffs table claims the design uses 429 back-pressure; cancellation of a job already in CANCELLING is specified as 409 Conflict in the state-check list and then as a de-bounced 202 two paragraphs later; and it rejects RPC-style verbs while modelling cancel as PATCH with an action field, which is precisely RPC-over-REST. Smaller errors compound: Idempotency-Key is attributed to RFC 7231 (it is an IETF draft, not part of 7231), the naming convention arbitrarily mixes snake_case URLs with camelCase bodies, and 'embedded SQLite/Vectorized job store' is not a coherent thing. B does have three genuine advantages A lacks — OpenTelemetry tracing with nested spans, per-client token-bucket rate limiting with the standard X-RateLimit headers, and bearer-token auth scoped per tenant — and its split of /health from /ready is the correct Kubernetes-style distinction, which A collapses into one endpoint. Those are real gaps in A, but they do not outweigh B's contradictions and the substantially thinner treatment of the lifecycle, idempotency edge cases, and rejected alternatives."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both propose a multi-signal weighted score with a hybrid/review band and an upgrade path to a small supervised model, but A's signals are sounder and its formulas actually point the way they claim. The decisive difference is the referential dimension: A defines in-degree (tables that FK-reference this one) minus out-degree (FK columns it contains) and correctly identifies master as the hub with high in-degree and low out-degree. B's Referential Connectivity Ratio counts 'records that foreign-key reference another table' — an out-degree measure, which is the transactional signature — yet assigns master a threshold above 0.7 and justifies it with an inbound example (one customer to many orders). That is a directional contradiction at the heart of the strongest structural feature. B's entropy treatment has the same problem: it asserts master data has low entropy because keys are 'dense, controlled', but a customer or SKU master key is maximally high-entropy by construction, whereas a transactional table's status or type columns are low-entropy; A gets this right by distinguishing descriptor columns (low entropy) from event-id columns (very high entropy) and by looking at the distinct-value-ratio profile across all columns rather than one hand-picked key. A also contributes signals B lacks that a practitioner would actually find discriminating: insert-to-update ratio and append ratio, row growth rate, the presence of effective-dating columns (valid_from/valid_to) as an SCD marker, and the time-of-day entropy of created_at to separate batch-loaded reference tables from continuously arriving events — a genuinely clever and cheap feature. Its caveats are the sharper ones too: small tables are statistically indistinguishable so prefer rate-based metrics, run over a window rather than a snapshot, and expect an SCD-type-2 bucket between the two classes. B offers copious numeric benchmarks (UFR under 5% per month, RSI over 0.85, TDR over 0.95, H under 2.5 'on a 0-10 scale') presented as derived from typical enterprise data but with no stated basis, which is false precision rather than calibration; several are also self-undermining, since master rows almost always carry created/updated timestamps so its TDR numerator would be near 1, and its 'mean time-span of records' term is undefined. B's SQL sketch is not executable (FROM your_schema.*), and its RSI symmetric-difference formula is stated loosely. B does have real merits — a clean end-to-end workflow, the recommendation to emit a probability distribution rather than a binary label, and a steward spot-check with an 80% agreement acceptance bar — and A is not flawless (its composite mixes unnormalised terms such as in_degree minus out_degree with ratio-scaled ones, and its surrogate-versus-natural-key heuristic is dubious since surrogate keys are standard in dimension tables). On balance A is more accurate, more insightful, and more directly usable."}

The ship framework is also better: it is built on a minimum practically meaningful effect that the business defines, it distinguishes four distinct situations with different actions (ship, extend with a stopping rule committed in advance, partial rollout with a kill switch and a four-to-six-week soak to watch for decay, or escalate a guardrail trade-off to the product owner as a product decision rather than a statistical one), and it correctly frames 'three weeks elapsed' as no reason to stop an underpowered test. A covers the standard ground — confidence interval, power, temporal consistency, subgroups, multiple comparisons, business impact — and makes one genuinely good catch B does not: that '0.8 percent' is ambiguous between percentage points and relative lift, which materially changes the interpretation. But A is thinner on guardrails, has no SRM or peeking check, no concurrent-experiment or outlier robustness analysis, and no mechanism requirement, and it contains a muddled statistical claim that an underpowered test 'can yield p = 0.03 even for trivial effects' — the actual hazard is the opposite, that significant results from underpowered tests systematically exaggerate the effect. On cancellation, A uses POST /cancel returning 202 for the running case, reasoning that the request completes when the signal is sent rather than when the process dies, and rejects DELETE because the job record persists for audit and artifacts; B uses DELETE and returns 200 alongside a state of 'cancelling', which asserts synchronous completion it has not achieved. A's idempotency contract is materially more complete: keys namespaced by (api_key, key) so tenants cannot collide, a TTL with garbage collection, 201 on first write versus 200 on replay, and - the rule B omits entirely - 409 when the same key arrives with a different spec, which is the only thing preventing a silent spec swap under a reused key. A also separates the client's dedup handle from the server's identity and justifies server-minted UUIDv7 for free creation-time ordering. Beyond those, A covers ground B leaves empty: auth and tenant scoping with cross-tenant 404 rather than 403 to avoid leaking existence, a per-key token bucket distinct from the queue gate, cursor pagination justified by concurrent queue mutation, absolute deadlines with distinct semantics depending on whether expiry occurs while queued or running, partial-artifact flagging when a process is killed mid-write, crash recovery with a rebuilt queue and a runner_crash failure reason, and a real deprecation policy with Deprecation and Sunset headers, a migration link and 410 after sunset. Its rejected-tradeoffs table is both longer and better argued, and it anticipates and refutes B's own choices. B is competent and has a few things A lacks - queue position surfaced to the client, an admin 'paused' queue state, and useful metrics for cancel latency and queue wait time - but several of its arguments are weak or self-contradictory: it rejects SSE because it is 'awkward for bidirectional operations like cancellation' when cancellation is a separate request, it rejects client-generated idempotency keys and then specifies exactly that, it models a validation error as a job transitioning pending to failed rather than a synchronous 422, and it routes unversioned /jobs to the latest version, which invites silent breakage in a public API. A's only real blemish is an internal inconsistency where the job GET echoes the full spec while the tradeoffs section says it returns a spec reference instead."}

Both contain a directional mistake, but B's sits in the axis it itself calls the strongest signal and is self-contradictory within a single table: it labels a high insert-to-update ratio a master signal and constant churn transactional, which is backwards (transactional rows are inserted and thereafter immutable; master rows are few but repeatedly amended), and then two rows later correctly says a high append ratio is transactional. Its update-frequency-per-row row is reversed the same way, and the composite temporal score inherits both, so the highest-weighted term points the wrong way. B's cardinality claim that master tables have low average distinct-value ratio is also doubtful, since a small entity table's key and name columns approach a ratio of one while a large fact table is dominated by low-ratio foreign keys. A's error is real but localised: its normalised timestamp entropy is defined and interpreted backwards, since a normalised Shannon entropy is one when uniform and zero when concentrated, and it also has a garbled cell claiming transactional tables are referenced by master, which contradicts both the adjacent in-degree row and its own foreign-key ratio rule. It supplies override heuristics for exactly the cases a statistical score will get wrong - fewer than fifty rows means defer rather than guess, a pure lookup with tiny per-column cardinality is reference data, a monotonic surrogate key whose timestamp advances in lockstep is an event log, and valid_from/valid_to/version means slowly-changing dimension and therefore master - where B only notes in prose that such hybrids exist. It specifies validation on roughly two hundred manually labelled tables with a per-class F1 target before production trust, a monthly drift monitor that alerts when a table flips class because that usually signals a schema change, and an explainability contract emitting the five sub-scores plus the top contributing columns so a steward can audit the label. It also addresses cost, noting that catalogue statistics plus a stratified sample of five to ten thousand rows suffices for every calculation, names where the job runs in a data-quality pipeline, prescribes how to tune the weights against the holdout, and shows how the framework extends to a third reference-data class. But it undermines that with three serious defects. Its core formula, E = (1-(1-AR)^N)/AR, is structurally wrong (the accepted-prefix expectation is the geometric sum AR(1-AR^N)/(1-AR)) and it contradicts its own stated limit: at AR to 1 the given expression yields 1, not N, and the rest of the answer silently reverts to a crude AR*N linearisation. It then inverts the batch-size economics, which is the decisive qualitative fact here: decode at small batch is memory-bound, so verifying several tokens costs barely more than one, and the advantage shrinks as batch grows and the target becomes compute-bound. {"choice": "A", "rationale": "A gets the physics essentially right and B gets it backwards. A uses the correct expected-tokens-per-step identity mu = (1-alpha^(K+1))/(1-alpha), which includes the free token the verify pass always emits, separates the memory-bound from the compute-bound regime, and reaches the correct headline conclusion -- speculative decoding is a small-batch, memory-bound win whose margin collapses as the batch drives the verify pass into the compute-bound regime where the extra K positions cost real FLOPs. It also identifies the single most useful practical insight in either answer: that the per-position acceptance curve alpha_j decays, so a healthy alpha_1 can coexist with a mu far below the uniform-alpha prediction, and that this is the usual reason a deployment underperforms its projection. B's core equation, Speedup = k*p/(D/T + v/B), is wrong in two load-bearing ways. It models accepted tokens as k*p rather than the geometric sum and drops the guaranteed bonus token, and it divides the verification cost by batch size while leaving the baseline un-amortized, which is a category error since batching amortizes weight streaming identically for the no-speculation baseline and cancels out of the ratio. That error propagates to B's central claim -- that at B=32 you need only k*p > 0.05 and 'even terrible acceptance rates give speedup' at large batch -- which inverts the well-established result and would send an engineer to enable speculation in exactly the regime where it hurts. B is also visibly unfinished: it prints a table, says 'Wait - that's not right. Let me recalculate,' prints a contradictory one, proposes mean-max-probability as an acceptance proxy, computes a 6.08x speedup, says 'Wait, that's too high,' and abandons the method, leaving the reader to sort out which numbers survive. Both converge on a linear probe on target hidden states as the minimal pre-build experiment, but A specifies it far better: it measures consecutive acceptance per position rather than a single scalar accuracy, argues correctly that the linear probe lower-bounds any non-linear head so a pass is a guarantee and a wide miss is a genuine stop, insists on the deployment distribution rather than a generic benchmark, and terminates in an explicit go / gate-on-batch-size / do-not-build decision table. A is not flawless: its boxed compute-bound formula K*mu/(K+rho_c) contradicts its own numerical table (which correctly computes roughly mu/(K+rho_c) and shows slowdowns), and the 'compute-bound is easier to make profitable' aside and the alpha_c = 0.045 figure that follow from it are wrong. But that is one inconsistent subsection inside an otherwise correct analysis, whereas B's error is in the fundamental equation from which it says everything follows."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both correctly identify that the discriminator is progress rate rather than elapsed time, but B actually solves the problem the prompt poses while A only restates it. B's stall rule is self-calibrating -- time_since_last_token > k x the median ITL measured from that request's own first ~50 decode steps -- which is the key idea, because it simultaneously catches a 15ms/token request that goes silent for 150ms and refuses to fire on a request that was always at 200ms ITL under a large batch, and it never fires on a 4096-token generation at steady rate no matter how long it runs. A instead hardcodes absolute thresholds (no token for 8s, TPS below 0.5) that are wrong for any model or batch regime other than the one they were tuned on and that will page on healthy slow generation on a loaded server. B also handles the parts A skips: a separate prefill-phase rule because ITL does not exist yet there, a spec_stall detector keyed on repeated zero-acceptance verify rounds that diagnoses draft-model divergence, and a spec_speedup metric that catches speculation making things slower rather than only measuring acceptance rate -- directly on point for this server's architecture. On alerting, B uses multi-window multi-burn-rate SLO burn on per-step ITL with an explicit page/ticket/dashboard tiering, requires correlation between a request-level and a system-level signal before escalating, suppresses TTFT alerts under known-good conditions, and excludes user_cancel and oom_reject terminations from SLO math; A's 'two of N conditions over a 2-minute window' plus rate limiting is a reasonable but much blunter instrument, and it still pages on memory above 95 percent and on throughput collapse with no correlation requirement. B is the only one to treat the memory cap as architecturally distinctive, separating slow occupancy creep (alert on regression slope over an hour, not a level) from eviction thrashing (eviction rate above zero AND hit rate below 0.5), and correctly assigns both to ticket tier unless they coincide with a stall. B alone addresses cardinality and cost, with an in-process ring buffer serialized into a span only at request completion or stall, and raw ITL series shipped only for the slowest requests. A's advantages are real but secondary -- a concrete tool stack and operator runbooks -- and its PromQL examples are not merely illustrative but incorrect: rate(generation_itl_seconds_count[8s]) > 0 is the inverse of the 'no token progress' condition it claims to express, and taking rate() of an acceptance-rate gauge is meaningless."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "The question asks for a software architecture, framed by what a winning business strategy demands, and A is the only one that actually designs the thing while B mostly names its layers. Its strongest move is empirical rather than assertive: it dissects how three incumbents actually won or fought -- CUDA plus cuDNN/NCCL/TensorRT and a decade of ecosystem compounding, XLA co-designed with JAX and sold through GCP, and AMD's HIP source-compatibility plus open-source ROCm as a fast-follower wedge -- which is the single most useful piece of strategy analysis in either response, and it yields the sharper conclusion that first-class PyTorch integration is non-negotiable and that vLLM and Hugging Face are now part of the required surface. Its lead principle, framework-agnostic by default, is also the weaker strategic read and is contradicted by the very incumbent history A documents, where the winners bet hard on one programming model or one framework. A's flaws are real but localized: the ASCII diagrams carry little information for their bulk, section 1 mislabels the whole-stack picture as the driver layer, and the PyTorch and JAX snippets are invented rather than real APIs (registration goes through the PrivateUse1 backend and a Dynamo backend, not torch.classes.register_library or a torch._C.Device subclass). {"choice": "B", "rationale": "B is stronger on every axis the prompt names, and A contains a disqualifying logic error at the exact point the question centers on. A's is_stalled pseudocode returns True only when system GPU utilization exceeds 0.9, so the canonical stall -- a hung kernel, an idle GPU, and an in-flight request producing nothing -- falls through every branch and is reported healthy; the detector is inverted relative to the failure it exists to catch, and the same function is wired directly to a PAGE row in the alert table. A also uses a fixed 30-second silence threshold, which is simultaneously too slow for a 25ms-per-token model and too aggressive under heavy batching, and it pages per-session with no deduplication, cooldown, or auto-resolve. B instead makes the stall threshold baseline-relative (time_since_last_token > N x p50 ITL for this model at this batch size, N drawn from the p99.9 of the healthy ITL distribution), which is the correct construction because it automatically tracks batch-size and model changes and structurally cannot fire on a long-but-steady generation. B then refuses to rely on that one signal, cross-checking GPU SM utilization and kernel liveness, KV tokens allocated per step, and batch membership continuity to catch a request orphaned by the scheduler after an eviction, and requires any two of those conditions for more than two seconds before declaring a stall. Both correctly reason that a collapsed acceptance rate is degradation rather than a stall, but only B grades it across a ladder from healthy to degraded to pathological to draft-hung and routes each to the right severity. B's granularity answer is genuinely engineered rather than asserted: it justifies one record per decode step as the atomic unit of progress, estimates the resulting 250 to 1000 records per second, and specifies ring-buffer plus rollup retention per layer to keep that affordable. Its alerting section contains the two best ideas in either response: an explicit anti-alert table codified as suppression rules so that total duration, session age, and token count cannot be re-added by a well-meaning engineer, and error budgets burned by stall and OOM events rather than by request count, so a 120-second generation with uniform 25ms ITL costs nothing. The implementation notes close the loop with the detail A misses entirely -- the stall detector and the GPU metric sampler must run out of process, because the decode loop is the component most likely to be the thing that is hung, and a self-reporting stuck process reports nothing. A is competently organized and its instinct to log rather than page on long duration and low acceptance is right, but it stays at the level of a metric list plus a broken watchdog."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B answers all five sub-questions more deeply and contains the two best ideas in either document. First, it states and then actually uses the governing asymmetry -- a false negative is bounded because the model can be re-evaluated next week, a false positive is unbounded because it consumes every downstream stage -- and derives the correct design rule from it: permissive early, strict late. A violates exactly this, gating stage 3 on 3-of-3 exact-match answers to trivial prompts, a brittle early filter that will fail good models on output formatting. Second, B's Champion's Burden rule re-runs the incumbent every week beside the new candidates and invalidates the entire week if the champion fails, which is a known-positive control on the harness itself -- the single most valuable honesty mechanism proposed anywhere in either response, because it catches the case where a favourite appears to fail due to a broken rig rather than a broken model. B also starts a full stage earlier than A, at zero-compute metadata triage (license, size versus VRAM, known-broken release, already-evaluated hash), which is literally the cheapest possible disqualifier and is the stage A omits. On re-testing, A offers only hash-match plus a 28-day expiry, whereas B reasons about partial invalidation: a different quantization restarts at stage 1 because quantization can break things, a fine-tune restarts at stage 2 because base capabilities are likely preserved. On honesty, A's guards are mostly audit plumbing plus a chi-square test on pass/fail counts that is statistically meaningless at a handful of models per week; B targets the actual failure mode, which is not a forged log but a motivated re-run -- pre-registered criteria changeable only with sign-off from someone uninvolved, a kill-switch forbidding 'let me try a different prompt,' a rotating devil's advocate who must write down three failure modes before promotion, and an honesty ledger. B is also the only one that grounds disqualification comparatively against the current champion rather than against absolute thresholds, which is what a weekly adoption decision actually requires; A's funnel completes in minutes, ends in a binary 'recommended' tag, and never asks whether the candidate beats what is already deployed. A is genuinely better on two narrower points -- its evidence record is more precisely specified (weight hash, environment hash, exact prompt and output, seeds, cache hit/miss) and its per-stage time and memory budgets treated as failures keep a stuck model from blocking the cadence -- and it is the tighter document. B's flaws are real but secondary: its stage 3 rules contradict each other, since disqualifying on falling below the champion on any benchmark is incompatible with promoting on exceeding the champion on at least one; the weekly-retrained performance predictor is not feasible at this data volume; and the sub-5-percent false-negative target has no stated measurement path."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both contain code defects, but B's are at the conceptual center while A's are at the periphery, and the core teaching is what matters here. B's headline 'Critical!' section asserts that sharding a weight requires an explicit jax.lax.psum and that without it JAX will error or return wrong results -- then demonstrates this on w_spec = P(None, 'model'), which is column-parallel and needs no communication at all, since the output is simply left sharded along the model axis. The all-reduce belongs to the row-parallel case, P('model', None), which B never distinguishes. Compounding this, the psum in B's 'Complete Working Example' sits inside a plain jax.jit with no bound axis name, so it raises an unbound-axis-name error rather than running, and the shard_map variant is internally contradictory because it reduces over 'model' while declaring out_specs=P('batch','model'). A reader following B would come away with an inverted model of when collectives are needed. A gets exactly this right and makes it the substance of the answer: column-parallel splits W along its output dimension, requires no communication, and yields an output sharded on the model axis; row-parallel splits W along its input dimension, consumes a model-sharded activation, and requires an all-reduce -- which is the Megatron pattern and the reason the two are chained. It extends the same reasoning correctly to vocab-sharded embeddings and to why normalization is cheap, and its checklist raises the genuinely operational concerns B omits: silent all-gathers inserted when a replicated-expecting op receives a sharded tensor, the memory arithmetic of sharding on both axes, and the requirement that checkpoints be reloaded under the same NamedSharding for the layout to match. Its closing ladder from Mesh to PartitionSpec to NamedSharding to shard_map to SPMD HLO is the clearest statement of the abstraction stack in either response. A's defects are real and worth docking: the auto_shard import and the Shardy sharding_specs helper are invented APIs presented without hedging, and the section 5 training step is incoherent (stop_gradient on the loss, a malformed value_and_grad call, pmap layered on top of shard_map). Both make the same beginner error of passing a flat jax.devices() list where a reshaped array is required, so that cancels. B's advantages -- brevity, links to the real documentation, and a closing offer to implement a specific pattern -- do not offset teaching the wrong rule about the one thing that makes tensor parallelism hard."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both set up the mechanism/verdict split competently, but B's taxonomy is finer and truer to how findings actually behave. A sorts each finding into one bucket; B repeatedly shows that a single finding splits -- the peak-memory formula is a mechanism while the fits/does-not-fit table derived from it is a verdict, the FLOP-and-byte analysis is a mechanism while the operator bottleneck ranking is a verdict, quantization's quality impact is a mechanism while its speedup ratio is a verdict. That decomposition is the actual difficulty of the task, and it is what stops a reader from smuggling a conclusion across by citing the principle that produced it. B also lands the one genuinely non-obvious correction in either document: model-quality numbers are not automatically transferable, because FP8 on Blackwell tensor cores has different rounding and accumulation semantics than the laptop's INT8 path, so quality must be re-measured per (model, precision, hardware) triple and only the shape of the quality-versus-precision curve carries. A treats quantization accuracy as an architecture property and misses this. On the report-structure question the prompt emphasizes, B's devices are stronger because they demonstrate rather than assert: the Discrepancy subsection walks a single mechanism through laptop, H200 and B200 (crossover batch 4, then 32, then 48) and attributes the shift to compute-to-bandwidth ratios of roughly 1:1, 8:1 and 12:1, teaching the reader the distinction by example; the cross-hardware table carries a Transfers? column with a checkable invariant (if V, the three columns are three different machines; if M, they should be identical and any one is usable); and the one-number-one-stamp rule plus the hardware tag in the stamp means a skimmer physically cannot lift a laptop figure into a server recommendation. B's writing-process guardrails are better too -- drafting mechanisms before verdicts so the separation is structural rather than cosmetic, the 'would this be true on an MI300X?' classifier (which probes more dimensions than A's 'would it hold if VRAM doubled?'), version-pinning on the grounds that a cuBLAS bump can move a GEMM 15 percent and that is itself a verdict, and requiring at least two runs so a verdict is reported with a spread rather than as a single sample. A's contributions are real: a third explicit category for re-measurement tasks, validation gates with acceptance criteria attached to each task, the rewriting rule that forces every carried claim to name the constraint that produced it, a standing clause forbidding H200-to-B200 generalization, and a second-engineer review pass. But A is also looser on facts -- it states B200 memory as 384 GB where B gives the correct 192 GB, and one verdict row mixes an RTX 4090 FLOPS figure with a B200 claim in a single incoherent sentence -- and its emoji-based labeling is a more fragile enforcement mechanism than B's bracketed stamps. B's own slip, describing H200's 60 MB L2 as per-SM, is minor by comparison."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "The decisive difference is factual grounding on the book itself. A dates it correctly to 2020; B dates it to 2024 and then builds a substantial portion of its synopsis on that error, claiming the book runs 'through the deep learning revolution, to modern large language models and reinforcement learning from human feedback,' that it illustrates specification gaming with 'modern LLMs that game evaluation benchmarks' and 'chatbot jailbreaks,' and that it devotes a theme to 'mechanistic interpretability, circuit analysis.' None of that is in the 2020 book, so roughly two of B's six themes and several of its supporting examples are invented. A gets this exactly right in the opposite direction, listing as an explicit limitation that the book predates LLMs and the alignment questions they raised -- reward modeling, RLHF at scale, constitutional AI -- which is precisely the fact B inverts. Neither captures the book's actual three-part structure (Prophecy, Agency, Normativity) or the fairness, bias and transparency material that dominates its opening third; A's four-part paraphrase attaches the paperclip maximizer to a part that is really about COMPAS and word embeddings, but its coverage of the reinforcement learning, reward hacking, inverse reinforcement learning and Russell-style uncertainty material maps well onto the real second and third parts. The bibliographies are comparably contaminated and both should be checked before use: A misattributes Coherent Extrapolated Volition to Soares in 2016 rather than Yudkowsky, and credits The Precipice to Bostrom when it is Toby Ord, plus at least two apparently invented entries; B invents a Hendrycks paper title, credits Interpretability in the Wild to Olah rather than Wang et al., and misdates both of Christian's own earlier books by three and four years respectively. That roughly cancels. A's critique section is also the more useful of the two, ending on the substantive objection that 'alignment' may be too narrow a frame and that the live problems are governance, power distribution and institutional design, and its closing advice to read the book as a companion to Human Compatible rather than a substitute is a concrete recommendation. B writes more fluidly and its 'Place in the Field' paragraph and inclusion of Christian's other books are genuine additions, but a synopsis whose central claims about what the book contains are wrong cannot win on prose."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both produce a sound critique and a role-specific decision dossier, and they agree on the essentials -- write the role charter before looking at numbers, report intervals not point estimates, surface tradeoffs, record assumptions and a revisit date. B goes materially further on the two things the prompt actually asks for. On uncertainty, A lists sources and adds confidence intervals; B specifies how they are produced (stratified bootstrap, or repeated evaluation across seeds reporting median and IQR for stochastic models), separates test-set interval from cross-validation variance as distinct kinds of uncertainty, and adds a distribution-shift stress test on a held-out set from a different time period or source so that fragility is measured rather than merely flagged as a worry. On conflicting evidence, A logs contradictions and resolves them in prose, which is good; B additionally handles the case that breaks most comparisons, where two models are statistically indistinguishable on the primary metric, by refusing to rank them and stating the tiebreaker explicitly, and it preserves recorded dissent on the grounds that the first question at six months is whether something was missed. B's failure-topography section is the strongest material in either response and has no counterpart in A: error shape by subgroup rather than just accuracy, a worst-five-percent analysis asking whether confident errors form a coherent input type that exists in production, reliability diagrams with the sharp observation that calibration becomes the primary metric whenever a downstream workflow is confidence-gated, and cross-model failure overlap to determine whether ensembling is even possible -- information that is structurally invisible to any aggregate score. B also derives the decision metric from an explicit asymmetric cost ratio in the charter rather than importing a generic one, which is the actual antidote to the Goodhart problem it diagnoses, treats hard-constraint failures as a different category of object rather than a low rank, assigns authorship to the owning and ops teams rather than the builders, and carves out one honest exception for a composite fragility score clearly labelled as a heuristic summary of curves. A is tighter and more readable, and it contributes two things B lacks: a worked sensitivity analysis that names the conditions under which the ranking flips, and the pragmatic insistence that the report be template-generated by the eval pipeline because manual reports will not get written. Its critique also catches benchmark contamination, which B misses. Those are real but narrower advantages than B's."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "This is a close pairing -- A is a genuinely strong answer that gets the central principle right (alert on progress anomalies, never on absolute latency), builds a per-request progress vector, requires two-of-three signal correlation before firing, scales grace periods to prompt size and cache hit ratio, and demotes 'long request' to an info-tier alert. But B executes the same principle more rigorously at the three points that decide the question. First, the stall threshold: A compares against a global STALL_THRESHOLD_MS and a hand-waved estimate_expected_rate, whereas B derives the threshold from the request's own median inter-token latency over its first fifty decode steps, so a request that was always slow because of a large batch is judged against its own baseline rather than a fleet constant -- and B separately notes that inter-token latency does not exist during prefill and supplies a distinct rule there, which A folds into a single expected-latency formula whose arithmetic goes negative once the assumed speculative speedup exceeds two. Second, alerting: B grounds the no-false-page requirement in multi-window multi-burn-rate error-budget alerting on an inter-token-latency SLO, which is the principled reason a steady 4096-token generation can never page (it burns zero budget), and adds targeted suppressions plus exclusion of user-cancel and oom-reject terminations from SLO math, a false-signal source A does not mention. A's tiering is reasonable but threshold-based and unanchored to any SLO. Third, cost: A instructs the server to emit a metric record at every token emission without ever addressing cardinality, which at realistic decode rates and concurrency is the failure mode that kills such designs; B confronts it directly with an in-process ring buffer serialized into a span only at completion or at stall detection, per-step data sampled for diagnosis, and raw series shipped only for the slowest requests. B also adds a speculative-decoding-specific stall detector keyed on repeated zero-acceptance verify rounds with inflated verify latency, diagnosing draft divergence, and treats the memory cap as two distinct failure modes -- occupancy creep detected on regression slope rather than level, and eviction thrashing detected by nonzero eviction rate with collapsed hit rate -- both correctly assigned to ticket tier unless they coincide with a stall. A contributes real things B lacks: a fuller metric catalog, a dashboard layout, concrete instrumentation call sites, and a session-memory-bloat alert for an aged session hoarding KV while producing few tokens, which is a good idea absent from B. It is not enough to overcome B on the discriminator, the alerting foundation, and the telemetry economics."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both build a mechanism-versus-verdict taxonomy with tagging, a decision matrix and structural safeguards, but A contains the one piece of reasoning that makes the study worth writing. Its section on rankings that almost transfer identifies that the naive split -- quality findings are mechanisms, performance findings are verdicts -- fails precisely where it does the most damage, because the laptop's constraints silently redefine what was evaluated. It names three concrete traps (rank reversal induced by quantization when one model is more low-bit-sensitive than the other, rank reversal induced by context truncation where a model scored zero only because the task never fit, and behavioral change between batch 1 and batch 32 from padding or positional-encoding handling) and distils them into a checkable rule: a ranking is a mechanism only if the effective model -- weights plus quantization plus context window plus batch size -- is held constant across platforms, otherwise it is a verdict wearing a mechanism's clothes. B's taxonomy admits no such boundary and would wave every accuracy finding through as transferable. A makes the same move again on the candidate set, observing that which models could be evaluated at all was a laptop artifact, and that expanding the set on the server is a different study whose results must not be merged into one ranking table. A's enforcement is also more mechanical than B's: the rule that an [M] finding may contain no throughput, latency, memory, power or clock number and that an [H] finding may contain no quality score unless explicitly framed as score-under-this-configuration is auditable line by line, and the restriction that the abstract and recommendations may cite hardware numbers only with a platform qualifier targets the actual leakage path, which is the executive summary. Its transfer table is worked rather than templated, including a row that demonstrates a real reversal, and its fixed-schema hardware profile with a laptop-equivalent line makes the delta visible at a glance. A's re-measurement list also catches things B misses: confirming identical sampling parameters and RNG backend, re-checking per-task truncation, recalibrating any time-limited task, and recomputing the minimum detectable effect at the larger N the server affords. B's advantages are real -- its transferable mechanisms are more systems-substantive (layer-wise quantization sensitivity, KV dominance beyond 32K, the shape of the batch-throughput curve, MoE routing overhead), it attaches explicit validation gates with acceptance criteria to each re-measurement task, it states a standing clause forbidding H200-to-B200 generalization, and it adds a second-engineer review pass. But it is also looser with facts, giving B200 as 384 GB where A correctly says 192 GB, and that error is load-bearing since the re-measurement plan instructs refitting at 384 GB; its emoji-based markers are a more fragile convention than A's bracketed tags plus running header; and its mechanism list is almost entirely about systems performance, which sits awkwardly with a prompt about an evaluation methodology for model quality."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "The two summaries flatly contradict each other on the two headline patterns -- A says early layers are most sensitive in a U-shape and that attention projections exceed FFN, B says depth increases sensitivity and that the FFN gate/up/down projections exceed Q/K/V/O -- and the literature genuinely supports pieces of both, with first and last blocks and the FFN down projection all commonly flagged. What separates them is calibration: A presents its patterns as converged and 'remarkably consistent,' while B devotes a section to what is not settled (the ordering among attention sub-projections varies with GQA versus MHA and with per-tensor versus per-group schemes, cross-scale stability is open, and most findings assume weight-only rather than joint weight-activation quantization). Given that A's attention-over-FFN claim is the more contestable of the two, asserting consensus is the wrong posture. B is also more accurate on mechanism, correctly locating GPTQ's Hessian in the layer-wise reconstruction objective weighted by activation outer products rather than, as A has it, the Hessian of the loss with respect to weights. On procedure, B works at weight-tensor granularity (Q, K, V, O, gate, up, down separately) rather than A's whole-block granularity, which matters because the usual real-world answer is to promote one projection inside a block, not the block. B also decomposes the signal properly: a clean local perturbation with only the target layer quantized, a separate final-logit KL that captures the downstream amplification a local metric cannot see, and an explicitly incremental cumulative score for error accumulation, with distributional weight and activation features as a prior where the perturbation signal is weak. A's single sequential measurement keeps every predecessor quantized and calls the confound a feature, but it makes each layer's score depend on accumulated upstream degradation and on the traversal order, so the resulting ranking is not comparable across depths -- the exact failure B avoids by separating local from cumulative. B further formulates the allocation as an integer program when the budget is in bits rather than layers, and its assumption table gives a per-row consequence-if-violated, including the important note that the additivity approximation holds for a coarse 8/4 split but breaks if 3-bit is added. On validation B is clearly ahead: pre-registered numeric acceptance criteria (delta perplexity under 0.1 to 0.3 nats, mean logit KL under 0.05, top-1 agreement above 95 percent), generated-text divergence to catch compounding error a single-step KL misses, activation-distribution and singular-value checks, and above all the sensitivity-curve knee test, which validates the procedure itself by confirming that the chosen k sits where returns diminish rather than merely confirming the artifact. A's real contribution, which B underplays by deferring labelled evaluation to a later phase, is the practical observation that MMLU, GSM8K, HellaSwag and ARC ship with their own labels and can be run immediately at no annotation cost; its explicit ablation against uniform 4-bit and uniform 8-bit baselines is also the right control, though B's k-sweep subsumes it."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both responses are technically unreliable - neither's code would run, and both repeat the same core misconception that shard_map inserts collectives for you, when shard_map is explicitly the manual per-device mode in which you write psum/all_gather yourself and jit with NamedSharding is the mode where XLA inserts communication. {"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is the deeper and more operationally credible design. It reasons rather than enumerates: it explains why a KV cache cannot survive a swap between different architectures (layer count, head dim, rotary params) and therefore what actually survives is the message list plus a re-prefill cost, which it then treats as the user-visible price of a swap; it gives a step-by-step swap procedure with a per-step timing breakdown and a watchdog deadline on each step; and it handles the awkward case B skips entirely - an interactive request arriving mid-load - with an explicit abort-versus-complete heuristic based on how far the load has progressed. Its preemption model is better too: an arriving interactive request suspends the benchmark generation at a token boundary and preserves kv_offset for resumption rather than killing it, with the correct caveat that this only works while both share the model. The memory accountant is predictive and self-checking - it computes predicted peak before dispatch and reconciles bookkeeping against driver-reported usage every five seconds, treating divergence as a bug class of its own - which is a materially stronger answer to 'memory accounting' than B's static tracking dimensions. The failure-mode section is prioritised by consequence (silent corruption first, then liveness, QoS, operational), and each row pairs a specific instrument with a specific recovery, closing with a named metric set. A also shows real judgment in section 8 by naming alternatives it rejected and why: no small resident model alongside the big one, KV spill to pinned RAM synchronously with the NVMe write async, benchmarks as a yield class rather than a throttled background class, and the inference engine in a child process as the key isolation boundary. B is a competent, well-organised design and is stronger in a couple of spots (prefix-cache dedup across benchmark prompts, fragmentation tracking, swap I/O budgeting so prefetch does not starve interactive decode), but it stays at the level of bullet-point assertions, leans on arbitrary thresholds without derivation, and contains technical slips A avoids - 'mmap weights into VRAM' is not a real operation and cudaGetDeviceProperties does not expose ECC error counters. A's own blemishes (a muddled example VRAM budget table, and SHA-256 over a multi-gigabyte KV buffer on every spill/restore presented without acknowledging its cost) are real but minor beside the gap in depth."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A gets the fundamentals right where B gets them wrong, and goes considerably deeper into what model parallelism actually means. {"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both are strong, well-structured answers that hit all three parts of the prompt - critique, four-axis scheme, trade-off guidance - and both correctly insist on gates before weights and on showing distributions rather than means. Its critique is sharper because it is worked rather than asserted: the 60%-in-10-minutes versus 12%-in-2-minutes pair that lands on an identical 36 successes/hour makes the conflation concrete, and its decomposition of the time denominator into intrinsic generation speed, algorithmic efficiency (retry cycles to convergence) and runaway time is the single best observation in either response - it shows the metric actively *credits* a 55-minute loop that ends in a correct three-line fix, which is precisely the runaway pathology the prompt is pointing at. Its metrics are more operationally defined and more clearly measurable: diff minimality against the gold diff, scope-creep and regression rates, multi-edit coherence, steps-to-convergence separating slow-per-token from needs-six-attempts, the planning-versus-emission time split, and a context-window degradation curve reported as pass rate at 1k/4k/8k/32k. The methodological caveat on the ceiling test - cap the wall clock and record a cap-hit as 'unresolved' rather than 'slow' so the ceiling stays honest - and the framing that the report is a data table not a verdict, re-weightable without re-benchmarking, are exactly the right disciplines. Its gate-floor-weight sequencing is crisp and its narrated trade-off example is a nice touch. But several of its axis entries stay at the level of named concepts, and B covers most of A's ground while adding the temporal decomposition, the failure taxonomy, per-use-case weight vectors and version-over-version tracking that would surface a silent edit-competence regression."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both arrive at the same defensible conclusion - start with retrieval, add fine-tuning for style later, hybrid is the endpoint - but A reasons its way there while B largely checklists it. A opens with the reframing that actually resolves the question: classify your failures as knowledge gaps versus behaviour gaps, and build a 200-500 example labelled eval set tagged on that axis before touching a GPU, because retrieval fixes the first and fine-tuning fixes the second. That framing then drives a genuinely discriminating experiment sequence, which is the part of the prompt that most separates the two answers: fine-tune on behaviour only with factual content deliberately excluded, then fine-tune again with knowledge added, so the delta between the two isolates which bottleneck you actually have; a staleness test restricted to questions whose answers changed in the last thirty days, which prices the maintenance tax directly; and a composition test that checks the subtle failure where a fine-tuned model starts ignoring its retrieved context - a real interaction effect B never mentions. B's experiments are closer to a list of evaluations to run, and its Experiment 2 does not separate style from facts even though it poses that as the key question. B does have real strengths A lacks: a broader pre-work checklist covering source attribution, data as moat, team ML depth and product lifetime; an explicit out-of-distribution robustness test; and a breakeven formula with a worked example. But the quantitative cost table that is supposed to be its differentiator is badly wrong - it prices Llama-class inference at roughly $300 per million input tokens and $1,000 per million output tokens, three orders of magnitude off, and then contradicts itself two lines later with a plausible $0.001-0.005 per query - and it lists Mistral Large among open-weight options. Wrong numbers presented confidently are worse than an honest qualitative model, and A's closing point - that the framing as a binary is itself the error, since one component supplies what to say and the other how to act, and each can be swapped independently - is the sharper insight."}

B answers it by running raw ALTER TABLE statements at request time through Prisma, which silently desynchronises the Prisma schema and generated client from the database and is precisely the anti-pattern a migration-first ORM exists to prevent - and B never flags the risk. {"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both are specific, credible design documents, but B is more accurate on the integration details the question explicitly asked about and more rigorous where clinical AI actually fails. B names the right standards and uses them correctly: DICOM Structured Report with LOINC-coded findings attached to the original study, FHIR R4 DiagnosticReport/Observation for modern sites, and HL7 ORU^R01 as the legacy fallback, with an explicit SR-versus-FHIR trade-off. A repeatedly invents 'ORU^RDS' and 'ORU^OBS' as message types, conflates MPPS with the modality worklist, and - more consequentially - places DICOM de-identification in the production inference path as 'a hard FDA/HIPAA requirement', which confuses training-dataset de-identification with treatment-context processing inside the covered entity; B correctly scopes de-identification to the data pipeline. B is also stronger on validation and safety: temporal plus site splits with explicit leakage control, AUC-PR for imbalanced data, sensitivity at fixed specificity, ECE targets with temperature scaling and MC-dropout intervals, pre-specified subgroup fairness across age, sex, scanner vendor and habitus, and a prospective multi-site clinical endpoint. Its architecture section offers a real choice (3D Swin v2 with medical MAE pretraining versus 2D ConvNeXt with attention pooling) and prices the trade-off in latency. A's most distinctive architectural decision is its weakest: to hit a self-imposed sub-second target - far tighter than triage requires, as B's 30s/10s SLAs reflect - it discards all but 32 slices chosen by a cheap HU-histogram anomaly detector, and never acknowledges that this can drop the very slice containing a small hemorrhage or pneumothorax, which is the exact false-negative harm the system exists to prevent; the accompanying '90%+ of the 3D model's AUC' claim is asserted without support. A does contribute two genuinely excellent things B lacks in the same form: the design rule that the score is an annotation rather than a hidden re-sort with radiologist override preserved, and a week-by-week shadow-to-tiebreaker go-live sequence with a quantitative acceptance criterion. B has its own small fabrications - a brain window written as 80/100 rather than W80/L40, and a config.pbtxt with fields Triton does not have - but they are peripheral, where A's errors sit in the PACS/HL7 layer and in the core modelling decision."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "A is well organised and its decision logic is crisper in one respect - explicit numeric pass criteria per experiment plus a summary table mapping each threshold to the next step - but its scientific design is weaker in ways that matter. A's Experiment 1 rests on 50 questions with 3 models x 3 temperatures, far too small to support the per-domain, per-component claims it wants to make, and its arc (baseline, RAG, fine-tune, cross-domain, human study) is a conventional pipeline that never isolates the causal mechanism. Most damagingly, A's entire metric suite is one-sided: hallucination rate, component accuracy, citation F1. Nothing in A penalises the degenerate solution of citing less or not at all, so every intervention it proposes could 'succeed' by suppression, and its fine-tuning loss that up-weights ungrounded citation tokens is exactly the kind of objective that would exploit this. B avoids that trap deliberately: it frames the problem as three separable failure modes and builds a controlled three-condition design (source-provided, no-retrieval, full pipeline) that actually identifies which mode dominates before choosing an intervention; it tracks omission rate, false rejection rate, net citation utility and abstention rate alongside fabrication; it flags reward gaming ('the model learning to never cite anything') as a specific risk; and it ends with an ablation that measures each component's marginal contribution rather than asserting the stack works. B is also better calibrated at the agenda level, stating what would invalidate the whole programme (fabricated citations memorised in pretraining would make retrieval and verification symptom-treatment), what would accelerate it, and where it does not apply, plus a dependency-aware timeline separating the critical path from parallelisable arms. B's flaw is that several 'expected outcomes' are written as if already found, with point estimates presented as key findings, which overstates confidence for a pre-registration; A hedges marginally better there. That is outweighed by B's superior identification strategy, metric completeness and explicit scope limits."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "B is the tidier engineering artifact - a four-stage table with a named cheapest disqualifier per stage, a real SQLite schema with a known-failures index, suite versioning with dependency-aware cache invalidation, a 10 GPU-hour weekly cap with FIFO queueing and checkpointing, and honesty metrics that are actually measurable (time-to-disqualify P80, skip rate, zero unlogged overrides). Promotion is gated on absolute floors (60% on a fixed 50-prompt set) and deployment SLOs, so a merely adequate model that meets TTFT and VRAM targets is promoted while the question 'is this better than what we already run' is never asked, and the entire capability assessment is one 50-prompt stage before 1.5 GPU-hours of deployment profiling. {"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both reviewers reach the same defensible conclusion - do not ship on this evidence - and both cover the standard checklist (SRM, peeking/multiple comparisons, novelty decay, segment heterogeneity, guardrails, phased rollout). A is cleanly organised and its trust/distrust split plus pass-fail decision table are easy to act on. B is better on every axis that requires actually thinking about this specific test. It opens with the question A never asks - 0.8% of what - and insists the effect be re-expressed against a baseline and in business terms before anyone calls it a win. It makes the decision rule turn on the lower bound of the interval rather than on the point estimate crossing a threshold, which is the correct framing for a marginal result and is exactly where A stops short (A demands the analyses but still decides on pass/fail cells). It catches the ranking-specific confound A misses entirely: a ranking change is a position change, so the lift may be the position-bias gradient rather than a relevance gain, and B makes resolving that a hard blocker with position-level CTR curves as the evidence. It also adds experiment interference and traffic-layer contamination, a within-user correlation argument for why session-level randomisation would inflate significance, supply-side externalities, an achieved-power audit distinguishing the powered MDE from the observed effect, a trimmed-window sensitivity re-analysis, a cohort split to estimate the steady-state rather than the blended lift, and a long-horizon holdout. Its final decision is conditional and segment-aware rather than a single verdict, including the sensible branch of shipping only to the segment that shows the effect. B's flaws are minor: the flat-prior posterior figure quoted for p=0.03 is loose, and the SRM threshold sentence conflates the split ratio with the test p-value. A's novelty reasoning is also slightly off - it asserts new-user-driven lift implies novelty, when returning users are the ones with a prior habit to be disrupted. Net, B is the deeper and better-calibrated review."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "B is crisp, correct and well calibrated. Its opening asymmetry (MoE cuts compute per token, never memory) is the right frame, and its sharpest contribution - that the honest comparison is MoE(total=T, active=A) against dense(total=A), not against dense(total=T) - is the framing most discussions get wrong. Its three-branch decision rule is clean and its numbers are generic enough to stay true. But it is thin for the question asked. A covers the same ground and substantially more, and almost all of the extra material is both correct and load-bearing for a memory-constrained device: MoE sparsifies only the FFN, so the KV cache is unchanged and long-context interactive use erodes exactly the headroom MoE already strained (B never says this); the router is a discontinuous failure mode under quantization because a small logit perturbation flips top-k selection, which is why the gate must stay at Q8 or FP16 while experts go to Q4; at batch one there is no cross-token amortisation of the scattered expert reads that MoE's efficiency story assumes, so the access pattern defeats prefetch and costs measurable effective bandwidth; prefill and decode behave differently, so time-to-first-token and inter-token latency should be budgeted separately; and the open MoE ecosystem is less characterised under aggressive quantisation, which is a real risk-adjusted argument rather than a benchmark argument. A's decision procedure is also genuinely operational - measure usable memory after OS, runtime and the KV cache you actually need, then branch - and it closes by telling the practitioner to profile on their own chip because published figures will mislead. {"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both correctly diagnose the same core flaws - conflation of finding a fact with using it, a binary cliff that discards the shape of the falloff, and uncontrolled confounds like position and information density - and both propose replacing the scalar with curves. Its separation mechanism is real rather than asserted: the retrievability gate pre-tests each of the N spans in isolation and admits an item to the reasoning curve only if the spans were actually recoverable, so a reasoning failure is attributable to integration rather than a missed needle. B's equivalent is to run reasoning items at a context length 'well above the EC50 of retrieval depth', which is backwards - EC50 is by construction the length at which retrieval is already failing half the time, so B's reasoning curve would be contaminated by exactly the retrieval failures it claims to exclude. A also treats position as a first-class variable with an explicit fractional sweep and a 2-D accuracy surface, making lost-in-the-middle a measured property rather than a caveat; B mentions position only as something to control. It then does the arithmetic: a variance decomposition with a stated source for each component, the SE of a language mean and of a pairwise difference, and separate power statements for the omnibus test (roughly 70-75%, adequate for screening) versus pairwise contrasts (a few percent after Bonferroni, about 24% unadjusted for a 15pp gap). That honest split - the budget buys an omnibus answer and a ranked list, not clean pairwise significance - is the central finding the question was fishing for, and B puts it in the abstract. A instead spends all 200 runs on single attempts at 40 tasks per language and justifies the absence of repeats by claiming the five-language replication serves as the statistical repetition. That is wrong: language is the factor under test, so replication across languages cannot estimate run-to-run stochasticity, and for a nondeterministic agentic harness a single run per cell makes each cell a coin flip with no way to separate sampling noise from a language effect. A's power derivation is also incorrect as written - the displayed formula solves for delta-squared, which at n=40 gives a detectable difference near 30pp rather than the 15-18pp claimed - and the assertion that McNemar on 40 paired tasks detects 10-12pp is unsupported, since paired power depends on the discordant-pair rate. Both understate power, but A understates it in the direction that flatters the design. On inconclusive reporting both are strong, and A's tiered evidence language, sensitivity re-analyses and explicit note that inconclusive is not equivalence are genuinely good. B is better still: it reports minimum detectable effect rather than A's post-hoc observed power (which is uninformative by construction and a known misstep), adds a Detectable? column so underpowered comparisons cannot be buried, defines a practical-equivalence band so overlapping intervals get a graded verdict instead of a binary one, frames Bayesian results as posterior probabilities of exceeding a decision-relevant threshold rather than a bare Bayes factor, and pre-registers the rule that triggers an inconclusive verdict before any run happens. That is the calibrated-uncertainty the prompt asked for, and B has none of it. A's procedure is properly specified: a local relative-L2 perturbation from quantising one tensor at a time, a global logit-KL term that captures downstream amplification the local metric misses, and an incremental cumulative pass that accounts for error accumulation, with hard pins on embeddings, lm_head and norm weights, and a note that the budget problem reduces to a trivial greedy sort. Its assumption table states each assumption together with the consequence if violated, including the key one - that additivity of per-layer sensitivity is only acceptable for a coarse two-level split and breaks if finer bit-widths are introduced. B instead validates mixed precision against uniform 4-bit, which is nearly guaranteed to pass since promoting layers to 8 bits can only help, so the check carries almost no information. B also has internal defects: its greedy rule in Step 5 is written backwards - it says keep a layer at 8-bit if the loss or KL increase exceeds a threshold, when upgrading precision should reduce error, and the stated threshold is ambiguous between a percentage and an absolute perplexity delta; its Proxy A criterion mixes a perplexity reduction with a loss-increase bound in the same sentence; and its asserted ordering places early FFN as the most robust layer type while the survey section two paragraphs earlier says early MLP layers degrade faster. {"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both are strong and largely agree on the core analysis: the model reads untrusted content and cannot distinguish data from instructions, so controls must be structural and live outside the model. B has the sharper closing formulation of that idea and covers two things A misses - approval fatigue as a named attacker with a fatigue-resistant approval UX, and per-session snapshot/rollback to make destructive hallucinations recoverable - plus it correctly elevates the model's own error (no adversary at all) to a first-class threat. Those are real gaps in A. But A's misses are narrower than B's. B never treats the LLM round-trip itself as an exfiltration channel: every file the agent reads is serialised to a third-party endpoint, which A ranks as attack path two, mitigates with credential isolation plus TLS/endpoint pinning against a swapped or MITM'd backend, and then closes properly by noting a local model eliminates that path entirely and should be a first-class option. B's credential redaction touches the edge of this but the compromised-or-adversarial backend never appears in its attacker table. B also has no kill switch, no per-process wall-clock timeout, and no process-group/resource caps, so a fork bomb or a runaway loop is unhandled. A is more precise technically - named per-OS enforcement mechanisms (Landlock/seccomp, sandbox-exec profiles, AppContainer/Job Objects), a hash-chained log written outside the sandbox root, AST-level command classification rather than regex, and the typed-tool-call design that refuses free-form bash strings - where B's package-script mitigation cites a pip flag that does not do what is claimed and suggests chroot for a developer workstation tool. A also reasons about ship order explicitly and correctly: contain the blast radius first because a contained failure is recoverable and a total compromise is not, and keep the agent autonomous for the safe eighty percent while gating irreversible and externally-visible actions, rather than B's v1 rule of approving every single command, which is safe but effectively disables the product it is modelling. Finally A is the more honestly calibrated of the two: its residual-risk section concedes that a sufficiently clever injection can still drive an allowed action toward an unintended end, that the developer who disables the sandbox voids everything, and that the agent's own dependency chain is itself a supply-chain target, and its closure matrix states for each path what remains open after v1 and which later control shuts it. B's design-principles section is memorable but does not do that accounting."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A identifies the property that actually makes this system different from any other dev tool - the agent's decision loop is not a trust boundary, because the model reads untrusted content (file comments, READMEs, commit messages, package metadata, PR descriptions) and acts on it - and then builds the whole model around that. Its attacker table includes the two cases that matter most and are easiest to omit: the model itself as a non-adversarial failure mode (a hallucinated rm or force-push produces the same blast radius as an attack), and the developer as a rubber-stamper under approval fatigue. Its path list is specific and sequenced by realism, including self-escalation (injected text tells the agent to append entries to its own allowlist), which A correctly notes defeats every other control in one step and answers structurally by making the agent's config unwritable by the agent. Its ship ordering is argued rather than asserted - egress denied by default so that stealing secrets leaves nowhere to send them, confinement to the project root so credentials are not merely off-limits but unreachable, install lifecycle scripts blocked, audit log built in v1 precisely because it is cheap now and expensive to retrofit and is the substrate for later anomaly detection - and it closes with principles that do real work, notably structural over behavioural: a model that decides not to read the SSH key is not a boundary, a sandbox that makes it impossible is. B is organised and readable, and several of its first-ship items overlap with A's (sandbox, audit log, least-privilege account, confirmation for dangerous ops), but it misdiagnoses the core threat. It frames the problem as classic command injection and prescribes stripping or escaping shell metacharacters from user-provided text before it reaches the LLM, and rejecting model output containing metacharacters. Prompt injection is semantic, not syntactic: escaping characters in a prompt prevents nothing, and blocking pipes and redirects breaks the ordinary commands the agent exists to run. B never once names injection via file content the agent reads, which is the highest-likelihood path on this system. Its remaining framing drifts off-target - an insider on the vendor's source pipeline, and full-disk encryption plus Secure Boot, which are irrelevant to a process already running as the logged-in user. It also offers no mapping from mitigation back to path, no residual-risk accounting, nothing on self-escalation, rollback, or approval fatigue, and its two-factor-per-dangerous-command proposal is unworkable at the frequency an autonomous agent operates."}

Its derivation sketch drops the square root and reports a detectable difference of 15-18pp for independent proportions at n=40 per arm when the correct figure is roughly 31pp, and the claimed 10-12pp for McNemar at 40 pairs ignores that paired power depends on the discordance rate; so its headline power claims are optimistic by about a factor of two, which is exactly the sort of error a power argument exists to prevent. Its task corpus is also a poor instrument for an agentic harness: HumanEval-style single-function problems with a hard tier defined as complex logic barely exercise a tool-using agent, and translating a public benchmark invites contamination it never addresses. {"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is both more accurate and more insightful. It opens with the asymmetry that actually governs the decision -- MoE cuts compute and weight-bandwidth per token but not resident memory, because you cannot know in advance which expert the next token routes to -- and then supplies the framing that most discussions of this get wrong: the honest comparison is MoE(total=T, active=A) against dense(total=A), which read the same bytes per token, not MoE(T) against dense(T). It correctly identifies that on bandwidth-bound hardware (CPU, unified-memory Apple silicon) MoE is genuinely faster than a dense model of equal total size, names the quantization mechanism precisely (sparsely exercised experts get thin calibration coverage, group granularity collides with small expert tensors, a quantized router can misroute, so practitioners hold the router at higher precision and give back some of the savings), and flags routing-induced load imbalance as token-rate jitter, which matters for an interactive assistant as much as mean speed. Its recommendation is conditioned on what is actually binding -- dense when the memory ceiling is the wall or when you must go to Q2/Q3, MoE when memory is plentiful and throughput is the constraint -- with a concrete default (dense 7-14B at Q4/Q5 with 20-30% headroom for KV cache) and an instruction to benchmark tail latency on the real device. B is well organised and its quantization-maturity and tooling-support points are fair, but it contains errors that undercut its analysis. It states Mixtral-8x7B has 1.6T total parameters (it is roughly 47B) and that active params are 2-4% of total (Mixtral's top-2 routing activates roughly a quarter). More damagingly, it conflates MoE's expert sparsity with structured sparse-kernel hardware support, concluding that MoE only wins on data-centre GPUs with sparse units or custom ASICs -- this inverts the real picture, since MoE's advantage is largest exactly where the bottleneck is memory bandwidth rather than FLOPs, which is the typical local CPU or Apple-silicon case that A calls out. B's claim that a 7B at INT4 often rivals a 13B at INT8 is asserted without support and cuts against the usual finding. Both land on dense as the pragmatic default, so the recommendations agree; A gets there with correct mechanisms and a sharper decision rule, while B gets there partly through a misdiagnosis."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "These are close: both reject the scalar, both replace it with a retrieval curve over context length and a reasoning curve over integration load, both make position a first-class variable, and both insist the threshold is a summary of a curve rather than the measurement. B's genuine advantages are real and I weighed them: retention thresholds expressed as a fraction of the model's own ceiling are better threshold semantics than A's absolute L95/L90/L80 crossings because they keep an 82%-ceiling model comparable to a 99% one; splitting reasoning into fact count N and step count S is a sharper decomposition than A's single K; and the reporting-specification table plus the explicit statement that the headline number is a convenience rather than the metric are good. But B's two signature moves have flaws -- the retrievability gate admits items where the model retrieved only N-1 of N spans, which cannot isolate integration failure since a missing fact makes the item unanswerable, and the composition formula multiplies per-fact retrieval probabilities as if independent while M is already defined conditional on a gate that tolerates one miss, so the factorisation does not line up with its own definitions. Its adoption measurement distinguishes leading from lagging indicators, proposes the stranger test (a new student reproduces a random three-month-old experiment in under an hour, unaided) as the real metric with everything else a proxy, tells you what a low reproducibility-test pass rate means (fix the platform, not the researchers), and uniquely lists metrics not to track -- notebook counts, logins, lines migrated, and survey scores, the last replaced by asking in person. The risk section is genuinely organisational: the PI as star topology whose private laptop kills adoption, the 'I'll migrate after this paper' trap answered by the next-experiment rule rather than a mandate, the platform owner as single point of failure with a maintainability standard (a competent engineer in two hours), the tool-versus-process confusion, the peak-and-decay curve with the instruction not to read the day-60 dip as failure, scope creep, and the budget cliff answered by a 0.1 FTE ongoing line framed as the cost of the lab's version control. A's measurement design is also far more credible: 5,000 queries across five domains with 500 annotated failure cases per domain and a stated inter-annotator agreement floor, plus deliberately degraded retrieval corpora to isolate whether low recall causes fabrication -- a genuine controlled manipulation rather than an observational sweep. Its cost model names the levers that actually decide it -- that a fine-tune's main economic payoff is licensing a smaller model at the same quality, that data curation and the retraining treadmill are the hidden cost, and that every base-model upgrade forces a re-fine-tune while the prompt+RAG arm just swaps checkpoints -- and it ties the verdict to volume tiers. But B repeatedly claims fine-tuning is the answer to hallucination, asserting a 30% reduction 'thanks to aligned weights' and routing sub-5% hallucination tolerance and regulated domains straight to fine-tuning. That is backwards for a support assistant: grounding in retrieved, citable source text is the mechanism that suppresses confabulation, and fine-tuning on answer text without retrieval tends to teach confident-sounding recall of stale facts. B's pilot also contradicts itself, requiring 1k-5k labelled examples in Part 1 and then proposing to sample 200 tickets and split them into train and held-out test in week one, which cannot support the fine-tune arm it is meant to evaluate. Its anti-paging section is the more direct answer to the question asked: never page on latency alone, never page when tokens are flowing regardless of TTFT, sustained-window evaluation with an auto-reset after a few seconds of renewed progress, rate-limited paging to prevent fatigue, and an auto-acknowledge checklist attached to each page so an on-call engineer can dismiss a healthy long request in three checks. It also threads the three named features properly, adding a soft cap at 85% that flushes idle sessions before the hard cap throttles, a fallback-rate guardrail on the draft model, and a token-indexed progress probe that gives an unambiguous still-alive signal.
