A's distinctive contribution is an operating-metrics layer that B lacks - CAC payback windows, an LTV-to-CAC target, and the observation that churn is the number one killer with quarterly business reviews as the countermeasure, which is a real gap in B - plus a useful pitfalls list. But A's numbers are its weak point rather than its strength: the 12-18 month payback and 3:1 LTV-to-CAC targets are imported SaaS heuristics that sit awkwardly against managed-services gross margins, and the claims that expansion revenue runs 3-5x the initial contract and that many MSPs draw 40-60 percent of revenue through partners are stated as established fact without support and are not obviously true. Confidently asserted statistics that may be wrong are a worse calibration failure than declining to quantify. B is tighter, better targeted to the specifics of this business model, and scopes its follow-up question along the dimensions that would actually change the answer."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both correctly diagnose successes-per-hour as a lossy scalar that entangles correctness with throughput, both separate the four axes, and both treat runaway behaviour as a gate rather than a dial - so the decision turns on completeness and on the quality of the decision procedure. B's critique is the more thorough and catches failure modes A misses entirely: the binary pass/fail discards partial credit in a workflow where a human reviews the diff; the metric is silent on how a success was obtained, so a model that deletes the failing test scores identically to one that fixes the bug; and once a team optimises the number, Goodhart pressure turns it into a measure of benchmark-gaming rather than capability. B is also right about something A gets materially wrong: edit competence cannot be derived from the same single-shot benchmark, and B operationalises it properly with behaviour-preservation, scope adherence measured by diff analysis, negative-constraint compliance, and context retention at turn 15 versus turn 1, whereas A reduces it to iterations-to-resolution, which measures retry-until-it-passes rather than competence at modifying existing code. B's decision procedure is the better answer to the actual question - gate on safety, floor on capability for the use case, then trade the remaining axes with explicitly documented weights, present the trade as a sentence the stakeholder can argue with, and revisit the weights when the use case changes - and it is careful to say a weighted sum is acceptable only after the gates and only with the weights visible. A leads with Value = w1*Capability + ... and only later carves out runaway as a veto, which is the weaker ordering. A is not far behind: its algebraic decomposition of the metric into success_rate times attempts-per-hour is the crispest single explanation of why the axes are unrecoverable, its observation that a runaway is reported as low throughput and is therefore indistinguishable from ordinary slowness is a genuinely subtle point B does not make as sharply, and its worked report card with bootstrapped intervals is concrete. But B matches A's concreteness with its own profile card plus a Pareto-frontier plot, adds calibration and human-judged quality to the capability axis, and covers more ground without losing structure."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is the far more serious design document. Its stage ordering is genuinely cost-ordered in the way the prompt demands - a zero-GPU static triage that kills candidates on licence, context length, and a memory-footprint calculation from config alone before any weights are touched - and it carries an explicit per-stage GPU-hour budget that sums against a stated weekly cap, with survival-rate estimates so the reader can see the funnel actually fits on one machine. Its promotion evidence is the right evidence: regression against the incumbent on a fixed prompt set, and a mean-score ratio against the model currently in production, which is what makes the decision actionable rather than abstract. B never compares against the incumbent at all. On avoiding repeated work A is substantially deeper: a content-addressed cache keyed on weights hash, quantisation, prompt id and sampling parameters, so a re-release with only a config.json change is a full cache hit; incremental battery evaluation that generates only the newly added prompt ids; a known_results table keyed including battery version so a model that failed three weeks ago is not silently re-queued; and delta-testing of fine-tunes restricted to the borderline band of the parent's results, explicitly labelled a heuristic with an override. B's caching is sound in outline but undercut by a 28-day expiry that contradicts its own claim of deterministic idempotency - if the weights hash and seeds are fixed, expiry only burns compute. The honesty section is where the gap is widest. A's controls are structural and specific to the actual failure mode: pre-registration of the plan before the run, thresholds as versioned numeric constants with an explicit no-rounding rule, blinded and randomised human spot-checks, an asymmetric re-run policy (a failure may be re-run once and only for a logged technical reason; a pass is never re-run to confirm), a logged favourite tax, and - the sharpest control in either document - a quarterly re-run of the battery against three known-good reference models to detect whether a favourite is failing because the validator drifted rather than because the model is worse. B's equivalents are largely imported enterprise ceremony that does not fit a one-machine weekly cadence: an ethics-team annual review, HMAC-signed append-only cloud buckets, and a chi-square test on pass/fail distributions that is statistically ill-posed as a favouritism check, alongside a blinding claim that cannot hold when the operator chooses and downloads the releases. B's gates are also weak as instruments: exact-match on three trivial prompts will reject capable models on formatting, and a ten-question MMLU subset with a six-correct threshold has an interval far too wide to disqualify anything. A is not flawless - BLEU-1 against twelve hand-written references is a poor coherence detector and several survival rates are invented - but it also closes with a failure-modes table for the funnel itself and an explicit statement of what the funnel does not do (it gates, it does not rank), which is exactly the calibration the brief rewards."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both cover all five requested areas and both are well organised, but A is internally consistent where B breaks in its core mechanism. B's watermark table is incoherent: 'Low: <60% VRAM free = normal', 'High: 60-85% free', 'Critical: <85% free = mandatory swap' - at 50% free both the normal and the critical predicate are true, so the zone logic cannot be implemented as written, and this is the table that drives every swap decision in the design. Its swap cost model calls torch.save to serialise the resident model to a temp file before unloading, which is pure waste when the weights already exist on disk, and it then cites flash wear as a swap-thrash harm, a consequence only its own unnecessary write creates. Its swap-trigger pseudocode confuses model identity with traffic class (current_model == interactive), its session cache is declared immutable per prompt-hash and re-keyed when the prompt changes, which is incompatible with the incremental multi-turn KV reuse that makes interactive sessions cheap, and it asserts a measured 200ms bound on cancel-plus-rollback in a document that has measured nothing - an unforced calibration error. A's treatment is sounder on the points that matter for a one-model box: it states plainly that KV cache is model-specific and must be dropped on swap while the message history survives in RAM so the user does not lose the conversation, it tracks KV per session so eviction can free a known number of bytes, and its swap decision matrix is expressed per traffic class with a defer rule plus a benchmark starvation timeout, which is the actual scheduling question. Its failure-mode section is also the better answer to what would be instrumented first, because it is explicitly tiered by priority and each entry carries symptom, blast radius, named metrics, a concrete alert predicate and a recovery action - including cancellation leak detected as KV growth without matching session growth, and swap-storm throttling on per-model-pair swap rate. A closes with a rationale table that makes its trade-offs contestable. B does contribute several failure modes A misses and should be credited for them - scheduler deadlock, priority inversion, partial-weight swap corruption with rollback, allocation size-class histograms for fragmentation, and cancel arriving mid-swap - and its benchmark swap-budget bidding is a nice idea. But A's static per-spec VRAM figures and fixed safety margin are a milder simplification than a decision table that cannot be evaluated, and A's only real slip is a duplicated word in its rationale row on FIFO versus priority starvation."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A gets the central mechanism right and B gets it backwards. A models verification cost as T_v = T_t[1 + (K-1)*phi(B)], where phi is the fraction of target time that is arithmetic rather than weight-read-bound, and draws the correct conclusion: at batch 1-4 the weights are re-read anyway so verifying eight tokens costs about one token's time, which is exactly why speculation wins in the interactive regime, while as phi approaches 1 the profitability condition becomes E[accepted] <= K + r, which is unsatisfiable for any positive head cost - so in the fully compute-bound regime speculative decoding can never pay off at any acceptance rate. That is the sharpest and most useful statement in either answer. B's verify-cost model, c(N,B) = N^alpha * B^(1-alpha), is unmotivated and mis-normalised (at N=1 it yields B^(1-alpha) target-token-times for a single-token forward pass), and it leads B to the opposite and empirically false conclusions: it computes a break-even acceptance rate of about 0.95 at N=4, B=1, declares that speculation pays off best at B >= 8 and that slowdown occurs at B = 1, and attributes the whole effect to kernel fusion rather than to memory-bandwidth-bound decode. B's expected-accepted-tokens formula, (1-(1-AR)^N)/AR, is also simply wrong - it tends to 1/AR, roughly 1.11 at AR = 0.9, not to N as B itself asserts one line later - so the quantity on which every subsequent number depends is broken. B then compounds this with fabricated authority: a named 2023 linear-probe citation with a correlation of 0.94, a draft-cost exponent validated across ten-plus architectures, and prediction errors within 0.08 measured on three specific models. None of that is real, and inventing validation data is the worst calibration failure available in an answer whose job is to tell someone whether to spend weeks training a head. Its probe corpus of 300-500 tokens is also far too small to estimate an acceptance curve. A is not error-free: its K=8 column and its alpha=0.9 K=4 entry overstate the correct geometric sum (3.10 and 5.13, not 3.46 and 6.29, at alpha=0.9), its optimal-K expression is garbled, and its experiment measures the target's K-step self-continuation against ground truth when the quantity that actually bounds acceptance is the predictability of the target's own continuation from the hidden state - a conflation it only partly repairs with the optional linear probe. But the formula it states is correct even where the table is miscomputed, its experiment needs no head at all and separately pins down the three governing quantities (acceptance ceiling, head cost ratio, batch phase), and its stratified-subset extension actually explains the sometimes-1.8x-sometimes-slower behaviour and suggests gating speculation on a cheap runtime signal. Correct physics with arithmetic slips beats confident, well-formatted analysis whose sign is inverted."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both correctly identify the core defects - conflation of retrieval with reasoning, a binary threshold standing in for a curve, and an underspecified notion of retrieval question - but B goes substantially further on exactly the dimensions the prompt asks about. It treats the measurement as a statistical object: it points out that the original metric reads a single Bernoulli trial near p = 0.5, specifies at least 50 needles per cell, quotes the resulting confidence interval width (about plus or minus 6 points near 0.9), and requires bootstrap intervals on every reported number. Its protocols include the controls that make the separation of the two axes real rather than nominal: a needle-removed condition that must fall to chance, which is the only way to rule out parametric recall and which A omits entirely; a drop-one-fact condition establishing that all K facts are genuinely necessary; and - the sharpest design element in either answer - an adjacent-facts condition that places all K facts in one paragraph, so reasoning difficulty is measured net of retrieval difficulty. B also controls distractor lexical overlap and needle uniqueness, reports retrieval accuracy in position bands with a middle-to-edge asymmetry ratio that isolates lost-in-the-middle from general decay, and presents reasoning as a two-dimensional surface over (L, K) summarised by K_max(L) and L_max(K) with the iso-accuracy contour as the object of interest. On threshold semantics specifically, B is much stronger: report L95, L90 and L80 together and read their spread as cliff-versus-slope, compare against a position-matched chance baseline rather than zero, pre-register the cutoffs to block post-hoc threshold selection, and treat the threshold as a lossy summary of the curve rather than the measurement. Its worked example contrasting a single scalar against a paragraph that states where, how and how much the model fails makes the whole scheme concrete. A is a competent answer with the right high-level decomposition, EC50 and d80 summaries, and a clear comparison table, and its point that the two curves interact because poor retrieval poisons reasoning is well made. But it holds context length fixed while varying reasoning steps rather than mapping the joint surface, it specifies no sample sizes, no intervals, no memorization control and no distractor controls beyond a mention, and its claim that the axes are orthogonal sits awkwardly against its own observation that they interact. B is the more rigorous and more actionable measurement design."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "These are close - both summarise the literature, both score layers by the change in output logits when a single matrix is dropped to 4-bit on unlabelled calibration text, both force-protect the embedding, LM head and norms, and both validate with held-out perplexity plus logit KL. B wins on two things that matter. First, its summary is more accurate: it reports the U-shaped profile (early and late blocks more sensitive, middle blocks robust) and gives two mechanisms for the middle-layer robustness, redundancy and error-averaging in the residual stream, and it is more precise within the block, identifying the FFN down-projection as the most fragile because the dimensionality reduction concentrates error, with O next and Q/K/V least. A instead asserts a monotone depth gradient in which deeper layers are more sensitive and early error is washed out, which is not what the cited work shows and sits badly against the fact that middle-layer robustness is precisely what makes a mostly-4-bit allocation possible; A's within-block claims are also muddled, placing FFN above attention and then putting V and O 'in the middle'. Second, B's validation includes the check that actually tests the procedure rather than the artifact: Spearman rank correlation between the proxy scores used for allocation and the measured per-matrix perplexity increase, with an explicit fallback (switch from logit-MSE to Hessian trace) if the correlation is poor; plus allocation stability across a different calibration draw with a stated overlap threshold, an ablation demoting the force-protected matrices to confirm the disproportionate jump, and a comparison against the uniform all-4-bit baseline as the control. B's design is also cleaner where A's is underdetermined: A's composite score sums four weighted terms with coefficients alpha, beta, gamma and delta that cannot be tuned without the labelled data the problem forbids, and A's calibration corpus of one to five thousand tokens is an order of magnitude smaller than what activation-statistics estimation needs, where B specifies 128-512 sequences. A is not weak - its explicit 'what is not settled' section is the best-calibrated passage in either answer, its assumption table is thorough and names the right failure consequences, and its sensitivity-curve knee check on the choice of k is a good idea - but its broader coverage includes low-value additions (a top-ten singular-value comparison per matrix) and it pays for breadth with a shakier factual base and a scoring rule it cannot actually parameterise."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both are thorough, well-organised proposals with credible stacks, RBAC enforced server-side, JWT access plus rotating refresh tokens in httpOnly cookies, transactional bulk updates and audit logging, so the decision turns on the one genuinely hard design question in the brief: what it means for an admin to create and eliminate database fields. A confronts it directly, rejects runtime ALTER TABLE as risky, and proposes a dynamic-attribute model (an admin-managed attribute registry plus a JSONB value column validated against the active attribute set on write), explicitly labelling this as its interpretation of an ambiguous requirement - exactly the kind of flagged assumption the rubric rewards. B instead exposes an HTTP endpoint that runs ALTER TABLE on the devices table at request time; it does add sensible guardrails (a data-type whitelist, a schema_meta registry, deactivate-then-drop after a grace period, audit logging), but the design contradicts B's own stated principle of reversible Knex migrations as the sole path for schema change, and runtime DDL on a live table undermines migration provenance, generated types and prepared statements. B's library list also contains real errors: it prescribes express-mongo-sanitize replaced by express-mysql-sanitize, which is not a package that exists, and treats input sanitisation as the SQL-injection control when it is already using a parameterising query builder; it describes uuid as deterministic ID generation; and it pairs Redux Toolkit for inventory data with TanStack Query for server state, duplicating the same responsibility, while offering express-validator as an alternative to the Zod schemas it has just designated as the shared contract. A's stack is internally coherent - Fastify plus Prisma plus Zod schemas in a shared package consumed by both apps, BullMQ so bulk updates do not block the event loop, PgBouncer for pooling, Testcontainers for real-database integration tests - and its data model (attribute definitions, attribute values, audit log) actually supports the admin capability it promises. B is genuinely stronger in places and should be credited: a permission matrix traced line by line to the stated roles, a Definition of Done gating each sprint, optimistic locking on PATCH via an updated_at version check that A omits entirely and that matters for concurrent inventory edits, a concrete CSV path with per-row success and error reporting, and a hardening sprint with named load-test targets, indexes, dependency scanning and monitoring. But A's only comparable weakness is that it silently narrows the user role to updating its own records when the brief says users update individual records, whereas B accumulates a fabricated dependency, a wrong library claim, a redundant state layer and an architectural decision at odds with its own principles table. On soundness of the core design reasoning, A is the better document."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B is the sharper piece of thinking because it finds the decomposition that actually makes the decision tractable: separate the knowledge gap (the model does not know your pricing tiers or return policy) from the behaviour gap (it knows the answer but buries it, uses the wrong tone, or will not escalate), observe that retrieval fixes the first and fine-tuning the second, and then make the first deliverable a 200-500 interaction eval set with every failure tagged as knowledge, behaviour, or both. Every later step keys off that artifact, and its experiment sequence is genuinely discriminating rather than merely comparative: Experiment 2 fine-tunes on behaviour only with factual content deliberately excluded, Experiment 3 adds facts to the training mix, and the delta between them answers the one question that determines the architecture. It then adds two tests A has no analogue for - a staleness test on fifty questions whose answers changed in the last thirty days, which prices the maintenance tax directly, and a composition test that names the specific risk of stacking the two (a behaviour-tuned model may start ignoring retrieved context). Its cost model includes the line items that dominate in practice and that A omits: model-upgrade optionality (RAG is model-agnostic, fine-tuning pins you to a checkpoint), the discreteness and expense of each training run as an experiment, and ongoing labelled-example curation as the hidden cost, with a usable heuristic that retraining more than quarterly probably eats the inference savings. Crucially B gets the factuality logic the right way round, routing grounding to retrieval, whereas A's headline guidance sends hallucination-critical regulated domains to fine-tuning, which inverts the mechanism that actually constrains factual claims. A is not weak - its seven diagnostic questions are sensible, its dollar figures and phased pilot give it more surface actionability, and its retrieval-ablation and data-volume knee curve are two good ideas B lacks - but it is undercut by an internal inconsistency (it declares 1,000-5,000 labelled examples a precondition for fine-tuning and then proposes a pilot that splits 200 tickets into train and test), by weak metrics (exact match and F1 against gold agent replies), and by arbitrary win thresholds asserted without justification. B's only real slips are a garbled model name and one appeal to personal experience. B wins on soundness and on the quality of the experiments."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B is the better curriculum on coverage, sequencing and currency. It runs zero-to-research-ready across seven phases with a named milestone project at the end of every phase, and each sub-block carries a specific course or reading rather than a generic pointer, so a learner always knows what to open next. Crucially it covers the material that actually defines modern practice and that A barely touches: tokenization and BPE, positional encodings including RoPE, decoder-only versus encoder-only, LoRA and QLoRA, RLHF with DPO and GRPO, KV-cache and continuous batching, quantization schemes, FSDP and ZeRO with the four parallelism axes named separately, vLLM and PagedAttention, speculative decoding, state-space models, and mechanistic interpretability with sparse autoencoders. It also handles branching properly, with four specialization tracks and explicit instructions on where to enter given prior background, and its always-on loop (read, code, write, teach) plus a reproduce-two-papers-per-quarter habit is the most useful advice in either answer for sustaining progress. A is well organised and has one structural feature B lacks - an opening self-assessment table across math, programming and prior ML - and it closes by offering to tailor the plan, which is appropriate for so underspecified a request. But A is thinner and dated: no parameter-efficient fine-tuning, no alignment pipeline, no serving stack, distributed training reduced to a single bullet, and its capstone options stop at fine-tuning GPT-2. It also opens with a conceptual error, proposing logistic regression and decision boundaries for Boston house prices, which is a regression target, and it garbles several items (Vision Transformators, LSTM on stock weather or sensor data, DDIM/Predictor). Both invent source attributions, which is the main mark against each: A misattributes Grokking Deep Learning, while B is the worse offender with a nonexistent Elements of ML credited to Cortes and Vapnik, an invented LLM book and YouTube tutorial, a course code that does not correspond to the Stanford generative-models class, and DPO miscategorised as a pre-training objective alongside CLM and MLM. Those are real calibration failures, but they are decorative citations around a substantially deeper, better-staged and more current plan, whereas A's gaps are in the syllabus itself."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both are complete, well-staged pipelines with honest scale-and-cost reality checks, and both contain a similar number of code defects, so the decision turns on which defects matter and which guide reflects what building an LLM actually involves. A's worst bug is silent: TextDataset already returns x as tokens[:-1] and y as tokens[1:], and then train_step shifts again with logits[..., :-1, :] against targets[..., 1:], so the model is trained against targets offset by two positions - the loss will still fall and the user will never see an error, but the resulting model is quietly wrong. Its MixedPrecisionTrainer also constructs a fresh GradScaler inside every train_step, discarding the scaler state that is the entire point of the class, and it puts the parameter count of its own small config at roughly twice the true value. B's errors are mostly API-name mistakes that fail loudly on first run (train_from_iterator called on the trainer rather than the tokenizer, encode_batch(...).data, a nonexistent FSDP.set_auto_wrap_policy, an undefined get_batch, a GradScaler wrapped around a bfloat16 autocast that B itself has just said needs no loss scaling), which a reader fixes in minutes rather than shipping unnoticed. On substance B is the more useful guide: it builds what a current decoder-only model actually is - RoPE, grouped-query attention, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, F.scaled_dot_product_attention - where A builds a GPT-2 replica with learned position embeddings and a hand-rolled attention matmul, and it then covers the parts that decide whether such a project succeeds and that A omits or waves at: data curation as a first-class stage (MinHash dedup, quality filtering, weighted domain mixing, PII removal), a table distinguishing DDP from tensor, pipeline, ZeRO-3 and sequence parallelism by what each actually shards, batch size expressed in tokens per step (2M-16M) rather than sequences, warmup as a percentage of training, throughput and gradient-norm monitoring, KV-cache and PagedAttention and speculative decoding for serving, and SFT plus DPO/GRPO as the step that turns a base model into something usable. Its closing judgement - that data quality, distributed-training stability and compute budget are the hard parts and the architecture is the easiest once built - is the single most valuable sentence in either response. A deserves real credit for two things B lacks: a perplexity evaluation phase, which is a genuine gap in B, and pitching the level closer to the stated audience of someone with only basic Python. But a modern architecture, a realistic account of data and distributed training, and loud rather than silent bugs make B the stronger answer."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both are well-organized and cover the standard ground (funnel decomposition, data sources, comparison table, practical tips), but B reasons rather than enumerates. It anchors on the shared identity Revenue = Traffic x Conversion x AOV and then explains precisely how each term is measured, modelled and constrained differently, which makes the contrast causal rather than categorical. B also surfaces drivers A omits entirely: hard physical capacity ceilings versus soft fulfilment/ad-budget constraints, the high fixed-cost floor that a B&M forecast must clear, per-store nodes and catchment dynamics, response latency to demand shifts (hours vs weeks), marketplace fee drag on net revenue, and online/offline cannibalisation in a hybrid model. Its closing synthesis - online is a demand-and-channel problem, physical retail is a location-and-capacity problem - is a genuine insight that gives the reader a model to reason with, whereas A's bottom line restates its own table. A is accurate and slightly tidier visually, and its shared-best-practices section is useful, but its content stays at checklist altitude with thinner actionability (no channel-level modelling guidance, no forecast-horizon or adjustment-band advice) and no explicit treatment of uncertainty. Neither calibrates uncertainty well, though B at least offers concrete magnitudes hedged as ranges and proposes a worked example as a next step. On depth, insight and actionability B is clearly ahead."}

But those are three isolated advantages against B's broader and more mechanism-aware coverage on both halves. B edges it on depth and actionability; A is the better choice only if measurement uncertainty is the reviewer's chief concern."}

B also has a misaligned table row. Net: B is the better template, A is the better argument and the better methodology, and on soundness and insight A takes it."}

It scores each item numerically on both requested axes so the reader can see where effectiveness and cost diverge, and it converts the ranking into a dated rollout, including the genuinely clever move of reusing the production loop detector as a component of the RL reward so the training objective and the production monitor share a metric. {"choice": "B", "rationale": "A is well-written, economical and academically well-formed - a single-paragraph scope followed by six cleanly abstracted limitation categories - but it stays almost entirely at the level of category labels. It never states what effectiveness will actually be measured, so the reader cannot tell whether the study quantifies radial deviation, concentricity, positional repeatability or something else, nor how many trials per condition constitute the 'statistically robust series' it claims. B operationalises exactly these things: it names the dependent variables and the dispersion statistics, gives a trial count per condition, specifies the material categories by hardness and machinability with the mechanisms of interest (density, grain structure, friction), and defines the experimental factor space to include bit diameter, feed rate, spindle speed and surface condition - which is what actually makes 'delineate the operational window' a testable aim rather than a slogan. On the limitations half, B covers everything A does - single configuration, bounded material and dimensional envelope, controlled versus field conditions, operator variability, finite trials and wear, excluded economic and ergonomic factors, guarded generalisability - and adds several substantive items A misses entirely: hole depth-to-diameter ratio, stepped and non-perpendicular holes, minimum guide engagement thickness for thin stock, named machine-specific confounds such as spindle runout and table flatness, and the specific failure modes (delamination, burr formation, anisotropy) that motivate excluding composites and exotic alloys. B also converts its limitations into future-research directions, which is what a scope-and-limitations chapter is expected to do. A's brevity is a genuine virtue and its prose is tighter, but on depth, specificity and actionability B is clearly the stronger research document, and length is not counted against it since the structure keeps it readable."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is the more rigorous design and, crucially, gets the hard semantics right. Its cancellation contract is precise - cooperative SIGTERM with a 30s grace and a SIGKILL backstop, with the API promising only 'will be stopped within grace plus kill timeout' and recording force_killed, honored_at and a classified error reason. B rejects hard cancel outright in favour of checkpoint-then-release, which assumes every job is checkpointable and leaves no answer for a process that ignores the signal; on a host with exactly one GPU that is precisely the failure that wedges the service. A also makes cancel idempotent and forgiving, returning 200 with the current state when the job has already terminated, and explicitly argues why the more 'honest' 409 is worse because it forces every client to handle an otherwise no-op race - B chooses that 409 without noticing the cost. A's idempotency is fully specified, including the case B omits entirely: same key with a different body returns 409 with the original job id, plus 201-versus-200 so replays are distinguishable. A's back-pressure reasoning is sharper (503 with Retry-After because the client did nothing wrong, 429 reserved for per-tenant rate limiting so one tenant cannot starve the queue), it separates liveness from readiness so an orchestrator can drain rather than kill mid-run, and its versioning section does the thing most designs forget - states are an open enum and clients must tolerate unknown fields and new states. Its rejected-tradeoffs table is also genuinely reasoned rather than a restatement, covering DELETE-as-cancel, client-supplied ids and IDOR, automatic retries causing duplicate side effects, and synchronous create dying at proxy timeouts. B is not weak: progress, live GPU metrics, an error-code schema with details, ETA and queue position, and webhooks are real additions A lacks, and webhooks-over-SSE is a defensible call for a host that restarts. But B's state diagram contradicts its own transition list with a running-to-queued arrow, it labels cancelling an internal state while returning it to clients, it has no list endpoint, no log access, no job timeout and no terminal-state immutability rule. A is the stronger answer on soundness and completeness."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both open with the right framing - that training a frontier-scale model is out of reach and the tractable project is a small GPT you actually understand - but A executes the pipeline far more soundly. Its architecture section implements the causal mask explicitly, uses pre-norm blocks, weight tying and sensible initialisation, and its sampling code implements temperature, top-k, top-p and a repetition penalty correctly. B's model never actually applies a causal mask: it calls nn.MultiheadAttention without attn_mask and relegates the fix to a parenthetical note, so the code as written leaks future tokens and does not train a language model at all - the single most important correctness detail in this task. B compounds this by applying the final LayerNorm after the vocabulary projection rather than before it, loads a tokenizers.Tokenizer from a directory saved by transformers, uses .ids and ['ids'] inconsistently across two files, writes scaler = autocast(), references GPT2LMHeadModel without importing it, and closes with a one-file demo that fine-tunes pretrained GPT-2 while being presented as the from-scratch build - which contradicts the whole premise. A is not clean either: its dataset already produces shifted x and y and then the trainer shifts a second time, an off-by-one that wastes a token per sequence, and it constructs the GradScaler inside the training step so its state resets every iteration. But those degrade training rather than invalidate the objective. A is also the more complete curriculum - quality filtering heuristics, custom BPE training, gradient accumulation, mixed precision, distributed options, perplexity evaluation, a parameter-count and cost reference table, and a staged learning path - whereas B skips evaluation entirely. B's genuinely better contributions are its caveats section (data curation matters more than architecture, from-scratch is rarely the efficient path, bias auditing) and its tighter project scaffolding, and its brevity is a real virtue for a beginner. It is not enough to offset code that would not do what it claims."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "The decisive design question here is how to buy power from 200 runs, and B gets it right: a common task corpus instantiated in all five languages makes the comparison paired, so task difficulty is differenced out and McNemar-style analysis extracts materially more power than five independent groups. B states that tradeoff explicitly, and it also confronts the repeats question head-on - zero repeats per task-language cell, spending the budget on task diversity instead - and justifies it rather than eliding it. A's allocation is nominally similar but it describes its 40 runs per language as independent attempts with fresh prompts and different seeds, conflating repeats with distinct tasks, and it never exploits pairing at all, so it leaves the largest available power gain on the table; its model specification also misfires, since a random intercept per run is unidentifiable when there is exactly one observation per run (the grouping should be per task). Both power arguments contain arithmetic errors of comparable severity: A computes a noncentrality of 50 at four degrees of freedom and then reports 81 percent power, which is far too low for that lambda, while B rearranges its sample-size formula without taking the square root and so quotes a detectable difference roughly half the true value for independent proportions. Neither plans for multiplicity across ten pairwise comparisons. On inconclusive reporting A has one clear advantage - TOST against an explicit region of practical equivalence, which is the right way to distinguish absence of evidence from evidence of absence, and B omits equivalence testing entirely. But B's reporting section is otherwise more operational and more honest: worked example numbers, a tiered evidence-language table that binds claims to interval width and power, sensitivity analyses showing whether the verdict survives task removal and difficulty reweighting, and a summary table with an explicit note that inconclusive does not mean equivalent. Net, B's superior design reasoning and more concrete uncertainty reporting outweigh A's broader metric set and its equivalence test."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both are honest about the central fact - 200 runs buys roughly a 30-percentage-point pairwise MDE and nothing finer - and both reach it by essentially the same arithmetic, so the separation is in the quality of the design reasoning around that constraint. B is markedly deeper. It runs a pilot outside the budget to obtain the per-tier success priors the power calculation then depends on, and it uses those priors to allocate runs by Bernoulli information content rather than splitting evenly: p(1-p) weighting puts the largest share in the Medium tier where the language contrast is most identifiable and the least in the ceiling-effect Easy tier. That is a genuine, quantified allocation argument; A's flat split across tiers is defensible but unjustified beyond divisibility. B also propagates the task random effect through the power calculation via an explicit design effect and ICC, so its effective n is smaller and more honest than the nominal n, and it computes separate MDEs for the language main effect, the difficulty main effect and the interaction - then states plainly that the interaction is severely underpowered at roughly 65 pp and refuses to bury that. It reserves a 10 percent buffer governed by a pre-registered, logged reallocation rule, plans Holm correction across the ten pairwise contrasts, pre-specifies sensitivity analyses including a partial-credit re-scoring, adds a Bayesian supplement reporting P(effect greater than a pre-registered practical threshold), and includes a threats-to-validity table covering the two failure modes that actually invalidate cross-language agent evals: benchmark memorisation (handled with multiple fresh hidden-test variants) and task-idiomaticity bias (handled by authoring one semantic spec and having native developers rate the translations). Its section on what it will not do - no post-hoc task dropping, no bare p-values - is the strongest inconclusive-reporting protocol in either answer. A is clean, correct, well-calibrated and makes one good strategic call, pivoting the study's purpose from ranking languages to locating difficulty-tier failure modes given the power it actually has, and its 20-tasks-per-language design has better external validity than B's 9 tasks. But its claim that two repeats is the threshold for valid variance estimation is weak for a binary outcome, it omits multiplicity correction entirely, and it offers no allocation argument beyond balance. B is the stronger plan."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "The prompt asks for a comprehensive list plus three detailed summaries, and the two responses split those halves. B's list is nominally longer at twenty items but is badly padded: entries 15 through 20 are not frameworks at all, they are pairwise combinations of the same three frameworks already listed, and two of them (PARA plus Zettelkasten, listed twice as separate items) are outright duplicates of each other; item 11 restates item 1 under a different name, and items 12 and 13 are generic placeholders with no identifiable source. But on the detailed half A is clearly stronger: each of its three summaries gives a numbered operating procedure, a separate best-practices list with concrete thresholds (two to three links per new note, a ten-to-fifteen-minute weekly review, the ten-percent distillation rule), an explicit ideal user, and expected outcomes, whereas B's summaries largely restate each framework's own vocabulary without telling the reader how to run it. A also closes with the most useful reasoning in either answer - how the three compose (PARA as structural backbone, Zettelkasten as the idea-generation engine, CODE as the habit loop) and a selection rule keyed to the reader's actual friction point. Both share the same weaknesses: each picks two Forte frameworks for its top three despite PARA being a component of CODE, each misattributes progressive summarization to Zettelkasten, and each has an attribution slip (A credits Personal Knowledge Mastery to the wrong author and overstates its number of disciplines; B attributes the digital-garden idea to the wrong practitioner). A's depth and actionability outweigh B's broader but heavily padded catalogue."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both design a sensible five-session arc from alignment through messaging, channels, timeline and measurement, and both chain each session's outputs into the next. A is the more usable facilitation artefact because it budgets time at the activity level - a timed agenda with breaks for every session - so the design is falsifiable: you can see that stakeholder mapping gets thirty minutes and judge whether that is enough. B gives only a session total, and its timings do not survive scrutiny: Workshop 2 packs affinity clustering of support data, a persona sprint, a full journey map with emotion curve, and a gap matrix into ninety minutes, while the accompanying tip prescribes strict five-minute timeboxes, which is internally inconsistent. A also handles the parts of facilitation that are about conflict and accountability rather than exercises: a decision log and parking lot as standing ground rules, explicit synthesis and circulation within twenty-four hours, reflection time between sessions, a rule that disagreements are surfaced and resolved or escalated, a launch-day run-of-show with failure branches, an internal-comms block that most launch plans forget, a pre-mortem for contingency, and - notably - success criteria for the workshop series itself, which is the kind of meta-discipline a facilitation expert should bring. B's real strengths are genuine: per-session facilitation technique that a novice could copy (silent-first-then-speak to stop dominance, round-robin for tone descriptors, dot voting to prioritise risk), richer communications craft that A omits entirely (tone and voice, funnel-aligned content pillars, proof-point mining, asset gap tracking, an accessibility and SEO check), concrete pre-work, and a post-work schedule that ends with a post-launch retrospective - the one structural element A lacks. It is a close call, and B would be the better pick for a team that needs the comms substance more than the process rigour. A wins on the strength of its time design, its handling of disagreement and ownership, and its overall operational realism."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B is the stronger threat model by a wide margin because it reasons from the specific mechanics of this system rather than from a generic checklist. It identifies the correct number-one path - adversarial text embedded in source files the agent must read, flowing through the model into an executed command - and names the reverse trust boundary that makes it possible (untrusted content entering the agent), which A never articulates; A treats injection only as something arriving from the model, missing that the repository itself is the injection channel. B's asset list is concrete where it matters (.ssh, .aws, .npmrc, lockfiles, git remotes, the agent's own system prompt and config as an asset whose compromise persists across sessions), its attacker table assigns likelihoods and explicitly rejects the nation-state framing in favour of what actually happens on a laptop, and its attack paths each carry a why-it-ranks-here argument. The v1 mitigations are implementable and named at the OS-primitive level - landlock and seccomp, sandbox-exec profiles, AppContainer and Job Objects, process-group kill on negative PID, an egress proxy with pre-registered registries, HOME redirected to a per-session temp dir so credentials are unreadable rather than merely forbidden. Two ideas in particular are genuinely insightful: forcing the model to emit a validated structured tool call instead of a raw shell string, which makes injected shell metacharacters syntactically inexpressible, and the reader/executor split where the context-reading model has no shell tool at all. B also closes with residual risks it does not claim to have solved, a refuse-to-run-as-root rule, a local-model option, and an explicit ship-order principle - shrink blast radius first because a contained failure is recoverable, shrink probability later. A is competently organised and its section headings cover the requested ground, but its content is largely generic: attack paths are described without ranking or mechanism, and its central v1 control is precisely the wrong one - rejecting output that contains shell metacharacters and whitelisting characters by regex is a known-bad sanitisation approach that B explicitly supersedes with AST-level parsing. A also omits package postinstall execution, the agent's own config as a persistence target, egress control in v1, and any residual-risk discussion."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "The prompt asks specifically for experiments that discriminate between the options, and A is the only one that designs for discrimination rather than measurement. Its organising idea - decompose the gap into knowledge versus behaviour, because knowledge belongs in the retriever and behaviour belongs in the weights - gives every subsequent step a decision rule, and two of its experiments are genuinely sharp: the ablation that reruns the fine-tuned model with retrieval removed, which distinguishes a healthy style-and-protocol fine-tune from one that has baked perishable facts into weights, and the negative control that fine-tunes on off-domain data to confirm the eval can detect a fine-tune effect at all rather than reporting noise. Neither appears in B. A's per-axis delta reading is also more decision-useful than a pass/fail threshold: three points on accuracy but twelve on tone tells you to keep retrieval for knowledge and fine-tune only for behaviour. Its cost model names the item most TCO tables miss - that every major base-model release forces a re-fine-tune, so the open-weight fine-tune arm forfeits free upstream improvements - and it ties volume tiers to which cost line actually dominates. B is tighter and has real strengths A lacks: a four-arm design that includes a prompting-only baseline, an explicit break-even formula with a volume range, a decision-flow diagram, a failure-mode taxonomy naming why each approach breaks, and the good observation that a five-point increase in escalations at fifteen dollars each can erase inference savings. But several of its numbers are asserted rather than reasoned, and one is substantively questionable: it sets a stricter hallucination target for the fine-tuned arm than for the retrieval arm, which inverts the usual relationship since grounding, not weight updates, is what suppresses fabrication. B also treats the decision largely as a threshold check, where A treats it as a diagnosis. A wins on experimental design, mechanism and calibrated conditions; B wins on concision and the break-even arithmetic."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "B is economical and well-written - a single flowing scope paragraph followed by six cleanly abstracted limitation categories - and its phrasing is arguably more polished than A's. But it stays almost entirely at the level of category labels: it never says which materials, which dimensional envelope, how many trials, or what quantity is measured, so a reader cannot tell what the study actually commits to doing. A specifies exactly that: named dimensional bands in millimetres for small, medium and large workpieces, material families enumerated by class (ferrous, non-ferrous, polymers and composites, wood products), flat versus curved versus irregular surfaces, and deviation from target centre analysed statistically against stated tolerances. On the limitations half A also reaches several boundaries B misses entirely and that matter for this particular instrument: drill-bit and host-machine variability as a confound, surface-condition effects such as painted or coated stock, and a scope-of-operations limit that explicitly excludes hole-diameter accuracy, surface finish, deep-hole and angled drilling - the last being a genuine and easily overlooked constraint on a centring guide. Both cover the common ground (single tool configuration, bounded material and dimensional envelope, controlled versus field conditions, operator variability, finite trials and long-term wear, no cost-benefit analysis). A's weaknesses are stylistic and mild: the phrase 'does not comprehensively' recurs as a hedge often enough to blur which exclusions are firm, it claims a trial count sufficient for statistical significance without naming one, and its scope promises a time-efficiency comparison while its limitations disclaim economic evaluation, a small tension B avoids by excluding productivity measures outright. Those do not offset the specificity gap. A is the more informative and more actionable scope-and-limitations section; B would be preferable only if brevity were the overriding constraint."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B reads like a review written by someone who has actually adjudicated ranking experiments. It leads with the integrity checks that decide whether the p-value means anything at all - sample ratio mismatch, pre-experiment covariate balance, and whether the randomisation unit was the user or the session - and then asks whether the test was stopped on a peek, requiring a sequential correction if so. A omits all four of these, and they are the most common reasons a marginal ranking result evaporates. B is also the only one to treat the specific pathology of ranking changes: novelty, tested concretely by splitting new versus returning users and inspecting whether the gap converges; metric gaming, where CTR rises while satisfaction or time-on-task falls; guardrails for diversity, spam and toxicity; negative controls that should not move; and the monetisation trap where engagement rises but CPM falls so net revenue declines. Its winner's-curse point about effect overestimation in underpowered tests is correctly stated, and its ship path is operational rather than notional - canary at one percent, a fast kill switch, a four-week persistence check, a post-rollout diversity audit - plus an explicit gate table and named rejection triggers. A is a competent review with two things B lacks: it flags the genuine ambiguity in '0.8 percent' between percentage points and relative lift, which materially changes the interpretation, and it asks whether the live result agrees with offline validation as an overfitting check. But A contains a real statistical inconsistency, twice recommending against shipping if the confidence interval includes zero when p = 0.03 already implies it does not, and its claim that an underpowered test can produce p = 0.03 for a trivial effect is muddled where B's framing is right. A's demanded analyses are also mostly statistical hygiene, with no safety or integrity layer. B is the stronger review."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both convert the user's sketch into a role-plus-template-plus-workflow prompt, both fence it for copy-paste, and both correctly identify the hard requirements: cumulative state, always return the whole document, leave irrelevant sections alone, justify rather than describe. A is the more directive artefact, which is what matters for a prompt that must produce consistent output over many turns. It specifies the internal shape of each section rather than just its title - named column layouts for the assumptions table, for the per-table field table including a constraint column, and for procedure parameters including direction - and it asks for Mermaid erDiagram syntax by name, a symbol legend, per-relationship cardinality and policy annotations, a numbered walkthrough of each procedure body, and a note on error handling. B's template restates the section headings with a sentence of guidance each, so two different runs could produce very differently shaped documents. A also handles the user's vaguest instruction better: it supplies literal placeholder text for sections not yet applicable, so the document's skeleton is stable from the first turn, and it adds a gap-analysis step that builds a checklist from the guidelines and records unaddressed requirements as Pending Items - the most direct answer to 'ensure every part of the assignment guidelines are assessed'. Its closing usage table plus the note about re-pasting the guidelines each turn versus citing only the relevant STEP numbers shows awareness of the real failure mode in long iterative threads, which is requirement drift as context is dropped. A additionally keeps the user's own 'Reaction Policies' heading, whereas B renames it to Referential Integrity and Cascade Policies - defensible as terminology and honestly flagged, but a deviation from a format the user may be graded against. B's genuine advantages are its named trigger phrases, the per-iteration status header summarising what changed, and the instruction to propose a defensible default when information is missing; A partly matches the first two with its Iteration Summary. On balance A's greater structural specificity and its explicit gap-tracking outweigh B's cleaner invocation protocol."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A has both the more complete taxonomy and the more careful account of where quality is lost. It covers grouped-query and multi-query attention as an architectural KV reduction and low-rank or layer-shared factorisation - two of the most consequential levers in practice - and B omits both entirely, which is a significant gap given that GQA alone accounts for most of the KV reduction in current open models. A's per-method analysis consistently answers the harder half of the question, not just the mechanism but the shape of the damage: the sliding window fails as a cliff rather than a curve; attention-score eviction is myopic because it scores what was attended to rather than what will be, so the failure is silent and distributed and shows up as a plausible-but-wrong identifier; quantisation error is uniform across the sequence with no lost region; gist compression loses granularity not gist, which is exactly wrong for exact symbol resolution. Its recommendation follows from that analysis, is quantified end to end, and correctly identifies silent symbol loss as the failure mode that matters for a repository agent. B is well-organised, its citations of H2O, SnapKV, KIVI and KVQuant are accurate, and it contributes two genuinely good points A lacks - that keys are more quantisation-sensitive than values, and that processing files in dependency order changes which tokens attention will have marked as important. But it has real soundness problems. It rates token merging as excellent for code while its own section concedes that merging can collapse distinct variable references; A's opposing argument, that near-identical identifiers are precisely what must not be conflated, is the better reasoning. It files Tree of Thoughts under hierarchical KV compression, which is a category error - that is a prompting and search method, not a cache technique - and its StreamingLLM placement under summary-based chunking is misattributed. Its pseudocode conflates token-level preprocessing with KV-cache operations, applying merging and SnapKV eviction to token lists before generation. Finally it dismisses retrieval outright for repositories, which is hard to sustain when a large repo exceeds any feasible resident cache; A's position - external KV with a code-aware, symbol-level retriever and gist tokens used as pointers rather than substitutes - is the more defensible design."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both responses cover the required six areas competently with structure-aware chunking, hash-based incremental re-embedding, hybrid BM25+dense retrieval with RRF and cross-encoder reranking, citation-mandated grounding, and layered faithfulness evaluation, so the baseline is close. B pulls ahead on depth and actionability at several load-bearing points: it makes the parent-child index an explicit architectural commitment (retrieve on children, generate on parents) rather than an afterthought; it bakes the embedding model version into the chunk hash and works through the consequence (a full re-embed migration with a dual-index cutover) instead of leaving the model-upgrade path undiscussed; it specifies ANN-time metadata filtering rather than post-filtering and correctly names the recall collapse that post-filtering causes at high selectivity; and it adds a calibrated confidence gate plus a second per-chunk relevance floor, which is the one mechanism in either answer that actually prevents the generator from being handed near-miss context. Its failure-mode section is also the stronger analysis: it timestamps each mode by when it would first appear, distinguishes the pure latency window from the genuinely dangerous case where old and new versions of a rewritten section coexist in the index, and its third mode contains the sharpest insight in either answer -- that blended paraphrase from tangential chunks slips past NLI faithfulness checks as 'neutral' rather than 'contradiction', with the follow-through that the neutral label should count as failure for code/config docs but not for prose. A is cleaner, better paced, and its closing framing (freshness and pipeline reliability over prompt tuning) is apt, and its catch about hashing parsed rather than raw text is a good specific detail, but its failure modes are more generic and its mitigations stop at the level of advice where B's stop at the level of a threshold you could implement. B's cost is some over-engineering and ASCII diagrams that add bulk without much signal, but its headings and tables keep it navigable, so the extra material does not damage clarity enough to offset the added substance."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is the more disciplined design document and answers the prompt's five asks more precisely. Its stages each carry an explicit budget cap, a single cheapest disqualifier, and a stated promotion criterion, and it adds a budget invariant (stages 0-3 must total under 60% of the weekly compute) that actually engages the one-machine constraint rather than just restating it. Its caching section is substantially deeper: results are content-addressed by the tuple (weight fingerprint, set version, prompt id, precision, seed), with the explicit warning never to key on display name because names get reused and forked, plus family-level memoisation that re-tests only the axes a prior version was weak on and structural memoisation that skips the smoke test when config and tokenizer hashes are byte-identical. The honesty section targets the right failure: it blinds the model name from the operator's own terminal during early stages rather than only from a human rating panel, makes stages 0-3 mechanical so the score is written before a human sees it, logs overrides with reason codes and tracks the override rate as a calibration signal, and fixes the incumbent rather than the favourite as the bar. B is broader in coverage and contributes two genuinely good ideas A lacks -- re-running the champion every week as an instrument check that invalidates the week if it fails, and a rotating devil's advocate -- but it is looser and contains real internal contradictions. Its stated core principle that false positives carry unbounded cost is directly contradicted by its stage-2 design choice to set thresholds low specifically to avoid false negatives. Its stage-3 disqualifier (below champion on any benchmark) is negated by its own promotion rule (within noise on all OR better on one). Its dedup table re-runs from stage 1 or 2 in nearly every row, so it saves little, and the results schema is keyed per model rather than per prompt and seed, which cannot support partial resume. The transfer-learning predictor is under-argued and its worked example is incoherent (predict a stage-3 failure, then skip to stage 3 anyway). Its funnel metrics set pass-rate targets, which is a gameable target that rewards failing candidates, and its false-negative-rate target is unmeasurable in a design that never revisits rejects. It also assumes a multi-person team (three evaluators, independent approvers, ceremonies) that sits awkwardly with the single-machine, likely single-operator framing. A is tighter, internally consistent, and more actionable."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "This is essentially a reference task -- name the frameworks and their originators -- so attribution accuracy carries most of the weight, and A fails it repeatedly. A invents a 'MAFIA Method (Memos, Articles, Files, Images, Audio)' and credits it to Ahrens; attributes Linking Your Thinking to Andy Matuschak when it is Nick Milo's; cites a Peter Elbow book title that does not exist; credits 'The Art of Thinking' to W. Edwards Deming; hangs the knowledge-management lifecycle on Senge; and asserts flatly that Matuschak coined 'digital garden' in 2020, when the gardening framing runs back through Caulfield and Bernstein and Matuschak's own term is evergreen notes. It also misreads Luhmann's addressing scheme, describing sequential IDs whose position encodes chronology, which inverts the point of the branching decimal system. B carries one clear error, attributing progressive summarization to Nick Milo rather than Tiago Forte, and repeats it, but otherwise its entries are real and correctly sourced, including the MOCs and LYT attributions A gets wrong, and its account of Luhmann placing a new note between existing ones to force articulation of where the idea fits is both accurate and the sharper observation. B's list is also better organized -- grouped by organizing principle rather than by workflow stage -- whereas A pads to forty entries with items that are reasoning heuristics rather than knowledge-organization frameworks (5 Whys, deliberate practice, dual coding, first-principles thinking), so its greater length buys less than it appears to. On the top three, A offers more procedural surface (review cadences, tool lists, explicit ranking justifications) and B offers more conceptual precision (evergreen phrasing, the title as the claim, the lattice, notes as executable interfaces), and B's choice of Matuschak's evergreen notes as the third entry engages the question's own 'Tools for Thought' framing more directly than A's digital gardens. Neither hedges its attributions, so calibration is weak in both; A's confident assertion of fabricated sources makes that weakness materially worse. B is the sounder answer."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "The prompt carries a constraint that is easy to skip past -- reduce runaways *without lowering answer quality* -- and B is the only response that operationalizes it, attaching an explicit quality-preservation mechanism to every single proposal rather than treating it as an afterthought. A raises the same concern only once, in a closing caveat about penalizing legitimate self-correction, which is a good observation but arrives after all eight of its proposals have been ranked without reference to it. B is also the more mechanism-grounded brainstorm: entropy-gated temperature scheduling keys the intervention to the entropy collapse that actually precedes a degenerate attractor rather than to the symptom, contrastive subtraction of the recent-context distribution from the logits is specified with a coefficient range, and adaptive token budgeting that reserves a fixed share for the conclusion is the one idea in either response that engages directly with the prompt's framing that the budget is what ends the response. Its hedging is distributed and specific (model-dependent, variable results, alpha needs tuning, risk of regression on other capabilities) rather than concentrated in a single paragraph. A's advantages are real but narrower: it is tidier, its two ranking tables list the same eight items so they can be read against each other, and its recommendation section reasons explicitly about effectiveness-per-cost by citing both ranks, which is more decision-useful than B's overlapping recommendation matrix.
