B's main cost is that its ranking tables bundle methods into composite rows with inconsistent groupings across the two lists (eight rows versus ten, different pairings), which makes cross-referencing effectiveness against cost harder than it should be, and several of its quality-preservation cells restate the same 'only intervenes on confirmed loops' line in near-identical wording. That is a genuine clarity cost, but it does not outweigh the added specificity and the fact that B answers the full question A answers only three quarters of."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B gets the central epistemic point right and A gets it wrong. B states that mechanisms transfer as directional hypotheses that must still be re-validated numerically, whereas A puts its transferable list under a heading reading 'No Re-Measurement Required (Validated)' -- which is precisely the confusion the prompt asks the report structure to prevent, committed by the report itself. The content of the two mechanism lists is not comparable either: B names real causal relationships (quantization error scaling with layer sensitivity, KV cache dominating memory past long-context thresholds, throughput scaling with batch until the memory bound, kernel routing accounting for a large share of performance variance, fixed per-token MoE routing overhead), while A lists things that are not mechanisms at all -- that the eval script is pure Python, that pip install works, that requirements are OS-agnostic. Worse, A asserts as a transferable mechanism that sampling produces an identical output distribution across devices at the same seed, which is false in practice given differing kernels, reduction orders and batch-dependent nondeterminism, and it presents cross-hardware agreement as already-observed evidence in a study that has not yet been run. B also catches the structural point A misses entirely: H200 and B200 are separate targets, and an H200 result must not be generalized to Blackwell, which B makes a standing clause and a separate column in its decision matrix while A treats the two as one bucket throughout. On actionability B again goes further, mapping each archived verdict to a specific re-measurement task with an expected shift and a numeric validation gate, against A's five-bullet protocol. The single sharpest idea in either response is B's classifier heuristic -- would this still hold if VRAM doubled; if yes it is a mechanism, if no it is a verdict -- which converts the whole taxonomy into something a reader can apply without the author. A's real contribution is its section-gating discipline (no hardware numbers in the mechanisms section, device-prefixed metric syntax, a read-only baseline archive, no cross-section speedup claims), which is concrete and good, but B's safeguards are equivalent in force and add a reference-but-never-carry-forward rule, an explicit banned-sentence pattern, and a second-reviewer pass. Both responses carry hardware-spec errors; A's are the more serious, understating H200 and B200 memory bandwidth by roughly a factor of four and inventing a PCIe generation, while B's main slip is an inflated B200 capacity figure. B is the better study."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "A is a competent but generic experiment review -- it would read the same for any A/B test of anything, and it omits several checks that a practitioner would treat as mandatory. B is written by someone who knows this specific problem. Its most important edge is putting sample ratio mismatch first, as a binary validity gate that forecloses any discussion of effect size if it fails, with the raw counts, the chi-squared p-value and a day-by-day count plot demanded; A never mentions SRM at all, and it is the single highest-yield instrumentation check in online experimentation. B also asks whether the randomization unit is the user rather than the session or request, and names the consequence (within-user correlation inflating apparent significance), which A misses entirely. The sharpest ranking-specific insight in either response is B's position-bias confound: a ranking change is by construction a position change, so the lift may be an artifact of moving already-high-CTR items up the well-known position gradient rather than any relevance gain, and B makes failure to resolve that an independent blocker. B adds the ecosystem dimension A has no analogue for -- result diversity and concentration, supply-side traffic shifts to smaller sellers, reformulation rate -- and correctly notes that three weeks yields only one 28-day retention window, so the long-horizon evidence is thin by construction. Its pre-registration questions are more precise (was this the pre-registered primary or the fourteenth metric on the dashboard; was the MDE larger than the observed effect, which would make the p-value close to meaningless), and it demands a trimmed-window sensitivity re-analysis excluding the novelty days, which is a concrete test A does not propose. Crucially, the prompt asks how the reviewer would decide, and B actually decides: no big-bang rollout, a conditional phased ship at 25-50 percent with pre-agreed kill criteria if the checks come back clean, segment-only ship if the effect is concentrated, and hard stop if the position artifact is unresolved. A stops at a framework and a hedge about a cautious rollout. A's genuine contributions -- flagging the percentage-point versus relative-lift ambiguity, and asking about false discovery correction across prior model iterations -- are both present in B in equivalent or stronger form. B's small imprecisions (its flat-prior posterior figure is a couple of points off, and the persona flourishes add nothing) do not come close to closing the gap."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is both the more accurate summary and the sounder procedure. On the literature, B asserts that attention projections are typically more sensitive than FFN weights, which inverts the consensus -- the FFN down-projection is the notoriously hard matrix, because the post-activation hidden state carries the outlier channels and the dimensionality reduction concentrates error -- and A gets this right, ranking down-projection and attention output above Q/K/V, with a stated mechanism. A also works at the granularity that matters for this task: individual weight matrices, with a budget equation tying the count of 8-bit matrices to the bit budget. B allocates whole transformer blocks, which is coarser than its own observation about within-block variation warrants, and leaves the budget as an abstract k. The decisive difference is the sensitivity measurement. A quantizes one matrix at a time against an otherwise full-precision model and scores the end-to-end change in output logits -- a clean isolation design measuring the quantity that actually matters. B measures sequentially, leaving each previously quantized layer quantized, so every score is taken against a progressively more degraded baseline and the resulting numbers are not comparable across layers; B presents this as capturing error propagation, but it confounds sensitivity with position in the sequence. Compounding that, B's metric is a local output perturbation of the layer itself rather than any end-to-end effect, and its pseudocode quantizes every layer to 4-bit in phase 1 without restoring, then re-quantizes in phase 3. A is also more honest about the stated constraint. B's validation section offers MMLU, GSM8K, HellaSwag and ARC under a heading claiming they require no labelling, which quietly redefines the no-labelled-data premise rather than working within it, and lists compression ratio as a validation method though it says nothing about quality, and validates on a split of the calibration set rather than a disjoint corpus. A stays label-free, insists the held-out corpus be disjoint from calibration, adds logit KL and top-k agreement as more sensitive than perplexity, checks allocation stability across calibration draws with an explicit overlap threshold, ablates the force-protected embedding and head to confirm the prior, and when it mentions an executable smoke test it flags that this is not labelled evaluation in the supervised sense. A's assumptions are the better-calibrated set, including the non-obvious one that the score only reflects irreducible error if the quantizer is well-behaved, and it names the limitation of isolated measurement -- that per-matrix scores do not perfectly predict joint degradation -- and adds a greedy swap step specifically to correct for it."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both answers get the shared skeleton right -- traffic or footfall times conversion times ticket size -- and both are clearly organised, so the decision turns on coverage and specificity. A opens by making the common formula explicit and then shows how each term is estimated differently on each side, which is a cleaner framing of 'what are the key differences' than listing two parallel approaches and hoping the contrast lands. It also names the methods a practitioner would actually use rather than just the variables: same-store or like-for-like sales analysis, which is the standard workhorse for an established retailer and which B omits entirely -- a real gap in an answer about forecasting physical retail. A adds capacity-constraint modelling, catchment-based location forecasting, cohort analysis by acquisition month, and the only quantitative calibration in either response, contrasting online apparel return rates around 15-30 percent against 2-8 percent in store, which is both roughly right and materially important since returns sit between gross bookings and recognised revenue. It further covers ground B leaves untouched: separate leading-indicator lists per channel, the reminder that revenue is not profit and that CAC, LTV, shipping and rent have to be modelled alongside it, and explicit guidance for hybrid operators to forecast channels separately and then model cross-channel effects such as buy-online-pickup-in-store and showrooming, which is the situation most real retailers are in. B's strongest contribution is genuinely sharper than anything in A: the observation that online you largely choose your traffic by choosing ad spend, so the forecast is partly a planning exercise rather than an extrapolation, with the corollary that the online model is driven by decisions you control while the retail model is driven by local conditions you do not. Its symmetric treatment of funnel leakage is also neat. But that is one insight against a broader and more actionable answer, and B's remaining content is largely a subset of A's, with a weak line about server capacity as an online ceiling. A's emoji headers are cosmetic noise and its length is greater, but the structure keeps it readable throughout, so length does not cost clarity."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "A looks far more substantial -- schemas, a thousand lines of code, architecture diagrams, a decision matrix -- but its central ML deliverable is unsound in a way that invalidates it. The win/loss classifier derives its target from deal_stage (target = stage == 4), trains only on rows where stage is 4 or 5, and then includes deal_stage itself in the feature matrix, so the label is perfectly determined by a feature; the model-comparison table it prints will show near-perfect accuracy and AUC and mean nothing. It then scores open deals whose stage values (0-3) never appeared in training, refits LabelEncoder separately on the open-deal frame so the product, customer and rep encodings do not match the training mapping, and feeds deal_duration_days, which is derived from closed_date and is therefore both null and leaky for open deals. The split is random rather than temporal, which is the wrong design for a pipeline that evolves over time, and none of this is flagged -- there is no validation discussion, no leakage caveat, no statement of assumptions, no uncertainty anywhere. Several blocks would also fail at runtime (aggregating a deal_count column that does not exist in the revenue frame, merging on product_name while it is the index), and the growth rate taken as last quarter over first quarter across pooled years is not a growth rate. The prioritization weights (0.35/0.30/0.20/0.15) are asserted without justification, and rank-percentile scoring is a weaker construct than the expected-value quantity the problem actually calls for. B has no code, and it does misread one requirement: the user explicitly asks to focus on products far from target, while B's tier-A criterion and its priority formula's (1 - |budget gap|) term both reward products already near target, and it repeats this in the takeaway without flagging the disagreement -- A handles the budget requirement correctly with gap severity tiers. But B's reasoning is otherwise the sounder of the two: it centres prioritization on expected revenue as deal size times win probability, proposes survival and stage-transition analysis for the funnel, derives stage-duration percentiles with a concrete trigger (auto-flag a deal lingering past the 75th percentile in Negotiate), adds what-if simulation to quantify what would actually close a target gap, maps each lifecycle stage to a monitored KPI, and closes the loop from lost-deal reason codes back into product and model decisions. It is also far easier to read and comes with a phased roadmap and deliverables. A's strongest single contribution is its revenue-versus-growth quadrant, which answers the high-revenue-versus-low-revenue question crisply, but that does not offset a headline model that is broken by construction and presented without a single caveat."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "The architecture code is the centrepiece of a from-scratch LLM guide, and A's is correct and current while B's is neither. A implements RoPE with the standard rotate-half formulation, grouped-query attention with the right repeat_interleave axis, SwiGLU with the correct gate/up/down wiring, RMSNorm, pre-norm residual blocks and tied embeddings -- all of it right, and each modern component is named and motivated. B's Block defines ln1 and then never applies it, passes attn_mask=None to nn.MultiheadAttention without is_causal, and so silently trains a bidirectional model on a next-token objective; that is the one bug that invalidates the entire exercise, and the comment claiming masking is handled does not make it so. B also calls self.apply(self._init_weights) without ever defining _init_weights, unpacks a single tensor as two in the training loop, and in generate concatenates a Python list with a tensor and then uses a top-k index position as if it were a vocabulary id (A gets that same mapping right via sorted_idx), while accepting a top_p argument it never uses. B's architecture is additionally a GPT-2-era design -- learned positional embeddings, LayerNorm, GELU, plain multi-head attention -- and it leans on nn.MultiheadAttention, which sits awkwardly with its own Phase 0 promise not to build on existing classes, as does its final instruction to clone nanoGPT and run train.py. A is also far deeper on the parts that actually decide whether the project succeeds: data curation with deduplication, quality filtering and domain mixing weights; a taxonomy of data, tensor, pipeline, ZeRO and sequence parallelism; inference optimisation covering KV cache, paged attention, speculative decoding and quantisation; post-training via SFT and DPO with appropriate learning rates; and a parameter-count-to-hardware-to-dollar table plus a staged week-by-month build order. A is not clean either -- it claims ~10M parameters for a config that is closer to 38M, pairs GradScaler with bfloat16 in the very loop whose notes say bf16 needs no loss scaling, gets the tokenizers train_from_iterator call and the ByteLevel argument name wrong, invents an FSDP.set_auto_wrap_policy API, builds a dataset from ragged lists, and overstates that nothing beyond 100M parameters fits on one GPU. But those are peripheral API slips around a correct core, whereas B's failures are in the model itself. B's genuine advantages are its explicit definition of what from-scratch means, its up-front expectation setting, and a concrete seven-day starter plan; A covers similar ground quantitatively with its cost table and its closing note that data quality, distributed-training stability and compute budget are the real obstacles. Not enough to offset a broken causal mask."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "The prompt asks for three things -- brainstorm, group, and rank on both effectiveness and cost to test -- and B executes all three completely while A only half-completes the third. A brainstorms roughly twenty ideas but its two ranking tables cover only eight, silently dropping half its own material, whereas B scores every single technique on both axes with a compact star rating and then folds them into a phased do-first/do-next/invest-if-budget list. B is also the broader and more substantive brainstorm, and several of its additions are the ones most specific to the long-thinking setting rather than to repetition in general: periodically compressing or summarising the prior reasoning trace to shrink the surface that seeds the loop, self-BLEU or self-ROUGE similarity monitoring that catches near-verbatim recurrence which exact n-gram blocking misses, entropy-based detection keyed to the low-entropy signature of a degenerate span, dynamic context truncation, and progress tracking in the prompt. Its closing design principles add real value that A has no counterpart for -- layered defence, detect as early as possible to avoid wasting compute, prefer summarise-and-continue over a hard stop, vary thresholds by task type, and track repetition rate as a standing quality metric rather than only suppressing it. B's calibration is distributed rather than concentrated but genuinely present, flagging that entropy stopping will also cut confident non-repetitive output, that post-hoc dedup can damage coherence, that context truncation loses information, and that anti-repetition instructions are unreliable because models ignore them. A's countervailing strengths are real: it opens with the mechanism (a degenerate attractor), its two rankings are internally consistent over one item set, its synthesis explicitly cites both ranks to argue effectiveness-per-cost, and it lands the single best caveat in either response -- that loop detection can truncate legitimate re-reasoning, with the operational fix of tuning the window against held-out good long traces. Since the stated failure is verbatim repetition, A's decision to rank exact-match n-gram detection first is also well matched to the problem, where B slightly penalises it for missing paraphrase. But A carries two weak entries (speculative decoding, whose purpose is to preserve the target distribution, and a prefix-cache 'break' continuation that is never made coherent), and B's own defects -- a muddled sampling-versus-decoding split that files n-gram blocking and contrastive decoding under sampling, a repetition-aware KV cache that is asserted rather than explained yet rated highly, and a priority list that drifts from its own cost ratings -- are sloppiness rather than unsoundness. On completeness against the instruction and on coverage of mechanisms, B is ahead."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B's taxonomy is substantially richer and more domain-correct on both sides of the line. Its transfer list contains real mechanisms -- layer-wise quantization sensitivity, attention-head and head-collapse diagnostics, KV-cache eviction policy effectiveness, the shape of quality-versus-context-length curves, failure-mode taxonomy, ordinal model rankings -- while A's list is padded with things that are not mechanisms at all, such as the eval script being pure Python and pip install working on both stacks. A also asserts as a transferable finding that sampling yields an identical output distribution across devices at the same seed, which is false given differing kernels and reduction orders, and it presents cross-hardware agreement as observed evidence for a study not yet run. On the non-transfer side B is sharper too, correctly flagging optimal batch size, optimal quantization choice (with the right mechanism: whether the bottleneck is bandwidth or compute), KV-cache sizing, multi-GPU scaling efficiency, cold-start and kernel-compilation cost, and PCIe bottleneck diagnostics as laptop-bound. B's single best contribution is expanding the binary into four states -- transfers, re-measure, re-optimize, and new -- where the 'new' category covers measurements the laptop could not produce at all, such as NVLink topology and multi-GPU collectives; A has no analogue and would silently leave that gap. B's anti-conflation machinery is also more concrete: a mandatory first-page legend, a transferability column on every table, a hardware tag in every figure caption, an explicit HARDWARE-BOUND prefix, a classification decision tree, the thought-experiment test, and a prohibited-patterns list whose mixed-sentence example (split 'fast and accurate' into an accuracy claim and a laptop-speed claim) is the most usable rule in either document. Its decision tree also correctly rules that relative speed ratios are hardware-bound because ratios move. Factually B is reliable where A is not: B gives H200 at 141 GB and 4.8 TB/s and B200 at 192 GB and 8 TB/s, all roughly right, whereas A understates both bandwidths by about a factor of four, misstates B200 capacity, and invents a PCIe generation. B additionally splits re-measurement into separate per-platform plans and tables, which structurally resists the H200-to-B200 generalization that A's single combined bucket invites. A's genuine strengths are its section-gating discipline, the red-line table forcing a status on every laptop metric, and the read-only baseline archive, but B matches or exceeds these in aggregate. Both share the same flaw -- calling mechanisms validated and requiring no re-measurement, when they should transfer as hypotheses to be re-confirmed -- so that does not separate them. B's redundancy, repeating laptop specifications in three sections, is its main cost and is not enough to close the gap."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both are strong, competent designs covering all six requested areas, but A handles the prompt's defining constraint -- a corpus that changes daily -- materially better. A explicitly rejects a nightly full re-embed, runs change-data-capture on a fifteen-minute cadence, and adds version-aware retrieval that filters to the newest doc_version plus a tombstone-on-landing rule, then reasons through the transition window where old and new chunks of a rewritten section coexist and the retriever can return both. B schedules its refresh nightly at 3 AM and then names the resulting twelve-to-twenty-four-hour staleness gap as its own first production failure mode; the mitigation (on-demand refresh for critical docs, a last-updated banner) is a patch on a choice it did not need to make. A is also the only one with an embedding-model-upgrade story, baking the model version into the chunk hash so an upgrade triggers a controlled full re-embed behind a dual-index cutover, and it is the only one to specify metadata filtering inside the ANN search rather than as a post-filter, with the correct observation that post-filtering collapses recall at high selectivity. On grounding, A's calibrated confidence gate plus a second per-chunk relevance floor prevents the generator from ever seeing five near-miss chunks, which is stronger than B's post-hoc verification pass that catches rather than prevents and costs an extra generation. A's failure-mode analysis is the deeper of the two: it timestamps each mode by when it would appear, and its third mode contains the sharpest observation in either answer -- that blended paraphrase from tangential chunks is scored neutral rather than contradictory by an NLI checker and therefore slips past automated faithfulness gates -- with the follow-through that neutral should count as failure for code and config docs but not for prose. Its gold set also carries per-question forbidden claims, which is exactly the right instrument for catching superseded values in a fast-moving corpus. B is not weak and contributes several things A lacks: routing documents to type-specific chunkers via a classifier, a separate code-embedding index with query routing to it, an explicitly stated idempotency guarantee on chunk IDs, iterative and co-citation-graph retrieval for multi-hop questions, structured JSON output with per-claim confidence, and numeric metric thresholds with a five-percent regression gate that blocks deployment. Its closing synthesis -- that all three failure modes are really about the gap between faithful-to-context and factually-correct -- is a genuinely good framing. But its retrieval-precision threshold is stated backwards relative to its own column label, it scores faithfulness on one hundred percent of answers with an LLM judge without flagging the cost, and its refresh deletes old chunks after upsert with no handling of the switchover. A is the sounder end-to-end design."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "B identifies the actual mechanism behind the prompt's puzzle and A does not. The reason the same head sometimes gives 1.8x and sometimes a slowdown is the memory-bound versus compute-bound transition: at small batch the K extra verify positions are nearly free because time is dominated by streaming weights from HBM, while at large batch the verify genuinely pays K times the FLOPs and the arithmetic inverts. B builds its whole analysis on that split, derives separate speedup expressions per regime, and closes with the right operational conclusion -- gate the feature on batch size. A, asked explicitly to analyse economics as a function of batch size, gets the sign backwards, claiming that B greater than 1 reduces effective verify cost by sharing prompt processing and often converts a marginal slowdown into a speedup; that is the opposite of the known behaviour and it is one of the four variables the question names. B also gets the MTP-specific cost structure right, noting that a parallel head costs one forward regardless of K whereas an autoregressive draft costs K forwards, a distinction A never draws. On the core formula B is correct that tokens emitted per step is (1-alpha^(K+1))/(1-alpha), including the free bonus token from the verify pass; A's expression omits it and so systematically understates throughput. B further treats non-uniform positional acceptance with the general product form and worked numbers, which is the most common real reason an MTP head underdelivers relative to the uniform-alpha prediction, and its memory-bound break-even result -- that the head's parameter fraction is the floor on required acceptance -- is a compact and memorable finding. The experiments are not close. B fits a linear probe from saved last-layer hidden states to the next K tokens, which is a minimal MTP head, measures the consecutive per-position acceptance curve directly, argues correctly that this is a lower bound on any non-linear head so clearing the bar is decisive, adds a cheap two-layer MLP probe to estimate the remaining non-linearity headroom, insists on the deployment distribution rather than a generic benchmark, and terminates in a three-row decision table. A instead uses target-model top-1 probability or entropy as a proxy for acceptance, which bounds what a perfect draft could reach but says little about what a small head will achieve, invents the entropy-to-alpha calibration constants, and describes an upper bound on alpha as conservative when for a go/no-go call it is optimistic. B is not clean: its boxed compute-bound formula carries a spurious factor of K, and the resulting critical acceptance rate of about 0.045 contradicts its own table, which correctly shows compute-bound speedups well below one for the same parameters; its arithmetic-intensity expression is also garbled, and calling the linear probe a guarantee overstates. Those are localized algebra slips inside a correct framework, whereas A's failures are conceptual and land on the question's central axis."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A supplies the organising idea the question needs and B does not: decompose observed failures into a knowledge gap and a behaviour gap, recognise that retrieval fixes the former and fine-tuning the latter, and make the first deliverable a labelled set of two to five hundred real interactions tagged by failure type. It then turns that framing into an experimental design that actually discriminates rather than merely ranks -- fine-tune on behaviour alone with factual content deliberately excluded, then fine-tune again with facts added, and read the delta between the two as the answer to whether knowledge belongs in weights at all. That isolates the causal factor, which is what the prompt asks for; B's parallel horse race across prompting, RAG, fine-tuned and hybrid configurations tells you which wins but not why, and its failure-mode section stays generic. A also carries several subtler correct points B lacks: that RAG is model-agnostic so you can swap base models with zero retraining while fine-tuning pins you to a checkpoint; that dense product vocabulary is a parsing problem, not only a knowledge problem, which is a legitimate reason to tune weights; that a behaviour-tuned model can start ignoring retrieved context, so the composition has to be tested rather than assumed; and its staleness test on fifty questions whose answers changed in the last thirty days is a crisp, cheap probe of the maintenance tax. B's real advantage is quantitative rigour on the cost model -- an explicit break-even volume formula with numeric ranges and a stated crossover band, a metrics table with thresholds, shadow-mode routing of a slice of live traffic, escalation cost as a line item that can swallow inference savings, ML engineering time treated as capital with a sprint-capacity trigger, plus a month-by-month roadmap and a drift-retrain trigger. Those are genuine contributions and A's cost section is qualitative by comparison. But B also contains a substantive error on the dimension that matters most for a support assistant: it sets a tighter hallucination target for the fine-tuned configuration than for the retrieval one and lists near-zero hallucination tolerance as a reason to choose fine-tuning, which inverts the standard result that grounding in retrieved evidence is the remedy for fabrication while baking facts into weights is a common source of it. Its ten-thousand-turn data bar is also high for the style-and-format tuning that is the strongest case for fine-tuning here, where A's one-to-five-thousand figure is better calibrated. On three of the four things the prompt asks for, A is the stronger answer."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both are polished, correctly formatted SMART sets in a credible CIO voice, so the decision rests on whether the plan actually holds together as a schedule -- which is the substance of a six-month roadmap. A's does not. It states in Goal 1 that the approved IRP is a prerequisite for effective tabletop exercises and in Goal 2 that the exercises validate the IRP, yet it runs Exercise 1 in Week 8 while executive sign-off does not land until Week 12, and it never says the early exercise is deliberately run against a draft. Worse, its summary timeline closes all remediation items by Week 24 while Exercise 4 occurs in Week 26 and its after-action report is not delivered until Week 28, so Goal 3's commitment to close ninety percent of critical items identified across all four reports is unachievable on its own dates. Its headline metrics also have weaker construct validity than their precision suggests: mean time to detect and mean time to contain are production telemetry, and a twenty-five and twenty percent reduction in them cannot be established from discussion-based exercises inside six months, while a thirty percent readiness-score gain sits awkwardly alongside separately enumerated sub-targets that partly restate it. Measuring the plan itself by a forty-page minimum is a proxy that rewards padding, where B measures completion against twelve required sections, named approvers, publication to document control, and cross-reference into the business continuity plan. B's sequencing is coherent -- draft by Month 2, sign-off Month 3, publication Month 4, then three escalating exercises in Months 4 through 6 feeding a scoped v2.0 revision -- and its exercise design is the richer of the two operationally, with scenario cards and timed decision points, an attendance floor for designated responders, a minimum finding count per report, and an eight-dimension competency rubric with a composite target by the third exercise, which measures improvement across the series rather than mere satisfaction as A's 4.0-out-of-5 feedback score does. Its third goal is also the better third goal, institutionalising the capability through LMS-verified role-based training with pre- and post-knowledge checks, a standing quarterly governance review, and a staffed on-call rotation with handoff procedures, and it is candid that the first quarterly review necessarily falls in Month 7. A retains real advantages -- NIST 800-61 and ISO 27035 grounding, eight named playbooks, a twelve-role RACI, FEMA exercise-facilitation guidance, an explicit budget line, and a consolidated milestone table -- and its three-to-four-hour exercise length is realistic where B's sixty minutes is far too short for a multi-vector scenario with fifteen cross-functional participants. B also has a smaller version of the same ordering slip, folding the third exercise's findings into v2.0 by Month 6 when that report is due ten business days later. But those are local defects inside a sound plan, whereas A's contradictions break the causal chain between its own goals."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "A is the more technically sound and more deeply reasoned threat model. Its trust-boundary analysis is the key differentiator: it explicitly names the reverse boundary -- untrusted content flowing from source files, dependency error output and build logs into the agent's context -- as the prompt-injection boundary, and then designs against it architecturally by splitting a read-and-analyse LLM with no shell tool from an execute LLM that receives only a validated summary, and by requiring the model to emit a typed, validated tool call rather than a raw shell string so that injected shell metacharacters are syntactically inexpressible. It also insists on AST-level command parsing rather than regex, and names real platform primitives (landlock plus seccomp, bwrap, a macOS sandbox-exec profile denying reads of the credential directories, Windows job objects and AppContainer), pointing HOME at a per-session temp directory and killing runaway trees by process group with wall-clock and resource budgets. Its command classification gate is the better resolution of the autonomy-versus-safety tension than B's blanket confirmation default, because it auto-runs read-only and build commands while gating destructive, network, install and permission-changing ones, preserving the product's value proposition instead of negating it. A also reasons explicitly about ship order in the way the prompt asks -- version one shrinks blast radius and preserves reversibility, later versions shrink probability, because a contained failure is recoverable and a total compromise is not -- and closes with a matrix mapping each attack path to its v1 control, the residual risk after that control, and the later mitigation that closes it. Its residual-risk section is genuinely calibrated, conceding that no sandbox fixes a model built to comply with instructions in its input and giving a concrete surviving example of exfiltration through an allowed action to a pre-registered remote. B is well organised, picks the right top three risks, and contributes several ideas A lacks -- diff-based rather than whole-file editing for auditability, progressive autonomy with staged capability grants, OS keychain brokering, and a user-facing incident-response path -- but several of its controls are weak or counterproductive. Stripping comments, string literals and binary data from the context sent to the model would destroy the very context the agent needs while failing to stop injection through identifiers, test names, markdown or tool output. Recommending chroot or path validation as the filesystem boundary is the wrong primitive, vulnerable to symlink and TOCTOU bypass where A's kernel-enforced sandboxing is not. Blocking commands whose text matches secret regexes misses the larger channel, which is secrets entering the model context in the first place. And B defers all real isolation to phase two as lower ROI while its own conclusion asserts that the product cannot ship without phase one, leaving confirmation prompts and pattern matching as the only load-bearing controls at launch."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "Both are strong, well-organised transfer studies with genuinely enforceable reader safeguards, so the decision turns on the study's central epistemic claim, and B gets it right where A does not. B states up front that mechanisms transfer as testable hypotheses rather than validated conclusions, attaches a 'what to verify on H200/B200' column to every mechanism, and its migration protocol only promotes a mechanism to 'verified' after numerical re-validation on the target. A's legend instead reads 'TRANSFERS -- applies to any hardware platform, no re-measurement needed', which is the exact over-transfer the prompt is probing, and it produces an internal inconsistency: A files accuracy and perplexity as hardware-invariant while its own verdict table says the quantization configuration will be re-optimised on the new hardware, so the quality numbers it declares settled were measured under a dtype and kernel path that will not be the deployed one. B is also more actionable on re-measurement. Its table pairs each laptop verdict with a task, an expected shift, and a numeric validation gate -- accuracy drop under half a point, scaling efficiency above 85 percent at four GPUs, sustained-to-peak ratio above 0.95 over a thirty-minute run, memory headroom above ten percent -- whereas A's checklist mostly says re-measure or re-optimise with a one-line note. B's anti-conflation rule is the sharper one too: rather than merely banning unlabelled numbers, it forbids the inference pattern outright and requires the author to name the binding constraint and state that the constraint is removed on the target, which is the actual reasoning error rather than a formatting symptom. Its finding-ID scheme with a laptop-finding-to-H200-task-to-B200-task matrix gives traceability A lacks, and it adds a second-reviewer pass to catch implicit transfers. A's real advantages are breadth and accuracy of detail: a wider taxonomy that also covers attention diagnostics, error taxonomy, methodology validity, cold-start cost, utilisation metrics and cost per token; a four-state legend whose RE-OPTIMIZE and NEW categories usefully separate re-running a measurement from re-deriving an optimum from measuring something the laptop could not do at all; a decision-tree node correctly ruling that relative speed ratios are hardware-bound; and correct memory figures, where B inflates B200 capacity to 384GB, which is the dual-package number. Those are real but secondary -- greater breadth under the wrong transfer stance yields more findings wrongly marked settled, and the capacity slip does not touch the framework. B also carries a mild self-contradiction, asserting that software-hardware interface contracts are stable across generations and then hedging that FlashAttention behaviour may differ on Blackwell, and it leans on emoji as its primary labelling device. Neither offsets the difference on the core claim."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both rewrites correctly identify the original's core requirements -- cumulative full-document output, rationale over description, skip not-yet-relevant sections -- so the decision rests on which produces more deterministic, higher-quality output. A goes considerably further on exactly that. It prescribes the column schema for every table the model must emit (Item/Assumption/Rationale for assumptions; relationship with ON DELETE and ON UPDATE and rationale for reaction policies; Field/Data Type/Constraint/Rationale for each table; Name/Type/Direction/Description for procedure parameters), which converts vague instructions into a fixed output shape. It supplies the literal placeholder string for sections not yet in scope, resolving a real ambiguity in the original where 'leave as is' could mean omit or retain. It expands the stored-procedure section beyond the original with the full SQL body, a numbered walkthrough of what each block does and why, and a note on error handling and validation. It adds an explicit gap-analysis step that surfaces guideline requirements not yet met as Pending Items inside the relevant section, closes the specific iterative-prompt failure mode of the model writing 'see previous response' with a cumulative-integrity rule, prefers Mermaid erDiagram with an ASCII fallback rather than leaving the choice open, requires citing guideline requirements by reference number, and sets a calibrating audience -- a reviewer who must approve the design without seeing the assignment -- that implicitly forces self-containedness. Packaging the deliverable inside one fenced block also makes it directly copy-pasteable, and the usage table plus the note about pasting either the full guidelines or only the relevant STEP numbers shows awareness of context limits. B is not far behind and contributes two things A genuinely lacks: an instruction to wait for input rather than generating a document on receipt of the prompt, and a supersession rule stating that when a new fragment contradicts earlier documentation the change and its reason must be noted, which is the sharpest single insight in either response about iterative rewriting. B also enumerates the full set of referential actions rather than just cascade versus restrict, routes ambiguity explicitly into the Assumptions section, and preserves the user's original heading formatting verbatim where A silently renumbers the sections -- a small fidelity loss given the user asked for that format specifically. Those advantages are real but narrower than A's across-the-board specification of output structure, which is what most determines whether the model actually produces the detailed, justified documentation the user is after."}

{"choice": "B", "rationale": "A is a competent threat model with some genuinely good touches -- naming the agent's own hallucination as the highest-likelihood adversary, an explicit trade-offs table reasoning that allowlists suit commands while denylists suit paths, a residual-risk table with acceptance decisions, and the product-aware principle that controls must be fast because the developer is in a hurry. Its idea that the agent should see only truncated command output, so it cannot re-read secrets it accidentally surfaced, is a clever control B lacks. But B is the sounder and deeper document on the points that carry the design. B names the reverse trust boundary explicitly -- adversarial text arriving through source comments, string literals and dependency error output -- and calls it the prompt-injection boundary, then designs against it architecturally: the model emits a typed, validated tool call rather than a shell string, so free-form bash is rejected and injected metacharacters are syntactically inexpressible, and a later reader/executor split gives the LLM that actually sees injected text no shell tool at all. A instead filters shell strings through an allow/denylist and defers prompt-injection handling to a Phase 2 heuristic that greps for phrases like 'ignore previous instructions', which is a known-weak defence. On correctness, A's primary mechanism — jax.device_put with a NamedSharding — is the real API, whereas B builds its entire answer on jax.sharding.shard, which does not exist, uses it four times including in a tip advising readers to use it for validation, and adds two further inventions (jax.optim.sgd and a jax.sharding.replicate context manager). B's pipeline-parallelism section is also conceptually wrong: wrapping each layer in a shard_map with P('pipe', None) on both activations and parameters does not produce stage-wise pipelining, and reshaping devices to (4, 1) under a single axis name is malformed. A is not clean either: its gloss that P('data') means replicate along data inverts the semantics (and contradicts its own later correct usage), it constructs the Mesh from a flat device list while claiming a (2, 4) grid without reshaping (B gets this right), its training step is badly broken (differentiating forward rather than the loss, indexing value_and_grad's output as gradients, a stray stop_gradient, and pmap layered over shard_map), and its automatic-sharding section invents a jax.experimental.auto_shard module and hand-waves at Shardy. The difference is that A's defects sit in optional and illustrative sections while its core path is runnable, and its explanatory content is materially richer; B is cleaner prose over a foundation of nonexistent calls."}

{"choice": "A", "rationale": "Both propose the same sensible shape — profile features, score transparently, escalate to a trained model once labels exist, keep an ambiguous bucket — so the decision turns on which set of features is sharper and which document is internally coherent. A wins on both. Its strongest feature is one B mangles: referential graph position, where master data is the hub with high FK in-degree and low out-degree while transactional tables point outward at master. That single signal is close to definitional, and A states it correctly with a fallback (column-name heuristics and join-log analysis) when lineage is unavailable; B's analogous ReferenceDensity is defined as FK columns over tables referenced, which is near-meaningless, and it assigns high values to master data, which is backwards. A also contributes several non-obvious, correct signals B lacks: time-of-day entropy of creation timestamps to separate batch master loads from continuously arriving events, distinct-value-ratio profiles with spike detection, entropy of categorical columns, effective-dating columns as an SCD tell, and row-count magnitude relative to the tables that reference it. Its caveats are the right ones — hybrids need an explicit SCD bucket, small tables are indistinguishable so use rate-based rather than raw-count metrics, and the analysis must run over a window rather than a snapshot. Critically, A's composite is internally consistent: every sub-score is oriented so that higher means master, and the final thresholds follow. B's recommended rule-based scorer, its centerpiece deliverable, contradicts its own feature tables in at least three places — it adds UniquenessScore and StatusFlagPresence to the transactional side and SurrogateKeyRatio to the master side, while its tables define all three the opposite way — so anyone implementing it would get systematically wrong answers. B has real strengths I weighed: the edge-case table is more thorough than A's caveats (audit and log tables, reference data below a row threshold, IoT telemetry discriminated by entity-per-record ratio, warehouse fact and dim tables resolved from catalog metadata), it specifies a concrete validation loop with per-class precision, recall and F1, and it ties the work to DQ dimensions and to explainability via SHAP plus a confidence threshold for steward review, which fits the stated role well. A's one substantive domain error is the opposite of B's: it characterizes transactional data as update-churning and master data as rarely updated, when immutable inserts for events and in-place correction of master attributes is the more standard pattern. That is a genuine misread, but it affects one table row within an otherwise coherent scheme, whereas B's inversions sit in the code it recommends shipping."}
